full_judgment:
3. Then Haroon Matin filed Civil Appeal No. 16 of 1979 and the Appellate Division, after hearing, taking into consideration of the provisions of section 73 of the Banking Companies Act 1962 and the case of Official Receiver vs Das Bank Ltd reported in 27 DLR (AD) 133 by judgment and order dated 25-6-80 upheld the above judgment and order of the High Court Division dated 31-1-1977 with the observation that "there can be no doubt that the leases forming parts of the same transaction by fraud and collusion will fall together being void ab initio"; then during spot verification of the suit property in the year 1980 the Official Liquidator came to know that both the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 claimed title in the suit property and litigations are pending; further in reply to the query made by the Official Liquidator to the defendant No. 1 regarding the basis of his claim, the defendant No. 1 by his letter dated 28-11-80 informed the Official Liquidator that in the year 1907 Apparna Charan, his father, took lease of CS Plot No. 1748 from Sadar Khashmahal, Chittagong and the relevant documents of the above lease have been filed by him in the High Court Division in connection with the aforesaid First Appeal No. 115 of 1965. Further case of the bank was, that the suit property being requisitioned in LA Case No. 62/1942-43 during Second World War was taken over for use of the military but later on was derequisitioned on 12-12-1946, and possession was handed over to the bank on 20-1-1947 and that although the defendant No. 1 in his letter dated 28th November, 1980 claimed title over the suit property tracing back his title from the year 1907 but from the records it will be evident that the suit property was owned by Sarada Kripa Lala as recorded owner till 6th November, 1936 and thereafter the same was owned by the bank and that the defendant No. 1, without serving any notice upon the bank, got the suit property mutated in his name in JM Case No. 230A/11 of 1954-55. 

 4. The suit was contested by the defendant Nos. 1 and proforma defendant No. 6 who filed joint affidavit in opposition contending, inter alia, that the suit property actually appertained to original Jote No. 88/88 of Mouza East Nasirabad, which was created in Settlement Case No. 284 of 1907-1908 in favour of Aparna Charan, the father of the defendant No. 1, and the said jote comprised the lands of CS Plot Nos. 1609, 1736 and 1748 and on 29-11-1912 Aparna Charan, filed an application before the Khashmahal Office for demarcation of the said jote land which was registered as Judicial Miscellaneous Case (JM Case) No. 288 of 1911-12 and order was passed therein on 26-3-1912 for demarcation of the lands settled in favour of Aparna Charan and accordingly, demarcation was made by an Amin of the said office on 26-3-1912 and since the creation of the said jote Aparna Charan had been in exclusive possession of the suit property and he had brick fields therein as well as the adjoining lands and during RS operation major portion of the said Jote No. 88/88 was recorded in the name of the defendant No. 1 as RS Jote No. 81 and by mistake the remaining portion, i.e. the suit property comprising of RS Plot No, 2956 appertaining to RS Khatian No. 776, was wrongly recorded in the name of Sarada Kripa Lala as RS Jote No. 86 though he had no title or possession therein and that the defendant No. 1, after death of his father in the year 1929, had also been in continuous possession thereof over the statutory period of limitation and also used the suit land as a part of his brick field and after coming to know that the bank wrongly entered its name in the RS record in JM Case No. 236 of 1936-37, filed an application praying for mutation of his name upon correction of the aforesaid wrong entry in the name of the bank and the said application to the Khashmohal Office, Sadar, Chittagong, was registered as JM Case No. 230A/11 of 1554-55 and then notice was duly served upon the bank and in spite of receiving the notice the bank, having no interest in the suit property, did not contest the said application and then the right, title, interest and possession of the defendant No. 1 being found in Jote No. 86 after proper enquiry, by order dated 30-3-1955 the suit property, along with other properties, were recorded in the name of the defendant No. 1 and as far back as 1959 he sold a part of the suit land measuring 1.20 acres to Pakistan Tobacco Co Ltd, the predecessor in interest of Bangladesh Tobacco Co Ltd, the defendant No. 3, who after enjoying the said property till 1964 disposed of the same in favour of State Bank of Pakistan, the predecessor of Bangladesh Bank, the defendant No. 4, whose name has been duly recorded in the record of rights and who is in possession of the same by paying rents regularly; the defendant No. 5 is in possession of part of the suit property by virtue of his purchase from a subsequent transferee of the defendant No. 1 and the proforma defendant No. 6 is in possession of part of the suit property by virtue of direct purchase from the defendant No. 1 and defendant No. 1 has made similar transfers from the suit property to various other purchasers and they, after constructing pucca buildings on portions of the suit property so purchased are in possession of the same long over the statutory period of limitation openly and adversely and since they were not made parties, the suit is bad for defect of parties and neither Sarada Kripa Lala nor the bank had ever any possession, right, title or interest in the suit property. 

 5. The defendant No. 2 also contested the suit and filed separate affidavit-in-opposition contending that Sarada Kripa Lala never mortgaged the suit property to the bank the suit property did not become the subject matter of the mortgage suit as well as the execution case and that the suit property was rightly recorded in the name of Sarada Kripa Lala during RS operation wherein his status has been recorded as a sthitiban raiyat and he on 4-3-29, made a will bequeathing the suit jote to Madhabi Lata Lala, his daughter-in-law, who, on 17-12-1940 after obtaining probate in Probate Suit No. 4 of 1939 was in continuous and uninterrupted possession of the same on payment of rent and she, after obtaining per-mission from the concerned authority under section 9 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and also obtaining Income Tax Clearance Certificates, sold the suit jote to the defendant No. 2 by kabala dated 29-9-1958 and thus the defendant No. 2 became the absolute owner in possession of the suit jote and his title has also been perfected by lapse of time and that the defendant No. 1, having fraudulently got his name mutated in RS Jote No. 86 and resisted the mutation of the name of this defendant and also the possession of the defendant No. 2 in the suit jote, he filed Other Class Suit No. 49 of  1959 for declaration of his title in the suit jote and also for recovery of khas possession which being dismissed he preferred First Appeal No. 115 of 1965 before the High Court, Dhaka which is pending. 

 8. As regards defect of parties, the High Court Division held hat Order I, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure makes it clear that misjoinder or non-joinder of parties is not fatal to a suit provided the suit is of such a nature that the rights and interests of the parties before the Court can be effectively disposed of without the presence of parties not joined and that in the present case, the transferees of the defendant No. 1 will stand or fall along with the said defendant No. 1 and so in their absence the right, title and interest of the parties may be effectively disposed of and so the suit will not fail for non-joinder of the parties who purchased lands from the defendant No. 1. 

 "The learned Advocate for the defendants have not opposed Dr M Zahir's plea to consider the case of adverse possession. They have of course argued that adverse possession has not been established, which I shall duly take note of. In those circumstances I do not think that the defendants will be prejudiced at all if the plea of adverse possession, raised by the plaintiff is considered in the light of the entire evidence on record, though not specifically raised in the plaint. In support of his case of adverse possession Dr M Zahir has relied upon Exhibit 4, certified copy of the proceedings of JM Case No. 236-37, Exhibit 1, the certified copy of the corrected RS Record of rights of the suit khatian and Exhibit 5 the copy of the proceedings of LA Case No. 62 of 1942-43." 

 Exhibit 5 is the next document relied upon my Dr M Zahir. It is the certified copy of the proceeding of LA Case No. 62 of 1942-43. It appears from the compensation schedule that RS Plot No. 2956 was requisitioned by the land Acquisition Department during the World War II in the said LA Case and occupied by the Military authorities on 30-11-1942. It also shows that the Mahluxmi Bank Ltd, was entered in the compensation schedule as the owner in possession of RS Plot No. 2956  ..... That finding recording the contemporaneous possession of the Bank remains a strong piece of evidence in favour of the plaintiff unchallenged subsequently by Sarada Kripa Lala. He or any one also claiming through him did not file any suit challenging the recording of RS Plot No. 2956 in favour of the Mahaluxmi Bank Ltd, as far back as in 1936. Although it is quite probable that the bank took possession of the suit plot on 24-10-1932 when it took possession of the other mortgaged properties of Sarada Kripa Lala, I shall not go by probabilities, but evidence. I shall take Exhibit 4 as the evidence of contemporaneous maters, not as an evidence of matters past. I have also taken note of the fact that Exhibit 4 remains unchallenged by the defendants. It has also not been assailed on any ground whatsoever." 

 10. The High Court Division also found that the defendant No. 1 claimed that most of the land settled in favour of Aparna Charan, his father, were in RS Jote No. 81 but some part thereof was recorded wrongly in the name of Sarada Kripa Lala in RS Jote No. 86 and after coming to know about the same from the defendant No. 2 for the first time in the year 1954 he filed JM Case No. 230 of 1954-55 but the above claim is not correct as there is no corroboration from any witness in this regard and the fact that Aparna Charan did not take settlement of the full CS Plot No. 1748 and took settlement of a part of it is evident from Exhibit F, i.e. the order sheet of Miscellaneous Case No. 284 of 1907-08 for settlement, Exhibit G i.e. the list of tenants, Exhibit H i.e. the kabuliyat executed by Aparna Charan, Exhibit S(6) i.e. sale deed dated 26-7-1939 executed on behalf of the defendant No. 1 in favour of Jibendra Lal Dutta and Exhibit S(7) i.e. the sale deed dated 5-8-1942 executed by Jibendra Lal Dutta in favour of the defendant No. 1 which will show that the Aparna Charan entered into possession of the full CS Plot No. 1748 after demarcation of boundaries in the year 1912 and then, as will be evident from Exhibits A-A4, he retreated to the settled portion of CS Plot No. 1748 at the time of RS operation and was not in possession of RS Plot No. 2956 at the time of preparation of RS records as is evidenced by Exhibit E(1), the RS Khatian No. 776, and that is why RS Plot No. 2956 was recorded in the name of Sarada Kripa Lala who actually possessed the suit property at the time of RS operation and the defendant No. 1 has failed to rebut the presumption of RS records by any documentary or unimpeachable oral evidence and as has been held in the case of Alimuddin Munshi vs Mainuddin Talukder, 14 DLR 725, merely because there is no evidence to show the basis of the entries in the record of rights, the presumption under the entry is not rebutted and there must be further evidence to show that the entries are incorrect and the defendant No. 1 having failed to produce any documentary evidence or any convincing evidence to show that and further the non-payment of rent by the defendant No. 1 for RS Plot No. 2956 from 1930 to 1955 was not an inadvertence as has been urged and, on the other hand, such non payment supports that the defendant No. 1 and his predecessor had no interest in the suit property and that is why they did not pay rent for the suit property after the RS operation and further from 1930 to 1955 the defendant No. 1 and his predecessor were quite happy and content with the recording of the land settled in favour of Aparna Charan in RS Jote No. 81 and Aparna Charan paid rent for that jote in the justified belief that all the settled lands of Aparna Charan were included in it and several transactions were made in respect of the lands of Jote No. 81 with the clear understanding and belief that those dealings were in respect of the entire settled lands of Aparna Charan and the defendant No. 1 took certified copies of his father's settlement papers, Exhibits F-H in the year 1954 and he failed to show any other certified copy taken before 1954 and further, taking advantage of the moribund condition of the bank in the year 1954, the defendant No. 1 went into possession of the suit property in the year 1955 and showing interpolated Exhibits F-H obtained mutation of the suit property in his own name and started the brick field during Pakistan period as unwittingly given out by DWs 1 and 2 and then he paid rent for RS Jote No. 86 from 1955 onwards and sold 1.20 acres of the suit land to Pakistan Tobacco Co Ltd in the year 1956 and in the year 1965 he stopped manufacturing bricks and on dividing the suit property into many plots started selling those to willing purchasers till an order of status quo was passed by the High Court Division and while the bank has been able to prove that it had possession of the suit land from 1934-55 by documentary evidence and, on the other hand, the defendant No. 1 has no documentary evidence and/or any reliable oral evidence in support of his title and possession of the suit land from 1930-55 and as has been held in the case of Keshav Raghunath Deshpande vs Govind Chimnaji Deshpande, AIR 1928 Bom 287 the fact that a stranger in the present case, the bank takes possession of a property under a mistake common to all does not make his possession any less adverse and it has also been held in a number of cases, namely, Govinda vs Mallayya, 311 C 678, Kunwar Sen vs Darbarilal ILR 38 All 411, Ram Piari vs Budhsen ILR 43 All 164, Priya Sakhi vs Manbodh Bibi, ILR 44 Cal 425, that a mortgagee, who does not enter possession in his character as mortgagee, may by 12 years' adverse possession, acquire a good title against a mortgagor and in a number of cases, namely, Zaibunnessa vs Parichit, 23, IC 611, Mula Singh vs Budh Singh, 25 IC 616, and Bhari vs Abbayanath, 41, IC 862, it has also been held that a mortgagee may by 12 years' adverse possession, acquire a good title to other land of the mortgagor which had not been validly mortgaged to him and that in the present case adverse possession of the bank against Sarada Kripa Lala and his successor started from the date of mutation on 7-11-36 and the bank continued in possession and its possession stood reconfirmed during the requisition and derequisition proceedings in 1942 and 1946-47 and that in the year 1942 the defendant No. 1 re-purchased RS Jote No. 81 being fully satisfied that this was the entire settled land of his father and further, the defendant No. 1 or Sarada Kripa Lala was no where in the picture during the requisition and de-requisition proceedings and therefore taking the date of the possession of the bank to be 7-11-36, the bank acquired good title to the suit land by adverse possession and so Madhabi Lata Lala had no saleable interest in the suit land on 29-9-58 and though Mr Mahmudul Islam, relying on the case of Sarat Chandra Maiti vs Bibhaboti Debi AIR 1921 Calcutta 584, submitted that when a property is requisitioned it passes into legal custody and during the continuance of requisition such custody is for the benefit of the true owner but the above cited case is a case of attachment under section 146, CrPC and there is nothing to show that such an order of attachment under section 146, CrPC is applicable in the case of mortgage. 

 12. Leave was granted on the submissions that the defendant No. 1 transferred the major portion of the suit property to others long before the institution of the instant suit and those transferees having not been impleaded inspite of objection taken and, as such, the suit is bad for defect of parties and the High Court Division, upon an erroneous view, held that since those transferees will stand or fall with the defendant No. 1; the learned Single Judge having found that the bank was not a mortgagee in respect of the suit property and that the suit land was wrongly mutated in the name of the bank as a mortgagee in JM Case No. 236 of 1936-37 and that "the actual mutation as a mortgagee in possession does not also reflect the correct position" and there having been absolutely no oral evidence of possession by the bank, committed grave error of law in finding title of the bank by adverse possession on the basis of the order of mutation of the suit property in the above JM Case No. 236 of 1936-37 specially when in their pleading the bank did not plead that they acquired title adverse possession; there having been no evidence whatsoever of the bank's entering into possession of the suit property the learned Single Judge was manifestly wrong in holding that the correct position was that the bank entered into possession of the suit property mistakenly as a mortgagee and such a finding is solely based on surmise and conjecture; even if it is assumed for argument's sake, without however conceding that the plaintiff bank entered into possession of the suit property in the year 1936, the learned Single Judge failed to notice that the bank claiming to have entered in possession as a mortgagee and having neither pleaded nor adduced evidence to show from when the plaintiff asserted absolute title to the disputed land;, the defendant No. 1 having examined a number of person to prove his possession in the suit property and there having been no evidence adduced by either the bank or defendant No. 2 in support of this adverse possession, the learned Single Judge ought to have held that the defendant No. 1, all through, had been in possession of the suit property; the learned Single Judge misread Exhibit 5, the certified copy of the proceedings of Land Acquisition of LA Case No. 62 of 1942-43 to find possession of the bank, inasmuch as Exhibit 5 neither shows that possession of the suit property was taken from the bank nor shows that the said property was redelivered to the bank upon de-requisition and even if it is assumed for argument's sake without however conceding that the bank was in possession of the suit property prior to 30-11-1942, when the government took possession of the same the bank being a trespasser could not tack the period between 30-11-1942 and 38-1-1947 for acquisition of title by adverse possession, inasmuch as the government having taken over possession of the suit property under the law, the possession of the bank was snapped and fresh period of limitation would start to run from the time the suit property was derequisitioned and vacated by the government, Exhibit A series, i.e. the proceedings of Boundary Demarcation Miscellaneous Case No. 288 of 1911-12 and Exhibit N, the rent receipt taken together with other documents clearly establish that Aparna Charan, the father of the defendant No. 1, took settlement of the entire CS Plot No. 1748 of which the suit property was a part and he possessed the same until his death in the year 1929, before RS operation, and the learned Single Judge upon untenable ground disbelieved the case of the defendant No. 1 claiming title to the entire CS Plot No. 1748 including the suit property and failed to consider that the documents produced by him and particularly, the records of Exhibit A series and the map prepared by the Amin therein, clearly established the claim of the defendant No. 1 and also shows that the entry of the name of Sarada Kripa Lala in the RS record of rights is completely without basis, the learned Single Judge on the basis of Report of JM Case No. 230A/ 11 of 1954-55, having found Exhibit R(1), that the defendant No. 1 was in possession of the suit property in 1955 and the defendant No. 1 adduced oral evidence in support of his possession, whereas there having been no evidence as to how the bank came into possession of the suit property, ought to have held that the defendant No. 1 was in possession of the suit property ever since it was derequisitioned in 1947; the present proceeding being for recovery of possession the burden of proof was on the bank, the plaintiff to, prove its possession and the bank having failed to adduce any evidence in this regard the defendant No. 1 was not required to adduce any evidence of possession and, in this state of affairs, when the preponderance of evidence regarding possession was heavily in favour of the defendant No. 1, the learned Single Judge ignoring the preponderance of evidence wrongly found that the defendant No. 1 was not in possession of the suit property prior to 1955; the finding of the learned Single Judge that Aparna Charan did not take settlement of the entire CS plot No. 1748 and that Sarada Kripa Lala was in possession of the suit property at the time of RS operation and that the defendant No. 1 failed to rebut the presumption of the RS record of rights and the defendant No. 1 went into possession of the suit property taking advantage of the moribund condition of the bank are all contrary to the evidence on record and are the result of surmise and conjecture. 

 13. Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned Counsel for the appellant, in his submission reiterated the grounds as stated above and also submitted that the High Court Division fell in error in relying on Exhibit AA, alleged traced copy of the CS map, to hold that CS Plot No. 1748 was sub-divided before RS Operation, inasmuch as Exhibit AA is only a traced copy and there is no evidence on record to show that any competent authority passed any order to treat Exhibit AA as an original CS map, and specially when it does not satisfy the requirement of section 83 of the Evidence Act and further, the High Court Division also fell in error in not taking into consideration the judgment and order passed in Civil Appeal No. 16 of 1979 as being not inter parties without considering that the said judgment and order, though not inter parties, was admissible under section 13 of the Evidence Act to prove the fact that the relevant original CS map along with a traced copy was filed in that suit and no division or Bata-dags were shown in the original CS map while such division was shown in the traced copy. 

 14. Mr Shafiq Ahmed, the learned Counsel for the respondent No. 1, submitted that although plea of adverse possession was not raised in the pleading but issue No. 6 specifically related to adverse possession and the defendants led evidence in this regard and before the witnesses were examined the learned Advocate for the bank made oral submission that the bank would claim title by adverse as well and the learned Advocate for the defendants did not oppose the above submission and argued that the defendant No. 1 failed to establish his adverse possession on the suit property by adequate evidence and, in view of the above, the High Court Division was competent in considering the case of adverse possession in the light of entire evidence on record and on consideration of evidence on record, particularly order sheet of JM Case No. 234 of 1936-37, Exhibit 4 the High Court Division rightly came to the finding that the bank entered into possession of the suit property in the year 1936 on the basis of order dated 7-11-36 passed in JM Case No. 236 of 1936-37 and continued its possession till 1955 and the Government took over possession of the suit property on 30-11-1942 in LA Case No. 62 of 1942-43 and then the same was returned to the bank on 8-1-47 and the period in which the suit land was under the occupation of the military has been rightly construed by the learned Single Judge to be the possession of the bank and further Exhibit 8, the judgment passed In Civil Appeal No. 16 of 1979, was rightly considered by the High Court Division in deciding the suit and the defendant No. 1, as DW 8, in his evidence clearly stated that his father Apama Charan took settlement of some land including the suit land in the year 1907 and the quantum of land was 36 acres but Exhibit A series showed that the total area of land alleged to have been settled was 64.32 acres and, as such, the above discrepancy falsify the above claim of the defendant No. 1 of taking settlement of 36 acres of land by Aparna Charan and further DW 8 in his deposition clearly stated that he has no documentary evidence regarding taking possession of the suit property prior to 1955 except his oral evidence and the other witnesses in support of possession of the defendant No. 1 having contradicted each other in material points, the possession of the defendant No. 1, since taking alleged settlement by his father in 1907, remained not proved and the defendant No. 1 also admitted that neither his father nor himself mutated their name before 1955 and, as such, the High Court Division did not commit any illegality in decreeing the suit. 

 15. We have perused the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and also other papers on record. 

 21. As it appears following the decision of 14 ILR Dr Zahir, who appeared in the High Court Division for the bank, before the witnesses were examined, made oral submission that the bank would claim title by adverse possession as well and the learned Advocate for the defendants having not opposed the above plea, the learned Single Judge was of the opinion that the defendants will not be prejudiced at all if the plea of adverse possession raised by the bank is considered in the light of the entire evidence on record, though not specifically raised in the pleading. 

 24. In the case of Niropoma Ritchel vs Md Abdul Jalil Mea 41 DLR 467, referred to by Mr Islam the distinction between lawful possession and claiming title by adverse possession was illustrated holding that the most essential elements of adverse possession is that the purchaser of a property by a person having no right to possess the property, such possession must be adverse to the true owner and the question of adverse possession in a case is to be determined on the basis of specific averment made in the plaint and that in a suit for declaration of title on the basis of adverse possession material consideration is the starting point of limitation and alternative title on the basis of adverse possession not having been pleaded and proved, decreeing of the suit by the trial Court without reference to the plaint and evidence on record is illegal and further no issue being framed on the vital question of adverse possession decree is also illegal. In the aforesaid case there was no assertion either in the plaint or in the deposition regarding adverse possession and no issue was also framed regarding acquiring of title by the plaintiff on the basis of adverse possession. 

 25. In the case of Mahaprabhu Ram vs Gopal Ram 42 DLR (AD) 154 referred to by Mr Islam the case of the appellants was one of acquisition of title by settlement which was not proved on trial and the trial Court conferred title on him on a gratuitous finding of adverse possession, unwarranted by pleading. The High Court Division held that the gratuitous conferment of title was uncalled for in a suit for partition and that of the precise title to which the plaintiff lays his claim is not supported by evidence on record, the Court cannot find out another source of title for him, by way of gratuitous relief. 

 28. In the case of Mahesh Chand Sharma vs Raj Kumari Sharma AIR 1969 SC 869 it has been held that a person pleading adverse possession has no equities in his favour. Since he is trying to defeat the rights of the true owner, it is for him to clearly plead and establish all the facts necessary to establish his adverse possession. For all the above reasons, the plea of limitation put forward by the appellant or by defendants Nos. 2 to 5 as the case may be is rejected. It was held that a person pleading adverse possession has no equity in his favour and since he trying to defeat the right of the true owner it is for the plaintiff to clearly plead to establish all the facts necessary to establish his adverse possession. 

 31. In 38 ILR it was held that a person could not acquire a title by adverse possession to land which was the subject of a usufructuary mortgage and therefore in the possession of the mortgagees, merely because he had managed to get his name recorded in the village papers for a series of years in respect of the mortgage property and it must be borne in mind that the equity of redemption where the possession remains with the mortgagor is quite different from the equity of redemption where the possession is with the mortgagee and there can be no doubt that an equitable estate, as distinguished from a legal estate, can be barred by time but it seems to us impossible that any person can be in possession of the right to redeem a mortgage where, under the terms of the mortgage, the mortgagee is entitled to the actual possession, and is in fact in possession thereunder. 

 34. In 25 India Cases question arose as to the effect of encroachment by the mortgagee on other land of mortgagor and also the effect of his being recorded in settlement paper as mortgagee of encroached land and it was held, that where a mortgagee encroaches upon his mortgagor's land not mortgaged to him, he holds it adversely to the mortgagor from the date of encroachment, although in the Settlement papers the encroached area is also shown as mortgaged property. 

 45. Further, Exhibit A series, i.e. the proceedings of Boundary Demarcation Miscellaneous Case No. 288 of 1911-12 and Exhibit N, the rent receipt, taken together with other documents established that Aparna Charan, the father of the defendant No. 1, took settlement of the entire CS Plot No. 1748 of which the suit property was a part and he possessed the same until his death in the year 1929, before RS operation and the learned Single Judge upon untenable ground disbelieved the case of the defendant No. 1 claiming title to the entire CS Plot No. 1748 including the suit property. The learned Single Judge also failed to consider that the documents produced by the defendant No. 1, particularly the records of Exhibit A series and the map prepared by the Amin therein, clearly established the claim of the defendant No. 1 in the suit property and also show that the entry of the name of Sarada Kripa Lala in the RS record of rights is completely without basis. The learned Single Judge on the basis of Report of JM Case No. 230A/ 11 of 1954-55, having found Exhibit R(1), that the defendant No. 1 was in possession of the suit property in the year 1955 and the defendant No. 1 adduced oral evidence in support of his possession whereas there having been no evidence as to how the bank came into possession of the suit property, ought to have held that the defendant No. 1 was in possession of the suit property ever since it was derequisitioned on 8-1-1947 and the present proceeding being for recovery of possession the burden of proof was on the bank, the plaintiff, to prove its possession and the bank having failed to adduce any evidence in this regard the defendant No. 1 was not required to adduce any evidence of possession and in this state of affairs, when the preponderance of evidence regarding possession was heavily in favour of the defendant No. 1, the learned Single Judge ignoring the preponderance of evidence, wrongly found that the defendant No. 1 was not in possession of the suit property prior to 1955. Further, the finding of the learned Single Judge that Aparna Charan did not take settlement of the entire CS plot No. 1748 and that Sarada Kripa Lala was in possession of the suit property at the time of RS operation and that the defendant No. 1 failed to rebut the presumption of the RS record of rights and the defendant No. 1 went into possession of the suit property taking advantage of the moribund condition of the bank are all contrary to the evidence on record and are the result of surmise and conjecture. It also appears that the learned Single Judge fell in error in relying on Exhibit AA, alleged traced copy of the CS map, to hold that CS Plot No. 1748 was subdivided before RS Operation, inasmuch as Exhibit AA is only a traced copy and there is no evidence on record to show that any competent authority passed any order to treat Exhibit AA as an original CS map and specially when it does not satisfy the requirement of section 83 of the Evidence Act and further, the High Court Division also fell in error in not taking into consideration the judgment and order passed in Civil Appeal No. 16 of 1979 as being not inter parties without considering that the said judgment and order, though not inter parties, was admissible under section 13 of the Evidence Act to prove the fact that the relevant original CS map along with a traced copy was filed in that suit and no division or Bata-dags were shown in the original CS map while such division was shown in the traced copy.

caseno: Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 380 of 1965.
lawyer:
A.T. M. Kamrul Islam ------- For Appellant.
B.N. Chowdhury ------- For Respondent.
parties:
Osman Ali Talukder ------- Appellant.
Vs.
Sukumar Majumder  ------- Respondent.
full_judgment:
2. The plaintiff respondents filed a suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession in the suit land by evicting the defendants. The plaintiffs' case, in short is that the suit land was recorded in C.S. Khatian No. 160 of mouza Borai and the plaintiffs, by an amicable partition amongst themselves and pro-defendants, were possessing the same; that during the last c.s. operation Jasmat Sardar  was possessing the suit land as a barga darunder Girish Chandra and others, the plaintiffs predecessors, on delivering half of the produce of the land from year to year; and that during Jasmat Sardar's life time the land was taken and given borga bandabosta to others. As Jasmat was possessing the land as borgadar his name was wrongly recorded in the C.S. record as tenant paying borga rent though he was never recognized as a tenant by the plaintiffs' predecessors. Acting on rumors, that lands recorded in the names of bargadars paying half the produce as rent, had vested in the bargadar's ; defendants, 1, 2, and 3, got fraudulent kabala from Jasmat's daughters, defendants 4 and 5 and forcibly dispossessed the plaintiff's from the suit land in Baishak, 1364 B.S. and hence the suit. 

 3. Defendant 1 contested the suit by filing a written statement where he stated, inter alia, that Jasmat Sardar was a recorded occupancy raiyat and defendants 3, 4 and 5 were the heirs of Jasmat Sardar  and he derived good title by purchase from them. His further case is that the landlords were present at the time of the preparation of the settlement records, that neither Jasmat nor his heirs over gave up possession of the land and the plaintiff never possessed the land by their borgadars, that during the revisional settlement operation the suit land had been recorded in the names of defendants 3,4 and 5 and they possessed the same on payment of money rent and that the suit was barred by limitation. 

 4. The learned Munsif dismissed the suit after finding that the C.S. record (Ext. 2) indicated that Jasmat Sardar has acquired a tenancy right in the suit land and that there was no evidence that during his life the land was taken back from him and given to some other persons as borga by the plaintiffs predecessors, that the plaintiffs had no possession within 12 years before the date of the institution of the suit. 

 5. The learned Subordinate Judge reversed the decision of the trial Court after finding that the C.S. recorded was not correctly recorded, and Jasmat was a borgadar and he was in possession till his death, 6/7 years back, and hence the suit was within 12 years of possession of the last recorded borgadar, and the transferee-defendants had no saleable interest in the suit land and as such the defendants were liable to be evicted. 

 6. Mr. A.T.M. Kamrul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, has submitted that the learned Subordinate Judge misinterpreted the decision in the case of Kumir Mondal Vs. Pramatha Nath Chowdhury (1962) in 14 DL:R 801 in as much as the principle laid down in the said case is that a borgadar recorded in the C.S. Khatian as tenant before the introduction of the proviso to clause (17) of section 3 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 by the amending Act of 1928 can plead tenancy right even after the introduction of the proviso. He has further submitted that the presumption of correctness of the entry in the C.S. Khatian cannot be held to have been rebutted merely because there is no evidence to show the basis of the entry. Mr. Islam, in support of his contention, has relied on Alimuddin Munshi Vs. Mainuddin Talukdar (1962) 14 DLR 725. 

 7. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the respondent has submitted that the presumption of the correctness of the record of right has been lost by passage of time, and that where it is on record that Jasmat Sardar  gave kabuliyat to the landlords as a borgadar before the preparation of the C.S. record and there is no other evidence that there had been any other agreement creating a tenancy in favor of Jasmat Sardar  the C.S. record must be held to have been wrongly prepared. 

 "that this proviso does not debar a person against whom a suit is now filed for recovery of a share of the crop as a bargadar, to set up the defense that he is not a bargadar but a tenant. In such a suit the presumption of correctness of the record of rights may also be invoked in aid as a circumstances supporting the defense but this will certainly not be a conclusive presumption. The presumption that attaches to a record of right under section 103 -B of the Bengal Tenancy Act is only this that the entry in the record of right represents the correct stale of affairs on the elate that it was prepared. Whether that state of affairs is continued even afterwards is not a presumption which arises under this section; but under section 114 of the Evidence Act, and its probative value diminishes progressively with the lapse of time. The older the record the less is its presumptive value. This is a matter therefore, of proof and it merely has the effect of shifting the onus upon the other side. It is certainly not a conclusive proof". 

 9. The C.S. Khatian recorded Jasmat Sardar  as a borgadar as well as a rayotisthitiban under Girish Chandra Majumdar and others at a rental of half of the produces inclusive of cess. The learned Subordinate Judge has found that Jasmat took borga settlement by a kabuliyat (Ext. 1) for a term of 7 years from 1321 B.S. and the preparatory works of C.S. operation started in the locality after 1327 B.S. and the record of rights was finally published in 1925 corresponding to 1332 B.S. He has observed that "it is quite likely that the settlement operation actually began at a stage when the term of the barga lease did not expire. It is, therefore, clear borga has been mentioned in the khatian. In the absence of any other stipulation between the parties Jasmat would be deemed to have continued in possession as a borgadar on the principle of holding over as enunciated in section 116 of the T.P. Act and as enunciated in principle in section 51 B.T. Act". 

 10. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury has empathetically urged that a finding as to the rebuttal of a statutory presumption is a finding of a fact and cannot be challenged in second appeal. In support of his contention he has referred 10 Aminuddin Biswas Vs. Miajan Biswas, (1960) 12 DLR 103, CharuBalaRudra Vs. Narayan Prosad Sen(1962) 14 DLR 159 and Dabiruddin Molla Vs. Prem Dasi(1967) 19 DLR 371. 

 11. A finding as to a rebuttal of a statutory presumption is no doubt a finding of fact and it should not ordinarily be disturbed in second appeal. In the present case, however, the finding as to the rebuttal of the presumption of the C,S. record is based on a material mistaken assumption that Jasrnat Sardar would be deemed to have continued in possession as a bargadar on the principle of holding over as enunciated in Section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act and as enunciated in principle under section 51 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury has conceded that neither section 166 of the Transfer of Property Act nor section 51 of the Bengal Tenancy Act is applicable to a bargadar. He has, however, contended that the principle of holding over has been applied by way of analogy. The right of holding over, unless conferred by a statute, cannot be implied or inferred by analogy. Long five years after the terms of the borga kabuliyat expired, the C.S. Khatian was published on 6-9-25. The assumption of the Court of appeal below that the settlement operation actually began at the stage when the terms of the borga lease did not expire is based on no evidence. 

 13, In 1929 by an amendment of the Bengal Tenancy Act, the Legislature sought to bring about a certain change with regard to presumption about the status of a person who used to cultivate lands under barga system, by adding the following provision to the definition of 'tenant' to section 3(17) of B,T. Act. 

 "It seems to us that the only change that the Legislature has labored to bring about is 10 lay down that; only in the first instance there will be a presumption 'that" a person holding under a system of adhi, barga or bhogis not a tenant, but this presumption will be rebutted only if it is established that he has been admitted by the landlord to be a tenant or is declared in a previous suit to be a tenant or if he can in a suit where this question is put in issue establish status as such tenant, In effect it seems that the Legislature has labored in in vain or worse avoided its responsibility and really thrown the burden upon the Court to resolve this question, for the net result appears, in substance, to leave the question where it was, apart from shifting the burden of proof on the tenant. To this extent possibly there has been a departure from the old principle." 

 “Merely because there is no evidence to show the basis of the entries in the 'record-or-rights, the presumption is not rebutted in view of the provision of section l03(B) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, and also the procedure as laid down in the several sections of the Bengal Tenancy Act followed by the officer concerned while preparing the final records-of-rights. There mutbe further evidence to show that the entries are incorrect. The absence of evidence for the basis of the entries may be a circumstance which along with other evidence may be to show that the presumption has been rebutted. " 

 The learned Subordinate Judge has not adverted to this case, though relied on by the learned Munsif. For want of proper approach to the material question in the matter and non-appreciation of the evidence on the records particularly the evidence of the D.Ws. he has arrived at an erroneous decision. In the present case, apart from merely asserting that the C.S. Khatian was 'Wrongly recorded, the plaintiff did not adduce any other evidence in support of his contention. There was no averment that Jasmat continued to possess the land on the expiry of the terms of the kabuliyat on the same terms and conditions. In fact there is no mention of a borga kabuliyat in the plaint. On the other hand, defendant No.1, apart from relying on the C.S. record, produced Defendant 2, the Tahsildar of the landlords, who stated that at the time of C.S. operation he himself and another amin looked after the preparation of the C.S. record and the suit land belonged to Jasmat on payment of paddy lent to the landlords. This witness admitted the kabuliyat to be written in his hand. He further stated in cross-examination that he held some lands of the landlords as bargadar but his name was recorded as mere borgadar possessor with an entry in the rent column. 

 16. I, therefore, hold that the presumption of correctness of the C.S. record has not been rebutted in this case. The next question is whether the presumptive value of the C.S. record, under section 114 of the Evidence Act, has been destroyed in this case or whether its presumptive value is still available to defendant 1. 

 17. D.W. 1 Osman Ali, stated that Jasmat possessed the land as tenant and after his death his heirs defendants 3,4 and 5 got the suit land ; that he purchased the interest of defendants 3, 4 and 5 by registered kabalas Ext. 1 and l(a); that the suit land was at first recorded in the names of defendants 3, 4 and 5 and the Majumdar landlords filed an objection, under section 19(1) of East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, and got their names recorded but the defendants, 3, 4 and 5 preferred an appeal, under section 19(2) of the said Act, and the land was again in their names. Ext. C is the certified copy of that judgment of the appellate officer. The Government also collected rent from the defendant No. 4 vide Ext. B Defendant's categorical statement that Jasmat got tenancy right in the suit land and after his death his heirs were possessing the same before his purchase are corroborated by D.W. 2 Haji Monsurulla, the tahsildar and D.W. 2 Majan Shah who held land contiguous to the suit land. 

 18. P.W. 1 is the only witness on behalf of the plaintiffs. He stated that the suit land was taken from Jasmat and was given borgabandabast to others. He did not state who used to cultivate the land after Jasmat but merely stated that when the defendant disposed the plaintiff Morlan Shah was the bargadar. Madan Shah according to D.Ws. 1 and 3 left for India long ago. Though P.W. 1 stated he had an account book for borga receipts he neither produced the account book nor any borga receipt. In the present case the presumptive value of the C.S. record under section 114 of the Evidence Act must be held to be still available to contesting defendant. 

 19. From the evidence on record it is clear that the predecessors of Defendant 1 never possessed the land as a bargadar of the plaintiffs and the defendant’s assertion that Jasmat and his heirs possessed the land in their own rights has been amply substantiated by the evidence on record. From Ext. 1it cannot be said, though contended by Mr. B.N. Chowdhury, that the subsequent possession of Jasmat was one of a bargadar . I do not find any mention of the kabuliyat in the C.S. Khatian. The learned Subordinate Judge has assumed, on a total misrepresentation of evidence on the record, that since Jasmat died 6/7 years back the sui t is within twelve years of possession through a recorded bargadar. From the evidence on record it is clear that the plaintiffs had no possession within 12 years before the institution of suit. The learned Munsif rightly dismissed the suit.

2. The facts of the case, in short, are that the plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 97 of 1985 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Mulladi, Barisal for partition of the land as described in the schedule-'Ka' to the plaint alleging, inter alia, that the suit land appertaining to Petty Settlement Khatian No. 70 covering and area of 9.02 acres originally belonged to three brothers namely Hamid Ali, Wahed Ali and Sabder Ali. The plaintiffs are the heirs of Hamid Ali and Wahed Ali. On the other hand, the defendants are the heirs of Sabder Ali. At the time of preparation of R.S. subsequent to S.A. Khatian, more share then that of the defendants were entitled, was recorded in the name of the defendants. The plaintiffs were entitled to get 2/3rd share covering and area of 6.02 acres as heirs of Hamid Ali and Wahed Ali. On the other hand, the defendants were entitled Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. to get 1/3rd share covering an area of 487 of 2007 3.01acres as left by their predecessor-in-interest, Sabder Ali. As the suit land was not earlier partitioned by metes and bounds so the plaintiffs requested the defendants to make partition of the suit land amicably but they did not pay heed, Hence the plaintiffs instituted the instant for partition. 

 3. The defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material allegation contending, inter alia, that the suit was not maintain it was barred by limitation and also barred waiver, estoppel and acquiescence. His specific case, in short, was that the suit land appertaining to Petty Settlement Khatian No. 70 covering an area of 9.02 belonged to Hamid Ali, Wahed Ali and Sabder Ali in equal share. Hamid Ali, Wahed Ali and Sabder Ali sold 1/3rd share covering an area of 2.226 acres of land from the Petty Settlement Khatian No. 70 to Rupjan Bibi, wife of Sabder Ali and mother of the defendants. Accordingly, Rupjan Bibi's name was recorded correctly in both R.S. and S.A. Khatians. The defendants have been possessing the said land. He prayed for dismissal of the suit. 

 4. Mr. Bivash Chandra Biswas, learned Advocate-on-Record, appearing for the petitioner submitted that Rupjan Bibi, the predecessor-in-interest of the defendants, purchased 2.226 acres of land from the admitted owner and on the basis of that .purchase R.S. and S.A. record of rights were prepared in her name and she took over possession to the said land and thereafter her successor-in-interest, the defendants, have been possessing the said land. In view of such categorical assertions and evidence as adduced by them onus squarely lies upon the plaintiffs to prove that the RS and S.A. record of rights were prepared erroneously in the name of Rupjan Bibi in order to rebut the title particularly to rebut the presumption attached thereto A rights Rupjan Bibi but the plaintiffs hopelessly failed to prove so. The learned Advocate further submitted that the last Court of fact on consideration of the evidence of record particularly, the R.S. and S.A. record of rights and title came to the conclusion that Rupjan Bibi acquired title in 2.226 acres or land, thereby modified the judgment and decree of the trial Court. 

 5. On considering the evidence of record the High Court Division found that the findings of the Court below were based on non-consideration of the evidence of record inasmuch as the presumption of R.S. record of rights has not been rebutted resulting in as error of law in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

full_judgment:
2. The land measuring an area of 0.40 acre appertaining to CS Khatian No.6359 and Plot No.16 originally belonged to Sheikh Kitabdi, who acquired title in the same by executing a kabuliyat on 24-4-1906 in favour of the landlords Girish Chandra Poddar and others. Sheikh Kitabdi died leaving two daughters Arjuda Begum and Meher Nigar. In SA operation, the said land was recorded in the name of Dhakeshwary Textile Mills Limited. The Government listed 0.27 1⁄2acre of land as enemy property in Enemy Property Case No.52/66-67. Arjuda Begum and Meher Nigar filed Writ Petition No.474 of 1969 and the High Court Division by a judgment and order dated 4-4-1977 declared that such enlistment as enemy property was unlawful. They sold 5 kathas of land to one Jakir Hossain by a deed dated 27-12-1969 who transferred 2½ kathas to Abdul Musabbir Hossain, father of the writ petitioners by another deed dated 20-4-1970. Arjuda Begum and Meher Nigar also sold 2 kathas of land to Abdul Musabbir Hossain by another deed dated 8-9- 1979. Abdul Musabbir Hossain constructed residential building therein and transferred the same by a deed of gift to the petitioners on 20-2-2007. RS khatian was prepared in the name of father of the petitioners and others in khatian No.468. In City Survey operation, the same was recorded in the name of the father of the writ petitioners. The Bangladesh Textile Mills Corporation (BTMC) filed Dispute Case No.667 which was dismissed by the Objection officer on 11-9-2000. The BTMC preferred Appeal Case No. 27938 of 2000, which was also dismissed. The BTMC, then, filed an application for re-hearing of the appeal before the Settlement Officer which was again dismissed on 20-3-2007 along with 26 appeals. Lastly, the Settlement Officer, Tejgaon, Dhaka by an order communicated under Memo No.13/42/4th/697 (4)-04 dated 6-8-2007 appointed one Saiful Azad, Charge Officer to re-hear the appeal who allowed the appeal along with 49 other appeals and directed to delete the names of the writ petitioners from the khatian and to insert the name of the BTMC by an order dated 22-8-2007. Then, the writ petitioners filed Writ Petition No.10535 of 2007 and obtained Rule which was made absolute by the impugned judgment and order. 

 3. The CS recorded tenant Sheikh Kitabdi died leaving his two daughters Arjuda Begum and Meher Nigar. Meher Nighar died leaving sister Arjuda Begum and, thereafter, Arjuda Begum died leaving only son Abdul Mannaf, father of the writ petitioner Nos.1-5 and wife, the writ petitioner No.6. They filed writ petition No.474 of 19691 and got declaration that the enlistment of 0.27 /2 acre of land out of 0.40 acre as enemy property was unlawful. In City Survey operation, the same was recorded in the names of the petitioners. The BTMC filed Dispute Case No.660 before the Objection Officer against the petitioners for correction of the khatian which was dismissed on 20-9-2000. Then, the BTMC preferred Appeal Case No.27938 of 2000 before the Appellate Officer which was also dismissed on 9-5-2001. The Settlement Officer re-opened Appeal No.27938 of 2000 which was again dismissed on 20-3-2007. Then, the Settlement Officer, Tejgaon, Dhaka by an order dated 6-8-2007 Suo moto cancelled the order dated 20-3-2007 passed in Appeal No.27938 of 2000 along with other appeal and appointed Charge Officer to re-hear the appeal who by an order dated 22-8-2007 allowed the appeal along with other appeals. Against the judgment and order dated 22-8-2007 passed by the writ respondent No.7 in Appeal Case No.27938 of 2000, the writ petitioners filed Writ Petition No.4757 of 2008 and obtained Rule which was ultimately made absolute. 

 4. One Kalachand Sheikh was the owner and possessor of the land measuring 0.31 acre by virtue of a kabuliyat dated 20-4-1906 which was duly recorded in CS khatian No.6196 and plot No.15. Kalachand died leaving two daughters Ramjan Bewa and Marium Bewa. Thereafter, Mariam died leaving Falu Mia as her only heir. Ramjan Bewa and Falu Mia sold five kathas of land from plot No.15 to Md Ali Hossain by a sale deed dated 30-3-1961. In SA and RS operation, the said land was rightly recorded in SA khatian No.1039 and RS khatian No.4388 in the names of said Md Ali Hossain and others. Ali Hossain died leaving four sons, two daughters and widow who effected partition by deed dated 30-7-1980. Md Anowar Hossain, Mst. Mariam, Mst. Huron Bibi, Mst. Sharifon Bibi, who are the heirs of Md Ali Hossain, transferred 0.0315 acre of land to the writ petitioners by deed dated 9-1-1992 who constructed dwelling homestead in the said land and have been residing therein. The BTMC filed Dispute Case No.680 before the Objection Officer, which was dismissed. Then, they preferred Appeal Case No.27957 of 2000 before the Appellate authority, which was dismissed on 9-5-2001. Thereafter, the said appeal was re-opened and again dismissed on 20-3-2007. By an order dated 6-8-2007, Settlement Officer, Tejgaon, Dhaka cancelled the order of dismissal dated 20-3-2007 and appointed Charge Officer to re-hear the same who by an order dated 22-8-2007 allowed the appeal. The writ petitioners, then, filed Writ Petition No.2687 of 2010 against the order dated 22-8-2007 passed by the Charge Officer in Appeal Case No.27957 of 2000 and obtained Rule. The said Rule was made absolute by the impugned judgment and order. 

 5. The land measuring an area of 0.31 acre appertaining in CS khatian No.6196 and plot No.15 originally belonged to Kalachand Sheikh who got the same by executing kabuliyat deed dated 24-4-1906. He, died leaving two daughters Ramjan Bewa and Marium Bewa. Thereafter, Mariam died leaving Falu Mia as her only heir. Ramjan Bewa and Falu Mia sold 0.10 acre of land from the said plot to Mirza Golam Hafiz by a deed dated 30-3-1961. In SA and RS operation of the said land was rightly recorded in name of said Mirza Golam Hafiz who transferred entire 0.10 acre of land to the writ petitioners by deed dated 1-3-1988 and delivered possession. The writ petitioners, taking over possession of the said lands, constructed two-storied building therein after obtaining necessary plan approved from the RAJUK. The writ petitioners filed Title Suit No.858 1997 against the writ respondent Nos.3-4 for declaration of their title and got decree on contest on 30-4-1998. The writ respondent No. 4 filed First Appeal No.354 of 1999 in the High Court Division, which was dismissed for default. They sold 0.045 acre out of 0.10 acre to Labu Ahmed, Md Kader and Md Masud Ahmed. The BTMC filed Dispute Case No. 677 before the Objection Officer which was dismissed. Then the BTMC preferred Appeal Case No.27954 of 2000 before the Appellate authority which was also dismissed on 9-5-2001. Thereafter, the said appeal was re-opened and again dismissed by an order dated 20-3-2007. Thereafter, by an order dated 6-8-2007, Settlement Officer, Tejgaon, Dhaka suo moto cancelled the said order dated 20-3-2007 and re- opened the Appeal again with some other appeals and by the impugned order dated 22-8-2007 allowed the said appeal along with other appeals. Then, the writ petitioners filed Writ Petition No.2692 of 2010 against the order dated 22-8-2007 and obtained Rule. By the impugned judgment and order, the High Court Division made the Rule absolute. 

 6. Hari Prashad Bandhapadday was the CS recorded tenant of the land recorded in CS khatian No.6362 and CS plot No.16. Hari Prashad Bandhapaddya died leaving four sons namely Sree Surendra Nath Benarji, Sree Narandra Nath Banarji, Sree Dherandra Nath Benarji and Sree Birendra Nath Benarji who settled 0.0530 acre of land to Jahura Khatun, mother of the petitioners from the said plot on 16-6-1944. In SA operation the same was recorded in SA khatian No.876 and plot No.2511 in the name of Dhakeshwary Cottons Mills Limited. Jahura Khatun filed Miscellaneous Case No.284 of 1986-87 for correction of record-of-rights which was allowed. Her name was recorded in Mutation khatian No.876/1. The BTMC then filed Review Petition, which was allowed by the Assistant Commissioner, Land by an order dated 12-1-1993. Jahura Khatun filed Miscellaneous Appeal No.14 of 1993 before tne Additional Deputy Commissioner, Revenue, Dhaka which was disallowed on 20-7-1999. Then, Jahura Khatun prepared Appeal Case No.86 of 1999 before the Divisional Commissioner, Dhaka which was allowed by the Additional Divisional Commissioner, Revenue, Dhaka by an order dated 20-7-1999. In RS operation, draft khatian No.2540 was prepared in the name of Jahura Khatun but finally the same was prepared in the name of the BTMC. Jahura Khatun mortgaged the said land and took loan from Sonali Bank Limited. She also got plan, approved from the RAJUK and constructed 4(four)-storied building therein. The BTMC as plaintiffs filed SCC Suit No.13 of 1992 in the 6th Assistant Subordinate Judge, against the Jahura Khatun for eviction claiming that she was their monthly tenant. The plaint of the said case was rejected. SCC Judge held that complicated question of title was involved in the subject matter. The BTMC, then, filed Title Suit No.169 of 1993 in the 6th Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka for declaration of title and khas possession. On transfer, the said suit was renumbered as Title Suit No.130 of 1994 in the Second Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka. The BTMC also filed Dispute Case which was dismissed. The BTMC, then, preferred Appeal No.27985 of 2000, which was also dismissed by the Appellate authority. The Appellate authority re-opened the said appeal and by the impugned judgment and order dated 22-8-2007 said appeal was allowed along with some other appeals. Challenging the said order dated 22-8-2007 passed in Appeal Case No.27985/2000, the writ petitioners filed Writ petition No.10535 of 2007 and obtained Rule. The High Court Division by the impugned judgment and order made the Rule absolute. 

 7. The land measuring 0.40 acre recorded in CS khatian No.6355 and plot No.16 belonged to Sheikh Kitabdi by virtue of a Kabuliyat dated 24-4-1906. Kitabdi died leaving two idaughters Arjuda Begum and Meher Nigar. 0.27 /2 acre of land out of 0.40 acre was enlisted as enemy property in EP Case No.52 of 1966-67. Arjuda Begum and Meher Nigar filed Writ Petition No.474 of 1969 and got an order from the High Court Division on 4-4-1977 that such enlistment as enemy property was unlawful. Arjuda Begum and Meher Nigar sold five kathas of land to Jakir Hossain by sale deed dated 27-10-1979 who transferred 21/2 kathas of land out of 5 kathas to AQ Ahmed Hossain, predecessor in interest of this writ petitioners Nos. 1-3 by sale deed dated 2-4-1970. In SA operation the land was recorded in the name of Dhakeshwary Cotton Mills Limited. The petitioners filed Miscellaneous Case before the Assistant Commissioner, land for mutating their names which was rejected. They preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No.119 of 1998 before the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Revenue, Dhaka which was allowed on 24-8-2002. In RS operation, the said land was duly recorded in the name of the predecessor in interest of the writ petitioners in RS Khatian No.468. The BTMC filed Dispute case which was dismissed by the Objection Officer. Then, the BTMC preferred Appeal Case No.27937 of 2000 before the Appellate Officer which was also dismissed on 9-5-2001. The said appeal was re-opened and allowed by the Appellate authority on 22-8-2007. Challenging the said order dated 22-8-2007 the writ petitioners filed Writ Petition No.2687 of 2010 and obtained Rule. The High Court Division by the impugned judgment and order made the Rule absolute. 

 10. It has been submitted by them that in view of the provisions of Rule 42 and 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 the Revenue Officer designated as Settlement Officer is authorized to correct the record-of-rights if fraud is detected in preparation of the same and in the instant cases respondent Nos. 6 and 7 exercising their power vested under those provisions of law had corrected the khatian and thus the High Court Division erred in law in passing the impugned judgments and orders. 

 13. Mr M. Qumrul Haque Siddique, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 1 in Civil Appeal No. 234 of 2015, respondent Nos. 1-6 in Civil Appeal No. 235 of 2015, respondent Nos. 1-3 in Civil Appeal No. 237 of 2015 has made submissions in support of the impugned judgement and order passed by the High Court Division. He also submits that the appellants have claimed that they had purchased the land in question from the liquidation cell through 5 registered deeds being Deed No.1936 dated 14-7-1988, Deed No.1618 dated 21-6-1988, Deed No.1619 dated 21-6-1988, Deed No.1620 dated 21-6-1988 and Deed No.1621 dated 21-6-1988 respectively and thus, BTMC became the owners, but in Deed No.1936 the disputed land CS plot No.16, SA dag No. 2534, RS dag No.4015 and Mohanagor dag No.4087, of the writ petitioner-respondent No.1 (in CA No. 234 of 2015), has not been mentioned, but the appellants by virtue of official position and force most illegally deleted the name of the writ petitioners and substituted the name of BTMC under the garb of a correction application without support of any rules after final publication of record-of-rights by an official notification dated 10-1-2000 and, as such, the judgment and order of the High Court Division declaring the order 22-8-2007 passed by Charge Officer, Settlement Office, Dhaka to have been passed without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect, is just and proper. 

 15. The learned Advocate further submits that admittedly no question of fraud was ever been agitated and, as such, in the absence of any allegation of fraud writ respondent No.7 cannot correct the record-of-rights in exercising power under section 42 and 42A of the state Acquisition and Tenancy Rules 1955 and, as such, the order dated 22-8-2007 passed by the writ respondent No. 7 deleting the record-of-rights of the respondent(s) is illegal. The learned Advocate lastly submitted that writ respondent No.7 in his judgment and order dated 22-8-2007 allowed the Settlement Appeal No. 27935 of 2000 along with 32 appeals deleting the record of right of present respondent(s) and substituting the name of the appellant in the said record-of-rights on the ground that ownership of the land has been settled in favour of the BTMC by a judgment passed by the this Division in an appeal, though in the aforesaid Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 390 of 2002 (arising out of writ petition No. 1416 of 1997) the property of respondent No. 1 was not included or the subject matter of the writ petition nor any way relates to the land of present respondent(s) even they or their predecessors were not party in the said writ petition and the findings of the this Division is based on statements of fact hence the said judgments passed by this Division is not binding upon the respondent No.1 and as has been rightly found by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 4758 of 2008 and, as such, the judgment of the High Court Division is just, right and proper and, as such, the appeal is liable to be dismissed. 

 17. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates for the parties concerned, perused the impugned judgments and order of the High Court Division and other connected papers on record. 

 "42A. Correction of fraudulent entry before final publication of record-of-rights-The Revenue-officer, with the additional designation of 'Settlement Officer' shall, on receipt of an application or on receipt of an official report for the correction of an entry that has been procured by fraud in record-of-rights before final publication thereof, after consulting relevant records and making such other enquiries as he deems necessary, direct excision of the fraudulent entry and his act in doing so shall not be open to appeal. At the same time the Revenue-officer shall make the correct entry after giving the parties concerned a hearing and recording his finding in a formal proceeding for the purpose of future reference." 

 20. It is now well settled by this Division that if fraud has been done or found in recording-of-rights before final publication thereof the Revenue Officer can hear the matter a fresh after consulting the relevant records, making such inquiry necessary, if he deems and can give an opportunity of being heard of the parties. In this connection we can rely on the case of Bhawal Raj of Wards vs Rashida Begum reported in 15 BLC (AD) 115, CA No. 2 of 2004 Government of Bangladesh and others vs Shamsul Hoque and another and CA No. 204 of 2004 Imam Shirajul Hoque and another vs Director-General, Land, Record and survey and others. 

 21. The appellants have failed to show us that the Settlement Authority had made any inquiry that the respondents fraudulently managed to entry their respective names in the record-of-rights as per provision of rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955. 

 23. It has been also argued that the appellant BTMC has failed to prove that in recording the record-of-rights the respondents had committed fraud in preparing the same. 

 24. If we considered these submissions of the learned Advocates for the writ-petitioners-respondents coupled with the above propositions of law, we find substance in the submissions of the learned Advocates for the respondents that repeated rehearing of the appeal under rule 31 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 is not permissible in law. Moreover, it is our considered view that before rehear an appeal under rule 31, the settlement authority had not made any inquiry whether fraud had been committed in recording of rights in the name of respondents. 

 25. Mr M. Qumrul Haque Siddique, learned Advocate appearing for the respondents in CA Nos. 234, 235 and 239 of 2015 submits that rule 42A provides correction of fraudulent entry before final publication of record-of-rights and in the instant cases the Charge Officer of Settlement office rehear the appeals repeatedly under rule 31 after the final publication of the record-of-rights, which was published in Bangladesh Gazette on January 24,2008. 

 26. The word 'before final publication of record-of-rights,' as mentioned in rule 42A of the Rule 1955 is very important and to deal with the above issue the scheme of law so far as relates to preparation of record-of-rights, as provided in rules 30-35 and 42 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 are required to be looked, which are as follows: 

 30. Objection—Blank forms of objection shall be supplied free-of-charge, and all objections shall, as far as practicable, be made in such forms, Along with the original objection, the objector shall file a copy or copies of the same for service on all other persons who, in the opinion of the Revenue-officer are materially interested in the case. The Revenue-officer shall issue notices informing the objector and all other persons so interested of the date and place fixed for the hearing of the objection and, with each notice to a person, other than the objector, he shall forward a copy of the objection. Objection regarding the ownership or possession of land or of any interest in land shall be decided summarily by the Revenue-officer. The record shall contain a brief summary of the evidence taken and an abstract of the reasons for the decision. Objections shall not be disposed of in the absence of any of the parties materially interested or their representatives, unless the Revenue-officer be satisfied, for reasons to be recorded, in writing, that the notice was duly served on the person concerned. " 

 (2) Before passing the final order on any such appeal, the Appellate Officer shall give the parties an opportunity of being heard and shall record in the proceedings an abstract of the reasons for his decision." 

 32. Preparation of Final Records—When all objections under rule 30 and all appeals under rule 31 have been disposed of and when the draft record of rights has been corrected in accordance with the original and appellate orders on all objections, the Revenue-officer shall proceed to frame the final record-of-rights. 

 In cases, however, where operations under Chapter XIV of the Act have been undertaken and fair and equitable rents have been settled and the settlement rent-roll has been finally framed under sub-section (3) of section 109, the Revenue-officer shall, after the draft record-of-rights has been corrected in accordance with the original and appellate orders on all objections, incorporate in the draft record-of-rights the rent determined in respect of each holding or tenancy on the basis of such finally framed settlement rent-roll and then proceed to frame the final record-of-rights. 

 Provided that in a case where the fair and equitable rent have not been so settled and the settlement rent-roll has been finally framed by the time the record-of-rights is ready for final publication, the Revenue-officer instead 

 of withholding final publication of the record-of-rights, may finally frame and finally publish the same noting the existing rents therein without incorporating the fair and equitable rent settled under Chapter XIV of the Act. 

 The final records shall be prepared in conformity with the draft records corrected as above and shall consist of a series of khatians prepared in forms which are generally similar to the forms used for the khatians of the draft record-of-rights. The Khasra shall not form part of the final record-of-rights. The final record shall be printed or prepared in manuscript according to the direction as may be given by the Provincial Government, by general or special order." 

 33. Publication of Final Records —The Revenue-officer shall publish the final record-of-rights by placing it for public inspection, free of charge, during a period of not less than 30 days, at such convenient place as he may determine. A proclamation shall previously be published in each village informing the Maliks and tenants and the Deputy Commissioner of the place at which the final record-of-rights of that village will be open to public inspection and the period during which it will be open to such inspection. 

 34. Certificate of final publication—(1) When a record-of-rights has been finally published under rule 33, the Revenue-officer shall, within sixty days from the date of final publication, make a certificate stating the fact of such final publication and the date thereof and shall date and subscribe the same with his name and official title. 

 (2) The Provincial Government may, by notification, in the official Gazette, declare, with regard to any specified area, that record-of-rights has been finally published for every village included in such area; and such notification shall be conclusive proof of such publication. 

 35. Presumption as to the correctness of record-of-rights—(1) When a record-of-rights is finally published under rule 33, the publication shall be conclusive evidence that the record has been duly revised under section 144 of the Act. 

 (2) Every entry in a record-of-rights finally published shall be evidence of the matter referred to in such entry, and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved by evidence to be incorrect. 

 42. Special Power of Revenue-officer appointed with the additional designation of Settlement Officer—A Revenue-officer appointed with the additional designation of Settlement Officer' may, at any time before the publication of final record-of-rights, direct that any portion of the proceedings referred to in rules 28 to 32 in respect of any district, part of a district, or local area, shall be cancelled and that the proceedings shall be taken up fresh from such stage as he may direct. 

 27. Upon perusal of the above rules, it transpires that rule 30 permits filing of `Objection' against any error or mistake appearing in the DP Khatian and requires the Revenue Officer to dispose of the objections after taking evidence. Rule 31 provides for appeal against the decision of the Revenue Officer given under rule 30. A Revenue Officer with additional designation of Settlement Officer is the forum for such appeal. Rule 32 provided that the Revenue Officer is to proceed to frame the 'Final Record-of-Rights,' which is to be 'printed' or 'prepared in manuscript'. 

 28. Rule 33 makes it mandatory for the Revenue Officer to publish final record-of-rights by placing it for public inspection, free of charge, during a period of not less than 30 days, as such convenient place as he may determine. And a proclamation shall previously be published in each village informing the Maliks and tenants and the Deputy Commissioner of the place at which the final record-of-rights of that village will be open to public inspection and the period during which it will be open for such inspection. Rule 34(1) requires that the Revenue Officer, within 60 days of such final publication, to make a certificate stating the fact of 'final publication' and thereof he shall subscribe with date, name and official designation. Sub-rule 2 of rule 34 says that Government may, by notification, in the official Gazettes, declare with regard to any specific area that the record-of-rights has been finally published and such notification shall be conclusive proof of such publication. Rule 35(1) speaks that when a record-of-rights is finally published under rule 33, the publication shall be conclusive evidence that the record has been duly revised under section 144 of the Act. 

 29. In the instant cases from the records, it transpires that final publication of the record-of-rights, as required under Rule 33 was completed and the certificate of final publication as required under Rule 34(1) was also completed vide notification ( প্রজ্ঞাপন) vide নং ভূঃ মঃ/শাঃ-২ (গঃ বিঃ)- ১১/২০০৫-১৬- dated 10-1-2000, though the said notification was published in the Official Gazette on 24-1-2008, which is optional and a mere formality to confer the status of "Conclusive proof" to the final publication. 

 30. In view of the above, we have no hesitation to hold that in the instant cases the settlement authority has proceeded beyond its jurisdiction to rehear the appeals repeatedly in the grab of rule 31 despite the notification ( প্রজ্ঞাপন) vide নং ভূঃ মঃ/শাঃ-২ (গঃ বিঃ)- ১১/২০০৫-১৬ dated 10-1-2000 which was published on 24-1-2008 in official gazette, and it remains unquestionable to testify the fact that, FINAL PUBLICATION under Rule 34 (1) by the 'Revenue Officer' was completed before 10-1-2000. In view of rule 35(1) when a record-of-rights is finally published under rule 33, such publication shall be conclusive evidence that the record has been duly revised under section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, and rule 35(2) speaks that every entry in a record-of-rights finally published, shall be the evidence of the matter referred to in such entry, and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved by evidence to be incorrect. Thus, the repeated hearing of appeals under Rule 31 or even under Rule 42 or 42A, by the Revenue Officers after final publication of a record-of-rights is without lawful authority, illegal and is of no legal effect. 

 31. Rule 42A does not give any authority to rehear an appeal under rule 31 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 by the concerned Settlement Officer after publication of the final record-of-rights, as the such publication is conclusive evidence (rule 35) and thus, in the instant cases the Settlement Officer has acted illegally and without jurisdiction in re-hearing the appeals repeatedly.
