2. Facts relevant are that the predecessor-in-interest of present respondent nos. 1(a)- 1(h) and respondent nos. 2 and 3 as plain-tiffs instituted Partition Suit No.57 of 1994 in thy Court of learned Subordinate Judge, 2na Court Bogra, impleading the petitioners herein alongwith the predecessor of present respondent nos.4(a)-4(f) and respondent nos.5-85 as defendants claiming saham of 1.48 1/6 acres of land out of the suit land measuring 13.35 acres, contending interalia, that the suit jote comprising 13.35 acres of land appertaining to C.S. Khatian No.10 of Mouza Khamarkandi under Police Station-Bogra, District-Bogra, originally belonged to Azim Uddin Mollah, Abdul Mollah and Sabu Mollah in equal share; During ejmali possession said Azim Uddin Mollah and Abdul Mollah transferred their shares to the extent of two third measuring 11 bighas and 17 kathas infavour of Asmat Ullah and Jasmat Ullah both sons of C.S. recorded tenant Azim Uddin Mollah by registered deed dated 09.06.1917 on condition that they would pay vendor's debt . of Tk.450/- to the ex-landlord; Since the sale was a conditional one, the vendors retained possession of the land; The said sale deed was never acted upon for non-payment of the debt to the ex-landlord in compliance with the condition stipulated in the deed; Azim Uddin Mollah died leaving three sons namely Asmat, Jasmat and Najem alongwith two daughters solebi and Sawabi; Sabu Mollah died leaving three sons namely Korban, Muslim and Moyez; Jasmat died leaving full brother Asmat; Said Abdul Mollah died leaving wife Amiron and three sons namely Kashem, defendant no.1 Chand, defendant no.2 Farid and 3 daughters namely Shukimon, defendant no.3 Rupban and Janina; Amiron died leaving two sons Ayetullah and defendant no.2 Farid and daughter defendant no.3 Rupban; Asmat Ullah died leaving two sons namely olam and Nasir and two daughters Toiron and Gendi; Najem died leaving a son plaintiff no.1 Jashim and daughter Lalbibi; Sawabi died leaving a son defendant no,6 Kuranu; Nasir died leaving a son plaintiff no.2 Khairuzzaman Mollah and daughter plaintiff no.3 Shahera; Golan died leaving wife defendant no,7 Kochimon and two daughters namely Jahanara, Jobeda and two sisters Gendi and Toiron; Salebi died leaving two sons Md. Nabir Uddin and Kalim Uddin, defendant nos.10 and 11 respectively; Korban died leaving three sons namely Buhl, Riaz and Kawser; Said Riaz died leaving four sons namely Md. Biraz Uddin, Md. Azizer Rahman, Md. Hafizar Rahman and Md. Abdur Rahman, defen-dant nos.13-16 respectively; Kawser died leaving only daughter defendant no.17 Mosammat Asma and brother Bulu; Moyez died leaving wife Fuljan, a son defendant no. 18 Md. Mojam Uddin and two daughters Most. Kallaton Nesa and Most. Potol Bibi; Fuljan died leaving husband defendant no.10 Md. Nabir Uddin, a son Mojam Uddin and three daughters Kallaton, Potol and Golapi, defendant nos.19-21 respectively; Moslem died leaving a son Samsul and three daughters Borki Bibi, Bull and Momijan, defendant nos. 22-25 respectively; Kashem died leaving a son Futu Mollah, defendant no.26 and three daughters Sonaban Bibi, Fatema Bibi and Rahima Bibi, defendant nos.27-29 respectively; Shukimon died leaving four sons namely Kazem, Sukra, Azo and Kachua alongwith one daughter Atopjan; Said Kazem died leaving defen-dant no.30 Kodban and Atopjan died leaving a daughter defendant no.31 Sharifon and three brothers Sukra, Azo and Kachua; Said Sukra died leaving wife defendant no.32 Hamidon and three sons namely Md. All Fakir, Md. Hachen Fakir and Md. Hamid Fakir alongwith daughter Shurjoban, defendant nos.33-36 respectively; Azo died leaving a son Yousuf Ali and two daughters Momena and Ayjon, defendant nos.37-39 respectively; Jarina died leaving two sons Rabia and Bacha; Said Bacha died leaving wife defendant no. 40 Achiron and brother Rabia; Said Rabia died leaving wife defendant no.41 Maim n, and five sons namely Abul Hossain, Gaffer, Hobibar, Sekander and Nur Hossain and three daughters Asarban, Nurbanu and Asma Khatun, defendant nos.42-49. respectively. Toiron died leaving five sons namely Asgar, Ahab, Dhalu, Bulu and Tutu and two daughters' Jarina and .lamina, defendant nos.50-56 respectively; Gendi died leaving a son defendant no.57 Dilbor and a daughter defendant no.58 Sahera; Kachu died leaving wife Kanchi and two sons Sobhan, Montu alongwith daughter Mariam, defendant nos.59-62 respectively; Defendant nos.1-62 are the co-sharers by inheritance to the suit jote and defendant nos.63-66 are the co-sharers by purchase to the suit jote; The plaintiffs are in ejmali possession; The plaintiffs demanded partition of the suit land from defendant no.26 on 15.06.1992 but he denied; Hence, the suit. 

 5. The case of the defendant nos. 67 and 68 are that the suit jote appertaining to C.S. Khatian No.10 originally belonged to Abdul Azim Mollah, Abdul Mollah and Sabu Mollah; During ejmali possession Azim Mollah and Abdul Mollah transferred their share to the extent of 11 bighas and 17 kathas in the year 1917 to Asmat and Jasmat but the C.S. record was not prepared accordingly; Azim Mollah, Abdul Mollah, Sabu. Mollah, Asmat and Jasmat transferred 22 bighas and 6.75 kathas of land to Shushila Shundari Gbosh, predecessor of the defendants, vide registered deed no.11.2 dated 05.01.1923 prior to the C.S. operation but C.S. record was prepared and published wrongly in the name of Azim Mollah, Abdul Mollah and Sabo Mollah; Though C.S. record was published wrongly but Shushila Sundari Ghosh possessed the purchased land through borgadars; Abdul Pramanik transferred 1.17 acres of land to Rajani Kanta Ghosh, husband of Shushila Sundari vide registered kabala dated 18.12.1928; Both Shushila Sundari and Rajanii. Kanta Ghush gave barga of the suit land infavour of Abdul Pramanik for 7 years by barga deed dated 02.04.1929; Shushila settled .55 acre of land to different persons and the rest to the extent of 10.59 acres was recoraed in the M.R.R. Khatain in her name Rajani Kanta died prior to publication of M.R.R. Khatian; Shushila Sundari died leaving two daughters Radharani and Raj lakshmi, defendant nos.67 and 68 respectively; During the war of liberation Shushila Sundari and her successors engaged Chand Miah son of Abdul Ariz as bargadar in respect of their share and left for India; On their return after liberation when they demanded usufructs from Chand Miah, he denied to give the same and then they filed Title Suit No. 2 of 1974 against Chand Miah which was decreed on compromise in their favour; Rajlakshmi transferred .24 acre of land by registered deed dated 25.06.1989 infavour of defendant no.22 son of defendant no.2; Rajlakshmi also transferred some lands to different persons; After transfer, the defendants retained possession to the extent of 7.43 acres of land; The defendants filed Case No.3713192 under Section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure against defendant no.26 and others which was disposed of in their favour on compromise; Plaintiffs are not entitled to get any saham/relief in the suit and the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 7. After hearing the parties and perusing the evidence on record, the learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 28.02.2000. 

 8. Being aggrieved, the plaintiffs i.e. respondent nos.l-3 herein as appellants filed First Appeal No.459 of 2000 before the High Court Division. Upon hearing the parties and considering the evidence on record, a Division Bench of the High Court Division allowed the appeal vide judgment and decree dated 02.05,2010 and decreed the suit giving saham to the plaintiffs as prayed for. 

 12. On the other hand Mr. A. J. Mohammad Ali, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent nos.1(a)- 1(h), 2-3 submits that the deed dated 09.06.1917 executed by Md. Azim Mollah and Md. Abdul Mollah infavour of Asmat Ullah and Jasmat Ullah was a conditional sale and the condition not being complied with, it was not acted upon and accordingly C.S. Khalian was prepared in the name of original owners but the trial court erroneously shifted the onus upon the plaintiffs as such the impugned judgment and decree shall sustain. He also submits that C.S. Khatian has presumption of its correctness which is suit rebatable by proper evidence but no evidence was adduced by the contesting defendants to discharge their onus which lawfully lies on them and the trial court failed to appreciate the evidence adduced by the plaintiffs and thus erroneously holding title and possession of the defendants. He again submits that Khatian has no presumptive value as such the impugned judgment and decree shall sustain and the appeal is liable to be dismissed. He lastly submits that the plaintiffs categorically stated in the plaint that: 

 15. it appears that the trial court dismissed the suit holding that the plaintiffs failed to prove their claim that the condition attached to the kabala dated 09.06.1917 was not complied with by the vendees of the kabala; The kabala dated 05.01.1923 (exhibit-'l ha') shows that Abdul, Azim, Sabu, Asmat and Jasmat together sold 22 bighas and 6.75 kathas of land to Shushila Sundari and thus the CS. recorded tenants Abdul, Azim and Sabu admitted the title of Asmat and Jasmat and therefore the plaintiffs cannot deny the title of the defendants who are the heirs of Shushila Sundari; The kabala dated 09.07.1923 (exhibit- ‘ga,') proves that the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs cultivated the suit land as bargadar of Shushila Sundari and thus they admitted the title of the defendant's predecessor-in-interest. Relevant portion of the judgment passed by the learned Subordinate Judge is quoted herein as under: 

 "Considering the evidence adduced by the defendant-respondents it does not appear that the consideration money for the deed dated 09.06.1917 i.e. exhibit 'Ica' was paid to the ex-landlord. It appears that trial court courageously fixed the onus of such proof on the plaintiff-appellants. The rebuttal onus always lies with the other side who wants to repudiates the presumption as the C.S. record of rights hold. 

 22. As per provisions of Section 90 of the Evidence Act there is a presumption infavour of a thirty years old original copy of a registered deed which is submitted in the court from proper custody. For proper appreciation Section 90 of the Evidence Act is reproduced below: 

 "90. Presumption as to documents thirty years old: Where any document, purporting or proved to be thirty years old, is produced from any custody which the Court in the particular case considers proper, the Court may presume that the signature and every other part of such document, which purports to be in the handwriting of any particular person, is in that person's handwriting, and, in the case of a document executed or attested, that it was duly executed and attested by the persons by whom it purports to be executed and attested. 

 23. From the provisions of above mentioned Section of the Evidence Act it appears that the exhibited copy of thirty years old registered document dated 05.01.1923 is being an original copy and produced before the court from proper custody as such the presumption infavour of deed no.112 dated 05.01.1923 is that the said deed is a genuine one. In such a situation the onus of proof of the allegation of the plaintiffs regarding lending money by taking signature in blank stamp and thereafter used the same to create forged document by the predecessor of the defendant nos.67 and 68 lies upon the plaintiffs. 

 30. From the aforementioned discussions, we are of the view that since the suit land was purchased by Shushila Sundari before C.S. operation, the C.S. record should have been prepared in her name. Again, on perusal of exhibit-'neo' i.e. M.R.R. khatian no.15 it appears that said khaitian was prepared in the name of Shushila Sundari in continuation of kabala dated 09.06.1917 and 05.01.1923 which are marked as exhibit-la' and ‘kha' respectively, as such said M.R.R khatian was prepared correctly. From the contents of kabala dated 18.06.1080 (exhibit-'pa') and another kabala also dated 18.06.1980 (exhibit-' fa' it appears that defendant no.69 purchased portion of the suit land from the heirs of Shushila Sundari. Thus Trial Court justly arrived at a finding that plaintiffs have failed to prove their title in the suit land. 

 42. It is to be noted that the view of the trial court regarding the credibility of the witnesses has a great weight and should not be lightly discarded inasmuch as trial court have the opportunity to evaluate the demeanour of the witnesses at the time of recording of evidences. 

 45. in the present suit plaintiffs hopelessly failed to prove their title as well as possession over the suit land. Since the finding of the trial court is based on proper appreciation of evidence on record, thus the same should not be discarded lightly.

vs

full_judgment:
13. The trial court after hearing the parties and considering the evidence on record decreed the suit and also gave saham to the parties as claimed by its judgment and decree dated 26-11-1974. 

 16. Mr M Liton Ahmed, the learned Advocate with Mr Sheikh Mosfeq Kabir, Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant-appellants submits that the trial court committed serious error in law in not considering the material facts of the case that the defendant Abdul Hakim Talukder the son of Mohammad Ali Talukder is the CS recorded owner and the three sisters of the defendants No. 1 did not take any step against the CS record even never claimed their saham but their successive heirs claimed saham without challenging the CS record. He further submits that not only the CS record even the SA and RS records were also prepared in the name of the defendant No. 1. He further submits that admittedly as per CS record the suit land belonged to Syed Ali and Amjad Ali sons of Tofani Talukder and Abdul Hakim Talukder son of Mohammad Ali Talukder and no dispute among them about the suit land but the trial court did not at all consider the said vital facts of the case. He further submits that the trial court committed patient illegality in decreeing the suit whereas it is settled principle that decree in case of partition cannot be given if the parties did not make prayer for declaration of title and challenging the record-of-rights which was prepared in the name of defendant No. 1 the predecessor of the present appellants. He further submits that the suit is not maintainable since CS operation was held on and between 1915-1919 and the instant suit was filed long after the CS record even thereafter the SA and RS record were also prepared but the plaintiffs did not challenge the said record-of-rights though they have knowledge about the records which the suit was clearly barred by limitation in support of his argument he referred the decision of the case of Akrab Ali vs Zahiruddin Kari and others reported in 30 DLR (SC) 81. The case of Md Sirajul Islam vs Taimuddin 13 ADC-349 and the case of Hriday Ranjan Dey vs Niranjan Dey being deed his hears Probate Dey reported in 10 BLT (AD) 137 = 54 DLR (AD) 16. 

 17. He further submits that as per provision of section 103 (b) (5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 every entry in a record-of-right finally published shall be the evidence of the matter referred to in such entry and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved to be incorrect but the trial court did not consider the said provision of law and erroneously passed the impugned judgment. 

 18. His further contention is that the CS record of schedule No. 1 prepared in the name of two sons of Tofani, Syed Ali and Amjad Ali as 6 annas share each and Hakimuddin for 4 annas share and Schedule-2 the khatian No. 40 stands in the name of Syed Ali and Amjad Ali for 4 annas shares to each and Hakimuddin for 8 annas shares and Schedule-3 appertains to khatian No. 152, stands in the names of Syed Amjad Ali and Hakimuddin as 1/3 share each, but the trial court held that the name of Hakimuddin was wrongly entered though it has not been challenged by the plaintiffs as such the findings of the trial court cannot be sustained. He prayed for allowing the appeal. 

 19. On the contrary Mr Abdus Salam Mondal, the learned Advocate along with Mr Abul Kalam Azad Advocate submits that the trial court rightly passed the impugned judgment. He further submits that the plaintiffs categorically stated that the suit land originally belonged to Tofani Talukder and Mohammed Ali Talukder but the CS record was wrongly prepared in the name of Syed Ali, and Amjad Ali son of Tofani Talukder and Abdul Hakim Talukder the son of Mohammad Ali Talukder and the plaintiffs are the successive heirs of Mohammad Ali Talukder and the trial court rightly found the same. He further submits that the presumption of correctness of the record-of-rights is to be rebuttable provided under section 103(b)(5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 and since the plaintiffs claimed that the CS record was wrongly prepared in the name of Abdul Hakim alone excluding the name of his three sisters namely, Rokabjan the predecessor of the plaintiffs, Phuljan defendant No. 64 and Rupjan defendant No. 65. He further submits that the trial court rightly found that the plaintiffs succeed to prove that the suit land was originally belonged to Mohammed Ali Talukder. The learned Advocate referred the case of Meherjan Bibi vs Naimuddin Dhali reported in 33 DLR (HCD) 126. He also referred the case of Akrab Ali vs Zahiruddin Kari reported in 30 DLR (SC) 81. 

 20. He further submits that as per provision of section 103(b) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 and section 114 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, though the entry of the records-of-right has presumptive value and when the plaintiffs claimed their right then onus shifted upon the defendants. In support of his arguments he referred the decision of the case of Pramatha Nath Chowdhury vs Kamir Mondal reported in 11 DLR (SC) 392. His next argument is that though initially no prayer for declaration of title of the suit land but ultimately through amendment before this court the plaintiff-respondents amended the pleadings and claimed declaration of title of the suit land so, no question that the suit is not maintainable without any prayer for declaration of title. He prayed for dismissal of the appeal. 

 21. We have heard the learned Advocates of both the sides, perused the impugned judgment of the courts below, the papers and documents as available on the record. 

 29. PW-2 Md Nawab Khan deposed that the parties are known to him. He deposed that he has land adjacent to the south of the disputed land and he is a Manager of the Co-operative Society, Chandpur and has collected loans and interest. He deposed that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land and it is not a fact that the sisters of defendant No. 1 gifted land to him. He deposed that the plaintiffs are in possession of the disputed property and he was about 8/9 years old at the time of CS operation and defendant No. 1 conducted the affairs for recording of their interest. 

 31. DW-1 Anwarullah Talukdar deposed that he is defendant No.I (Kha). Abdul Hakim Talukdar also known as Hakimuddin. He deposed that the Schedule-1 belonged to Mohammad Ali 4 annas khas, Tofani 4 annas and 8 annas and Khan Hakimuddin took settlement of 4 annas share. Syed All and Amajad Ali took bandabasta of 4 annas and schedule-3 belonged to the persons as alleged in the plaint. Mohammad Ali died in 1313 BS and at that time Hakimuddin was aged about 16/17 years. Tofani Talukdar looked after Hakimuddin during his minority. Rukubjan and Fuljan orally gifted their interest in favour of their brother Hakimuddin Talukdar and Tofani Talukdar accepted the gift on behalf of Hakimuddin Talukdar. Rupjan also orally gifted her interest in favour of Hakimuddin and Tofani gifted 4 annas interest of schedule-2 in favour of Hakimuddin before CS record. Hakimuddin had 4 annas in schedule-1 and 8 annas in schedule-2 and 1/3rd in schedule-3. He deposed that Amir Uddin Patwary got the interest recorded during the CS operation and he was a literate person of his relation. The kabalas in favour of the plaintiffs are fraudulent, collusive and bogus and were not acted upon. He deposed that the plaintiff earlier filed Title Suit for partition which was withdrawn by the plaintiffs and the grandsons of Tofani falsely filed this suit for harassing them. Karimjan and Alekjan relinquished their interest in favour of Syed Ali and Amjad Ali. It is not a fact that Mohammad Ali had 4 annas in schedule-1 and 8 arenas in schedule-2. It is not a fact that the CS Khatian was not correct. Rukubjan and her sisters never separated the homestead in dispute. 

 32. In cross-examination by the plaintiffs he stated that his present age is 35/36 years and he was not present when the oral gift was made by Rukubjan and others in favour of Hakimuddin and the persons who had knowledge of the oral gift all are dead. He stated that it is not a fact that there was no oral gift by Rukubjan and others in favour of Hakimuddin. He further denied that it is not true that Tofani did not gift his land in favour of Hakimuddin. He stated that he has no paper to state that the schedule-2 to the extent of 8 annas was settled in their favour and he has no paper to show that his father and sons of Tofani both made settlement of land of schedule-2 but stated that they have dakhila. He stated that he could not produce any witness to prove the factum of settlement and oral gift and it is not a fact that Mohammad Ali had 4 annas in schedule-1 and 8 annans in schedule-2 and Tofani had 8 annas share in schedule-2. He stated that after oral gift, the heirs of Rukubjan, Rupjan and Fuljan never leave or visit their house and they themselves also did not visit their house. Rukubjan died in the year 1941 AD. He stated that it is not a fact that Rukubjan and her sister visited their homestead and he did not see Amiruddin, supervising the works of record of interest and he was not present when the plaintiff got the kabala. He stated that it is not a fact that the plaintiffs are in possession of kabala land. He admitted that his father sold 0.91 cents to Meherjan wife of Golam Ali. Meherjan gifted the same to defendant Nos. 55-63 and they are in possession. 

 37. We have heard the learned Advocates of both the side, perused the impugned judgment, the evidence of the witnesses and the papers and document as available on the record. 

 38. The case of the plaintiffs is that the suit land originally belonged to Mohammad Ali and Tofani Talukder. Admittedly, the CS record was prepared in the name of Syed Ali and Amjad Ali sons of Tofani Talukder and Abdul Hakim son of Mohammad Ali Talukder. It is admitted that Mohammad Ali Talukder leaving behind only son Abdul Hakim Talukder and three daughters Rukubjan the predecessor of the plaintiffs, Phuljan the defendant No. 64 and Rupjan the defendant No. 65. In the instant case some of the heirs of Mohammad Ali Talukder claimed partition of their ejmali land. The plaintiffs claimed that the suit land originally belonged to Mohammad Ali Talukder but inadvertently, the CS record was wrongly prepared only in the name of Abdul Hakim Talukder son of Mohammad Ali Talukder excluding the name of three daughters of Mohammad Ali. The plaintiff Nos. 1-7 are the successive heirs of Rukubjan. The plaintiff Nos. 6-12 also the successive heirs of deceased Amjad Ali. The defendant Nos. 11-12 also claimed that they have purchased the land from Phuljan the defendant No. 64 and Rupjan defendant No. 65. 

 42. Admittedly, the CS record was prepared in the name of Syed Ali and Amjad Ali the son of Tofani Talukder and Abdul Hakim Talukder son of Mohammad Ali Talukder. Plaintiff case is that though the CS record was prepared in the name of Abdul Hakim Talukder the only son of Mohammad Ali Talukder excluding his sisters but the property belonged to Mohammad Ali Talukder and thus the plaintiffs are the co-shares of the suit land and which are ejmali land as such claimed saham. 

 43. We have examined all the documents but no where it is found that Mohammad Ali Talukder was the original owner of the suit land. Though the plaintiffs claimed that Mohammad Ali Talukder is the owner of the suit land and the plaintiffs claimed that Tofani Talukder is also the owner of the rest portion of the land. It appears that the CS record was not prepared in the name of Tofani Talukder and Mohammad Ali Talukder but which were prepared in the name of Syed Ali Talukder and Amjad Ali Talukder the two sons of Tofani Talukder and the name of Abdul Hakim Talukder the son of Mohammad Ali Talukder. It appears that the defendant No. 64 and 65 sisters of Abdul Hakim Talukder. The CS record was prepared in the name of Abdul Hakim alone but three sisters of Abdul Hakim did not challenge the CS record. Since it is the case of the plaintiffs that the CS record was prepared in the name of Abdul Hakim Talukder Hakimuddin and two sons of Tofani Talukder Sayed Ali Talukder and Amjad Ali Talukder in such a case they ought to have challenged the CS record. 

 44. It is settled principle that the plaintiffs should prove their case by adducing evidence. In the instant case the plaintiffs failed to prove that the suit land was settled in favour of Mohammad Ali Talukder and Tofani Talukder. But on perusal of the CS record it is found that the CS record was prepared in the name of Abdul Hakim Talukder and two sons of Tofani Talukder namely Sayed Ali Talukder and Amjad Ali Talukder. The plaintiff's side failed to produce any witness in support of the case that the land was settled in favour of Mohammad Ali Talukder and Tofani Talukder. Even on perusal of the Exhibit No. 3 it is found that Abdul Hakim Talukder transferred some land on 27-3-1943 before SA record. So, it is clear that the defendant No. 1 was the only owner of the suit land. But the trial court did not consider the said documentary evidence and erroneously decided that the original owner was Mohammad Ali Talukder. It appears that the successive heirs of Rukubjan claimed their saham by purchase and inheritance. They claimed that entire portion of the land of defendant No. 64 and 65 the two sisters of Abdul Hakim purchased by plaintiff Nos. 11 and 12. 

 45. At the time of hearing of this appeal the plaintiffs amended the plaint claiming title of the suit land and also challenged the CS record. 

 46. Mr M Liton Ahmed the learned Advocate argued that as per provision of Article 91 of the Limitation Act, any instrument should be challenged within 3 years even as per Article 120 of the Limitation Act, and the Limitation is only 6 years. The CS record was prepared in the year 1919 and the suit was filed in the year 1967 but the plaintiffs now filed application for amendment of the plaint claiming title and challenging the CS record long after about 100 years. It appears that at the time of filing the suit three sisters of Abdul Hakim Rokabjan, Phuljan and Rupjan did not challenge the CS record claiming that the suit land was originally belonged to their father even they did not file any document that the said land was settled in favour of Mohammad Ali. In such circumstance of the facts, it is our view that the case challenging the CS record is clearly barred by limitation. 

 47. The learned Advocate of the appellants submits that preparation of CS record under section 103(b) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 has presumptive value that every entry in a record-of-rights finally published shall be the evidence of the matter referred to in such entry and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved to be incorrect. In support of his argument he cited the decision of the case of Hriday Ranjan Dey vs Niranjan Dey being dead his heirs, Probate Dey reported in 10 BLT (AD) 137 = 54 DLR (AD) 16 and the case of Akrab Ali vs Zahiruddin Kari reported in 30 DLR (SC) 81 wherein the principle laid down that: "According to section 103(b)(5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act every entry in a record-of-rights finally published shall be evidence of the matter referred to in such entry and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved to be incorrect." 

 48. It is the case of the plaintiff that the suit land belonged to Tofani Talukder and Mohammad Ali Talukder. Though one of the successive heirs of Tofani Talukder deposed as DW-4 but in his deposition he did not claim that suit land was originally belonged to Tofani Talukder but he claimed that which was belonged to his father Amjad Ali Talukder and CS record was prepared in the name of Syed Ali Talukder and Amjad Ali Talukder. Plaintiffs also claimed that Abdul Hakim Talukder was minor when the CS record was prepared but no evidence from the side of the plaintiffs that he was minor at that time. The plaintiffs claimed that Tofani Talukder took initiative to prepare the CS record. But it is found that the CS record was not prepared in the name of Tofani Talukder which was prepared in the name of Syed Ali Talukder and Amjad Ali Talukder. So, it cannot be presumed that Tofani Talukder excluding the three daughters of Mohammad Ali Talukder namely Rokabjan, Phuljan and Rupjan recorded the land in the name of Abdul Hakim Talukder alone. But the trial court did not at all consider the said material facts of the case. 

 49. Mr Abdus Salam Mondal, the learned Advocate on behalf of the respondent submits that the ownership of land on the basis of CS record is not a conclusive prove and in support of his argument he cited the decision of the case of Pramatha Nath Chowdhury vs Kamir Mondal reported in 17 DLR (SC) 392 wherein our Apex Court held: "The presumption that attaches to a record-of-right under section 103-B of the Bengal Tenancy Act, is only this that the entry in the record-of-right represents that correct state of the affairs of the date it was prepared. Whether that states of affairs is continued even afterwards is not a presumption which arises under this section but under section 114 of the evidence Act, and its probative diminishes value progressively with the laps of time. The older the record the loss in its presumptive valuable. This is a matter, therefore, of proof and it merely has the effect of shifting the onus upon the other side. It is certainly not a conclusive prove." 

 50. Admittedly, the CS record was pre-pared in the name of Abdul Hakim Talukder who was the original defendant No. 1. Even the plaintiffs did not produce any subsequent record that by which the CS record was corrected or revised. So the aforesaid decision does not support the case of the plaintiff. 

 51. It is found that two sisters of Abdul Hakim Talukder Phuljan and Rupjan transferred some portion of the land in favour of Aftabuddin and Usafuddin. It appears that the defendant Nos. 11 and 12 claimed that Rokabjan and Phuljan by registered a kabla Exhibits-1 and 1(a) transferred the property in favour of defendant Nos. 11 and 12 in the year 1939 and 1942 and Amiruddin predecessor of the plaintiff No. 1-10 purchased 16 decimals land from defendant No. 6 by Kabla Exhibits-1(b) and 1(c) and also purr chased 10.14 decimals of land from defendant No. 2 by kabla Exhibits-1(d) and 1(e) and Nasiruddin husband of Rukubjan purchased 0.83 decimals by Exhibit-1(f) from the defendant No. 2 one of the son of Syed Ali the son of Tofani Talukder who was the CS recorded owner. (Since Syed Ali is the another CS recorded owner as such by the said purchase deed it cannot be said that the CS record was not rightly prepared in the name of defendant No. 1.) It appears that since the defendant No. 11 and 12 purchased land by Exhibits-1 and 1(a) in the year of 1939 and 1942 from Rokabjan and Phuljan though they have no right and title to transfer the property but the defendant No. 1 did not challenge the said deeds so, it is our view that by adverse possession they are entitled to get the said portion of the land. 

 52. The trial court also considering the evidence on record about the saham of the other defendants took view that they are entitled to get their respective saham. On perusal of the findings of the trial court we find that the said findings are on the basis of the evidence. So, we do not interfere with the said findings of the trial court. 

 53. Considering the aforesaid facts and circumstances of the case, it is our view that at the time of appeal challenging the CS record is clearly barred by limitation. However, considering the facts and circumstances of the case and the aforesaid observation it is our view that the judgment of the trial court should be modified. Thus we find merit in the appeal. 

 Send down the Lower Court's Records at once.

lawyer:
Abdul Quayum with Selim Reza Chowdhury, Advocates---For the Appellant. 
SN Goswami with Afsana Begum, Advocates---For the Respondent.
parties:
Motiur Rahman Bahadur ----- Defendant-Appellant 
VS
Hemanta Kumar Shill ----- Plaintiff-Respondent
full_judgment:
2. The facts as set out in the plaint, in short, are that 4.76 acre of land described in 'Ka' schedule of the plaint originally belonged to one Rajkamol Shill and Brindabon Shill in equal shares. Rajkamol Shill died leaving two sons, Lalit Kumar Shill and Rajmohon Shill. Brindabon Shill died leaving one son, Kalinath Shill. Lalit Kumar Shill died childless leaving his wife Kumudini Shill (Defendant-2). Rajmohon Shill died leaving two sons, Sharot Chandra Shill and Shashi Kumar Shill. Sharat Chandra Shill died leaving two sons, Hemanta Kumar Shill (plaintiff) and Surendra Nath Shill. Shashi Kumar Shill died leaving three sons, Anil Kumar Shill, Amulya Kumar Shill and Adhir Kumar Shill. SA record stands in the names of Kalinath Shill, Surendra Nath Shill, Hemanta Kumar Shill, Anil Kumar Shill, Amulya Kumar Shill and Adhir Kumar Shill in different shares and in the name of Kumudini Shill in 1/4 shares. Anil, Amulya and Adhir Kumar Shill having died unmarried their shares in the property devolved upon the plaintiff. As per her 1/4 share in the property Kumudini Shill possessed 1.19 acre land which she took out of plot Nos.353, 355, 356 and 359 by family arrangement as described in schedule Kha of the plaint. Kumudini Shill inherited the land from her late husband and thus she held the same in life-interest. The plaintiff is the grandson of the brother of Lalit Kumar and happens to be the nearest heir of the last full owner, i.e., Lalit Kumar. His interest is expectant upon the death of Kumudini Shill, the limited heir now in possession. 

 5. The defendant No. 1 (Appellant) contested the suit by filing a written statement wherein he denied all the material allegations made in the plaint. The case of the contesting defendant is apparently multi-directional. First line of his defense is that the suit land was not inherited by Kumudini (Defendant No. 2), his vendor, from her husband or any one else. It was her self-acquired property as such stridhana. The claim that the land was stridhana is testified by the fact that RS record was prepared in the name of Kumudini during life-time of her husband Lalit Kumar Shill. Subsequently SA record was also prepared in her name. Another fact that testifies the case of self-acquisition is that the plaintiff, Amulya and Kumudini jointly sold a piece of land from the suit plots to one Abdul Kader and Abdul Zabbar in 1956 which amounted to admission of absolute title of their vendor (Defendant No. 2) in the suit land. The second line of defense sought to be introduced during trial is that the land originally belonged to Lalit Kumar but he gifted the land to his wife Kumudini pursuant to a condition imposed by her father. The precondition imposed by the father of Kumudini was that unless Lalit had agreed to make a gift of a piece of land to his daughter he would not give his daughter in marriage with him. The third line is that Rajkamol and Brindabon did not belong to same family far less being full brothers. The plaintiff having claimed his descent from Brindabon, stands beyond blood relation of Lalit Kumar Shill and, therefore, does not come within the line of his heirs. By the same token the plaintiff is not the successor to the estate of Anil, Amulya and Adhir as reversionary. 

 14. Mr. SN Goswami, learned Advocate appearing for the respondent contended that the facts and evidence on records closely considered lead to the single conclusion that the suit land was inherited by defendant No. 2 from her deceased husband and she held the same in limited interest and that the plaintiff is the next reversionary of Lalit Kumar the last full owner of the suit land. It is also proved, he insisted, on convincing evidence that the suit land is sold with the primary intention of depriving the respondent, the next reversioner. He further submitted that there is an earlier decree against the defendant No. 2 passed in a suit for permanent injunction filed by the respondent, restraining her from disposing of the land on the ground that she took only limited estate in the suit land. Subsequently in the instant suit another Court of original jurisdiction again adjudged the defendant No. 2 as a limited owner of the suit land and found her not competent to transfer the same except for legal necessity. Mr. Goswami submits that the plaintiff has proved by preponderant evidence that he is the nearest reversioner of late Lalit Kumar and his interest in the suit land is expectant upon the death of Kumudini Shill who inherited the same from her husband and thus obviously. held the land in limited interest. 

 20. Defendant No. 2 Kumudini Shill herself was examined as DW 2. She tried to establish that she sold her own property not the property of her husband saying, inter alia, -'I have sold my own property not the property of my husband'. Her words are 'apparently vague in that the words- 'I have sold my own property' do not necessarily mean that the property sold was her stridhana in that stridhana is a highly technical word used strictly in technical sense. Even if the words are construed to mean stridhana there must be some evidence on records which in the circumstances of the case, must lead to the inference that the property was received or acquired by her in a manner which may constitute stridhana. There is none except two records of rights standing in the name of Kumudini and the factum of joint sale for stridhana to stand on. The question would be addressed at an appropriate stage of our judgment. 

 26. In view of the facts and evidence on records it may fairly be concluded that the respondent is a member of the Shill family and is the nearest heir of deceased Lalit Kumar Shill, the last full owner of the land sold. Respondent's case on this point is established by his own statement on oath and reaffirmed by the admissions made by the Dews in Court. It is also proved by the respondent that the land sold is a portion of the ancestral property of the Shill family and admittedly the vendor is the widow of late Lalit Kumar Shill. Respondent's clear case is that defendant No. 2 inherited the land from her husband. The appellant (contesting defendant), though denied acquisition by inheritance, has miserably failed to press home his own case by cogent evidence oral or documentary. Moreover, he appears to have taken multi-dimensional defenses going beyond his pleadings which again were contradicted by his own witness as is discussed above. 

 27. Back to the crucial question of record of rights and the joint sale. Mr. Quayum seems to have placed a good deal of emphasis on the fact that the RS and SA records stand in the name of Kumudini as well as on the joint sale of a piece of land from the suit plots with Kumudini and Amulya. The point he seeks to canvass is that the RoR standing in the name of Kumudini and the joint sale of land with her by the respondent amply suggest that the suit land is stridhana of Kumudini not inherited from her husband. He sought to buttress up his point submitting that the RS record was prepared in the name of Kumudini during the lifetime of her husband which clearly raises a presumption in favour of stridhana and further strengthens the case of the appellant. The trial Court, he stressed, committed an error of law having failed to take into notice such a decisive piece of evidence. We are not persuaded to agree with Mr. Quayum for the precise reason that the revenue records of the government by its nature does not squarely correspond to the intricacies and peculiarities of title of a person attached to a piece of land. For the purpose of revenue records one is not required to lay bare all the details relatable to title. Apparent interest in the land either as a proprietor, tenure-holder, raiyat, under raiyat, even pos-session as an occupant may form sufficient basis for preparation of record of rights. 

 28. It is a settled position of law that a widow as a limited heir is not a mere tenant-for-life, but is owner of the property inherited by her, subject to certain restrictions on alienation. The whole estate is vested in her for life and she represents it completely and her position is that of an owner. So long as she is alive no one has a vested interest in the succession. It is similar in incidents to an absolute estate. As long as a Hindu woman is found in possession of a piece of land either taken by her as life estate or as absolute interest she remains to be the owner of the land. In the circumstances, preparation of record of rights in her name remains to be a matter of course. It has nothing to do with the nature of her title to the land, limited or absolute. Nor such record of rights per se raises any presumption in favour of stridhana. 

 29. Over and above Mr. Quayum appears to be factually wrong in that the defendant No. 2 herself as DW. 2 stated in clear terms that the land was recorded in her name after death of her husband. Her own words read as follows: The appellant himself also did not stick to the point and said nothing on oath about the timing of preparation of RS record. Be that as it may, our view is that record of rights standing in the name of the widow even if found to have been prepared during lifetime of her husband, does not ipso facto raise any presumption in favour of stridhana. 

 33. The above statement of DW.1 made during trial (held in late 1999) shows that Kumudini was married at the age of 10 and lost her husband only 1½ years thereafter and her husband died 68 years ago. PW.1 (Respondent) on the other hand stated that Lalit died 50/60 years ago. The joint sale appears to have been made in 1956 allegedly for meeting expenses of sradhya etc. of Lalit. It is fairly deducible from the above evidence on records that Lalit died in mid-fifties. 

 39. For the reasons stated above we find substance in the contention of Mr. Goswami that, in view of the facts and evidence on records there is no justifiable reasons for interference of the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court. The appeal must, therefore, fail. 

 Send down the lower Court records at once.

lawyer:
SR Karmaker, Advocate ----- For the Petitioner 
Md Shahidul Alam Chowdhury, Advocate ----- For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Dayal Chandra Mondal and others ------ Petitioner
vs.
Assistant Custodian of Vested and Non-Resident Properties (L&B) and Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Dhaka and others ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
2. Maran Mondal, predecessor-in-interest of the petitioners as plaintiff, instituted a suit in the 3rd Court of Munsif Dhaka being Title Suit No. 732 of 1981 subsequently re-numbered as Title Suit No. 153 of 1984 before Munsif. Savar for declaration of his title in the suit land measuring 0.82 acre of nal land as recorded in CS Plot No. 787 under CS Khatian No. 137/24 corresponding to SA Plot No. 198 under SA Khatian No. 198 and RS Plot Nos. 1194 and 1204 under RS Khatian No. 225 of Mouza Barakakar, PS Savar, District Dhaka. The plaintiffs case, in short, is that the suit land originally belonged to Lakshman Mondal, full brother of plaintiff Maran Mondal and the same was correctly recorded in the CS and SA Khatians in the name of Lakshman MondaI. Lakshman Mondal eventually died as a childless widower at his native village Kakabo PS Savar District Dhaka leaving the plaintiff as his only heir to succeed him and since then he has been owning and possessing the suit property peacefully on payment of rent to the Government Acquired Estate. The plaintiff’s further case is that while he has been in rightful possession of the suit property the same has been correctly recorded in his name in the finally published RS Khatian No. 225 following which he has been paying rent to the Government in his own name in respect of the suit property. It was in late 1975 that at the instance of some greedy and unscrupulous persons the defendants illegally tried to treat the suit property as a vested property and threatened to oust him from possession by sheer force and under threats of imminent forcible dispossession he was constrained to pray for yearly lease of the suit property under protest but at the same time he filed an application before the appropriate authority for releasing the suit property from the list of vested property. It has further been contended by the plaintiff that the SDO. Dhaka who is defendant No. 2 in the suit after proper enquiry clearly found in his order dated 5-10-76 Ext. 5 that the original tenant Laksham Mondal had died 15 years ago at his native village Kakabo, Savar leaving plaintiff Maran Mondal as his brother and only heir to succeed him. The learned SDO in his order dated 5-10-76 further found that there was no occasion to treat the suit property as vested property and recommended the release of the suit property from the list of the vested property. The learned ADC (Rev) Dhaka eventually rejected the said recommendation of the SDO Dhaka illegally and arbitrarily and this necessitated the filing of the suit for declaration that the suit property is not vested property and the plaintiff is the absolute owner of the same. 

 3. The Assistant Custodian Vested and Non-Resident Property (Land and Buildings) and ADC (Rev) Dhaka contested the suit by filing written statements denying the material allegations of the plaint and contended, inter alia, that the recorded tenant Lakshman Mondal left Bangladesh long ago and permanently settled in India as a result of which the suit property has become a vested property by operation of law. It was further contended that since the plaintiff himself took lease of the suit property from the vested property authority and unsuccessfully tried for release of the same from the authority concerned he is estopped from challenging the legality or propriety of the vested property proceedings and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed. At the trial the defendant did not appear and contest the suit either by cross-examining the plaintiffs witnesses or by adducing any witness in support of the defence case. 

 4. The learned Munsif by his impugned judgment dated 12-1-85 dismissed the suit without discussing any evidence oral or documentary. It is evident from the impugned judgment that the learned Munsif dismissed the suit in a most casual manner without discussing and considering any evidence adduced by the plaintiff and the legal incidence of the documents exhibited in the case in support of the plaintiff’s case. It also appears from Ext. 4 and 5 that these do not contain any khatian number but the learned Munsif appears to have discovered a khatian number in the said exhibits, the basis of which is not available on record arid discarded the plaintiff’s case with reference to the baseless khatian purported to have been mentioned therein. 

 5. Mr SR Karmaker the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-petitioners submits that the learned Court of appeal below seriously erred in law in holding that the suit property is a vested property without any basis at all. The learned Advocate further submits that in the face of cleat assertions by the plaintiff and evidence led to substantiate the same to the effect that his brother Lakhman Mondal never left this country to settle in India and he died at his native village Kakabo leaving the plaintiff as his only heir and since then he has been owning and possessing the suit property and his name has duly been recorded in the finally published RS Khatian and he has been regularly paying rent to the Government Acquired Estate, there is absolutely no basis for treating the suit property as vested property on the basis of a VP Case started in late 1975. The learned Advocate further submits that in the face of the clear finding recorded by defendant No. 2 SDO Dhaka in Ext. 4 that the admitted tenant Lakshman Mondal had died in this country leaving the plaintiff to succeed him as his only heir and in the face of the unchallenged evidence of the plaintiff as PW 1 to the said effect the learned Court of appeal below evidently erred in law in arbitrarily ignoring the said evidence both oral and documentary by illegally shifting the onus of proof regarding the death of Lakshman Mondal and the same has resulted in error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice. Mr Karmaker further submits that from Exhibit 4 it is evident that the learned SDO Dhaka who is defendant No. 2 in the suit and himself conducted an enquiry in the VP Case himself found on local enquiry that Lakshman Mondal had died in this country as a citizen of the erstwhile East Pakistan and he never migrated to India and since Lakshman's death plaintiff Moran Mondal has been owing and possessing the suit property on payment of rent to the Government Acquired Estate and on such findings recommended the realse of the suit property from the list of the  vested property. the learned Court of appeal below evidently erred in law in completely ignoring these pieces of material evindence convincingly proving the plaintiffs case and the same has resulted in error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice. 

 7. The learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties finds it difficult to support the impugned judgments and frankly concedes that in the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record the impugned judgments do not appear to be proper and sustainable in law. 

 8. In support of his submissions Mr Karmaker has placed before me the case of Abul Khair vs. Bangladesh and others reported in 32 DLR (AD) 29 wherein their Lordships held that before a property could be treated as a vested property the authority concerned must prove that the original tenant migrated to India before the Enemy Property laws came into force in 1965. In the instant case there is absolutely no material on record to prove that Lakshman Mondal migrated to India at any point of time and settled there permanently but on the contrary there is convincing documentary and oral evidence to prove that the admitted tenant Lakshman Mondal had died in this country as its citizen leaving the plaintiff as his only heir to succeed him. The casual exercise made by the defendants in treating the suit property as a vested property without any legal basis whatsoever ostensibly at the instance of an irresponsible Tashilder who is accountable to none and an overzealous Superintendent lightly setting at nought the definite finding and recommendation of the SDO Dhaka must be held to be acts of malfeasance and witch-hunting at the cost of a citizen of the country whose name has duly been recorded in the finally published RS Khatian and from whom rent is being regularly accepted by the Government treating him as a tenant in respect of the suit property. 

 10. In the present case the plaintiff never abandoned his rights in the suit property and the defendants were never misled by his prayer for taking yearly lease so as to change or alter their position to their detriment and the prayer for temporary lease being obviously under protest and without any prejudice to the rights of the parties the doctrine of estoppel or waiver has no manner of application in the present case. Now here in the whole spectrum of deliberations the learned Courts below appear to have addressed themselves to the vital question as to whether the mere unsubstantiated claim of the vested property authority at the instance of an ever-exuberant and irresponsible Tahsilder whose action is never authenticated by any responsible officer of the Government is sufficient to throw away the unchallenged legal evidence both oral and documentary convincingly proving that the recorded tenant Lakshman Mondal had died in his country as its citizen leaving the plaintiff to succeed him as his only heir and thereby clearly fell in error in deciding the moot question involved in the case by misplacing the onus of proof. 

 11. It is evident that the instant Vested Property case was started as late as in 1975 and before that time there was no occasion to treat the suit property as vested property. In the absence of any legal foundation whatsoever to treat the suit property as a vested property the whole exercise made in this direction appears to be a malafide and superficial one at the behest of some irresponsible officials unnecessarily landing a citizen of the country and the Government in costly vexacious and oppressive litigations for an unworthy cause. Exts. 4 and 5 from the VP Case in question were admitted into evidence without any objection and, as such, it was absolutely unnecessary for the plaintiff to call for the records of the said VP case for proving the genuineness of Exts 4 and 5. The objection of the learned Court of appeal below on Exts 4 and 5 is totally unwarranted in the facts and circumstances of the case. It is apparent that the learned Court of appeal below totally misconceived the law bearing on the subject and clearly erred in law in discarding the case of the plaintiff who successfully proved his title in the suit property and the baselessness of the Vested Property proceedings in question. On a complete misreading of Ext 3 and 4 the learned trial Court mis-directed itself to find that the land described in the schedule to the plaint is different from that mentioned in Ext. 3 and 4. Unfortunately, the learned Court of appeal below failed to scrutinize Exts 3 and 4 as they deserved and fell in error by committing the same mistake. The misreading and non-reading of the said material evidence has obviously resulted in error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice. 

 13. Mr Karmaker also refers to the case of Arun Kumar Lal and others vs. Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property (Land & Buildings) and ADC (Rev) Dhaka reported in 1983 BCR 225 wherein his Lordship found that estoppel cannot operate against a statute. From the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record it is evident that the plaintiff was threatened with dispossession in a summary way by the defendants and it was under the instant threats of forcible dispossession he had to pray for yearly lease of the suit property for saving his possession albeit under protest and lost no time in coming to the Court for vindication of his grievance. Under such circumstances the learned Courts below erred in law in holding that the plaintiffs claim in barred by estoppel. 

 14. In this connection we may profitably refer to the principle which is incorporated in section 115 of the Evidence Act. The doctrine of estoppel in an equitable postulation which Jays down that if a person has acted to his detriment or altered his position on the basis of any declaration, act or omission of another that other person will not be allowed in any future suit or proceedings between himself and that other person or his representative to go back upon to the detriment of the opposite party. To establish a case of waiver or estoppel it is therefore, necessary to show that the party alleged to have waived his rights had acted in such a manner so as to lead the other side to believe that such rights will not be enforced in the future. Mere indulgence shown under exigency of circumstances in not enforcing one's legal rights or keeping the said rights suspended for the time being cannot constitute waiver or estoppel and give rise to the inference that the rights have been abandoned for all times. In the present case the plaintiff was always diligent in asserting his own title in the suit property and he never abandoned his claim of ownership over it nor the defendants were misled by his prayer for an annual lease so as to change or alter their position to their detriment and the prayer for temporary lease being obviously under protest and without any prejudice to the rights of the parties the doctrine of estoppel or waiver has no manner of application in the present case. The learned Court of appeal below acting on wrong premises evidently erred in law in holding that the suit is barred by estoppel and waiver. 

 15. The learned Courts below left the field of fact and strayed to fiction by finding fault with the plaintiff for not producing the death certificate of Lakshman Mondal which is not a requirement of law for proving his death particularly when his death was well proved by other convincing and unchallenged evidence. The learned Courts below appear to have approached the case from a totally wrong angle of vision unsupported by the established principles of law and thus misdirected themselves to dismiss the suit on misreading and non-reading of the material evidence on record affecting the merit of the impugned decision. 

 17. Order VIII rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that assertion of facts made in the plaint if not denied specifically or by necessary implication shall be deemed to be admitted. In our case under review the plaintiff clearly stated in the plaint that Lakshman Mondal had died in this country as a citizen of the erstwhile East Pakistan leaving the plaintiff as his only heir to succeed him and he led evidence to prove the said assertion by the unchallenged oral and documentary evidence and there being no contrary evidence on record the learned Courts below clearly erred in law in dismissing the suit ignoring the positive evidence on record by resorting to hypothetical assumptions and the same has resulted in error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice. 

 18. It may not be out of place to reiterate that laws relating to enemy properties now vested properties which are fairly well-settled by now by the consistent pronouncements by the highest Court of the country properties which assumed enemy character and became enemy properties by operation of law during the relevant time viz from 6-9-65 to 16-2-69 when emergency was formally lifted became vested properties and the Government may treat such properties as enemy or vested properties and take over possession thereof in accordance with law subject to the legitimate rights of co-owners co-sharers and the bonafide transferees in lawful possession therein. But before a property is treated as a vested property particularly on the basis of a VP Case started long after the lifting of emergency on 16th February, 1969 a heavy duty is cast upon the authority concerned to satisfy itself that the recorded tenant migrated to India before 1965 and settled there following which the property in question has really become vested property by conducting necessary enquiry into individual cases rather than relying on the stray noting of a petty Tahsilder who is accountable to none and whose report has never been verified by any responsible officer of the Government. There being as yet no authenticated and published enemy property list the scope for manipulations is wide open till now to unscrupulous officials to include any new property any time in the unending list of enemy property and play like toys with the rights of the citizens whose consequent engagements against the Government in protracted costly and oppressive litigations do not eventually serve any useful purpose either for the Government or for the members of the public the only beneficiaries being some capricious officials and the paraphernalia. 

 20. There is yet another special feature of the case which has been overlooked by the learned Courts below. Admittedly the finally published RS Khatian stands in the name of the plaintiff and the Government is regularly accepting rent from him thereby recognising him as the tenant in respect of the suit land. A finally published record of rights revised under section 114A of the SAT Act has a presumption of correctness and that presumption continues till it is otherwise rebutted by reliable evidence. Nothing has been done by the contesting defendants to dispel the legal presumption that attaches to the finally published RS Khatian in the name of the plaintiff. Recognition of the plaintiff as a tenant in respect of the suit property by the Revenue Authority of the Government is binding upon the Vested Property Department and the latter cannot claim the suit land as a vested property summarily discarding the finally published RS Khatian in the name of the plaintiff. The action of the ADC (Revenue) Dhaka who is the de facto head of the Vested Property Department of the District indulging in oppressive litigations must be deprecated. The case of the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev) Narayanganj vs. AKM Latiful Karim and others reported in 17 BW (HCD) 249 lends instant support to this view. The impugned judgment cannot be sustainable on that ground as well. 

 Send down the lower Court records at once.
