Zeyad Rahman and another------Petitioners
Vs
Delta Insurance Company Ltd and others------ Respondent
full_judgment:
The case of the petitioner in Company Matter No. 61 of 2010 in short is that he is a share-holder of respondent No. 1 company, being the beneficiary owner of Account No. 12025300375- 7944; that he holds 8098 (eight thousand ninety eight) share of public shares; that the Respondent No. 1 was scheduled to hold its 19th AGM on 19-9-2005 in respect of financial year ended on 2004 but upon an application, in Company Matter No. 114 of 2005, filed by a share-holders namely Mr AQM Nurul Afsar, this Court, by order dated 31-4-2005, stayed holding of the Annual General Meeting (AGM) of the Respondent No. 1 scheduled to be held on 19-9-2005. Eventually the said Company Matter was dismissed for non-prosecution by order dated 2-3-2010. In the meantime, the holding of  19th to 23rd AGMs of the respondent No. 1 for the financial years ending on 2004-2008 have fallen due and it became imperative for the respondent No. 1 company to hold the AGMs for the said periods. It is stated by the Petitioner that in the event this Court condones the delay in delay in holding AGMs for the aforesaid years, the respondent No. 1 company would need 2 fix a fresh record date as per SCE Notification No. SEC /CMRRCD/ 2008-183 / Admin/03-36 dated 5-10-2009; to constitute an election commission and the share-holders of the company would need to cast vote to elect the directors of the company. It has been stated by the petitioner that pursuant to section 76 of the Insurance Act, Board of Directors of an Insurance company shall comprise of 20 directors, out of which 12 directors ought to be elected from the sponsors, 6 directors to be elected from public subscribers and 2 directors to be elected as independent directors. It has been asserted by the petitioner that the shares issued by the respondent No. 1 are ordinary shares, with equal voting rights ranking pari passu to each other. Since its incorporation, the respondent No. 1 company had issued total 3,00,000 ordinary shares and some of them are yet in script/paper form, while majority share have been converted into script less/electronic shares. Script shares were converted into script less shares following establishment of the Central Depository Bangladesh Limited ('CDBL'). 

 3. All shares are required to be traded through the CDBL system. Approximately more than 60% of the shares from both groups of share-holders have already been dematerialized and merged. The petitioner also asserted that the Insurance Act, 2010 has not taken into cognizance of the Central Depository System ('CDS'), which is run by the CDBL, and CDS does not recognize classification of shares. It is stated by the petitioner that since the respondent No. 1, CDBL or the holders of dematerialized shares themselves are unable to ascertain whether the shares they are holding are either sponsor shares or public shares, and further in the absence of any discrimination between voting rights of all the issued shares of the respondent No. 1, the petitioner and owners of all script less/dematerialized share as well as holders of script shares are entitled to cost vote by way of two separate ballots in the election of directors amongst both the sponsors share-holders and public share-holders as envisaged in section 76 of the Insurance Act, 2010. It has further been stated by the petitioner that he is the holder of the dematerialized shares in his Beneficiary's Account No. 1202530003757944 and as a share-holder of the company, he is lawfully entitled to vote in electing the sponsor and public directors of the said company by two different ballots. The petitioner prayed for the following reliefs:— 

 ii. To direct the respondent No. 1 to hold the said AGMs within a stipulated period of time by fixing a new record date as per SEC Notification No. SEC/ CMRRCD/2008-183. 

 4. The respondent No. 1, the added respondent Nos. 2A and 2B contented the said application by filing respective affidavit-in-opposition denying material allegations set out in the petition. All these respondents although concurred to the prayer for condonation of delay for holding of the AGMs for the aforesaid years but opposed the consequential directions prayed for by the petitioner. The answering respondents in their respective affidavits-in-opposition in more or less the same terms contended that the board of directors having recommended for the 19th AGM to be held for the year 2004 and the board of directors having fixed book closure and the said date having expired, there is no scope for fixing a new record date for the said AGM in view of SEC Notification No. SEC/CMRRCD/2001-14/24/ Admin/-03 dated 26-11-2011 (Gazetted on 10-12-2001). It was further stated that fixing of record date is a matter that lies the issuer in view of section 2 (Chha) read with section 44 of the Depository (User) Regulation, 2003. The Securities and Exchange Commission also issued another Notification under section 2CC of the Securities and Exchange Ordinance, 1969 conforming that the board of directors of an issuer will fix the record date. It was contended that the fixation of record date is a legal compulsion, which is a duty assignment on the board of directors to discharge the same at the proper time when arrives and the Court may not interfere with regard to fixation of record date in a preemptive manner at a premature stage. It has further been stated by the respondent that the constitution of the Election Commission as prayed for is not permissible under Rules 15B(5), (6) and (7) of the Insurance Rules, 1958 (the said Rules). This concept is foreign to the Companies Act, 1994 as well. It is asserted by the respondents that the Rule, having spelt out the method of appointing Election Commission, this Court should not venture into the appointment of an Election Commission in contravention of the said in as much as, when no case been made out by the petitioner as to the neutrality of the chairman of the board. In the affidavit-in-opposition, it has further been stated that section 76(2) of the Insurance Act, 2010 (Insurance Act) makes it mandatory that the election of the directors shall be conducted as per the Rules prescribed. Relying on section 76(2) of Insurance Act read with Rules 15B(5), (6) and (7) of the said Rules the respondents contended that the prayer for independent election commission is barred. 

 7. Thus, the ratio of share-holding between sponsors and public was 50: 50 at all material time. All these issued shares were ordinary shares being equal right to dividend, voting participation in the meeting etc, without any discrimination/difference. The Articles of Association of the respondent No. 1, company did not provide for any limitation on the voting rights of the shares subscribed by the share-holders, in particular, in relation to the formation of a new board of directors where all the directors are elected pursuant to the change in law and the fact that AGMs of the company could not be held for the last six years. Therefore, the provision of Article 96 of the Articles of Association that addresses the voting rights of the shares when reelecting retiring directors is not relevant in the instant case. It has further been stated in the affidavit-in-reply that until 30-06-2010, out of total 300,000 ordinary shares as issued by the said company, the total 1,88,088 (one lac eighty eight thousand and eighty eight) shares stood in dematerialized form. Thus, the number of shares in dematerialized form constitutes about 63% of the total issued and paid up capital of the company. This means that the holders of dematerialized shares constitute majority of the share-holders of the company. But due to ulterior motive of the holders of the shares in script form who constitute a minority, the interests of these majority share-holders of electronic shares are at stake and therefore, the petitioner is seeking the protection of the Court through the instant company matter for protecting the best interests of the company. 

 12. Placing the prospectus Dr Zahir, the learned Counsel further submitted that the prospectus does not reflect any categorization of shares so as to give extra advantage to any group of share-holders in respect of anything including voting rights. He submitted that prospectus is an instrument of representation from the company to the public at large and the ordinary share-holders having acted pursuant to the said prospectus the respondent No. 1 company is stopped from doing anything to their detriment. He also submitted that the prospectus does not create any restriction in respect of voting of an ordinary share-holder toward election of sponsor share-holders. 

 19. Mr Imam, the learned Counsel submitted that section 76 of the Insurance Act, 2010 provides that the board of directors of an insurance company shall comprise of not more than 20 directors out of which 12 shall be sponsor directors, 6 shall be public subscriber director and 2 independent directors. He submitted that 60% of the directors of the company, i.e. majority of the directors are required to be sponsor directors. Moreover the majority of the directors of the company are required to elect the 2 independent directors of the company (SEC Order No. SEC/ CMRRCD/2006-158 / Admin/02-06 dated 09-01-2006, Corporate Governance Guidelines), condition 1.2 of which provides that independent non-share-holder directors should be appointed by the elected directors. Accordingly, sponsor shares are in a position to elect 14 directors out of 20 directors of an insurance company, i.e. 70% of the directors of the company. Mr Imam submitted that Article 96 of the Articles of Association of the respondent No. 1 company provides that sponsor share-holders shall re-elect sponsor directors, whilst the public subscribers shall re-elect public directors. However, as a result of dematerializing of the shares, 63% of the shares held by the share-holders of the company from the Stock Exchange are not aware as to whether they are holding sponsor shares or public shares. According to Mr Imam 63% share-holders of the company will not be able to exercise their voting rights for election of directors of the company pursuant to the provisions of the Article 96 of the Articles of Association of the company, which requires that sponsor share-holders be re-elected by sponsor directors and public subscribers re-elect public directors. Mr Imam submitted that respondent No. 1 company in its affidavit-in-opposition has stated that dematerialized share should be treated as public shares and accordingly these share-holders can vote in only for election of public directors. However, this position is not maintainable for the following reasons:— 

 20. Mr Imam, the learned Counsel also submitted that the 3,00,000 shares that have been issued by the respondent No. 1 company are all ordinary shares with no special rights and privileges attached to any particular class of shares; accordingly all share-holders enjoy equal rights in respect of voting and dividends which are the principle rights that shares carry. 

 21. Mr Imam also submitted that since all issued shares were of one class i.e. ordinary shares ranking pari passu i.e. with equal rights in all respects, these rights will continue even after dematerialization, which does not in any manner alter the rights attached to the shares particularly because of the merger of the identity of the sponsor and public shares of the elimination of any/all distinction between them in the CDS system CDBL has no means of maintaining such distinction even on re-materialization into script from. He submitted that section 76 of the Insurance Act, 2010 read with SEC Notification No. SEC/CMRRCD/ 2006-158/ Admin/02-064th January, 2006 in respect of election of 2 independent directors effectively means 28.84% sponsor shares elect 14 out of 20 directors of the respondent company. According to Mr Imam the consequence of disfranchising the majority share-holders from electing the majority of the directors (i.e. 14 out of 20) would destroy one of the most fundamental concepts of company law i.e. majority rule as enunciated in the classic case of Foss vs Harbottle (1843) 2 Hare 461. 

 22. Mr Imam submitted that prospectus governing the issue of public shares does not limit their rights, unlike other share-holders, to elect only public directors. He submitted that section 91 read with the compulsory regulations of the Companies Act, 1994 guarantees the rights of the ordinary share-holders in electing the directors of the company. Section 76 of the Insurance Act, 2010 does not deal with voting rights to elect directors and Rule 15B of the said Rules is inapplicable and/or overridden by the CDBL system having a non-obstante clause in the governing law i.e. The Depository Act, 1999 and the Depository Regulations, 2003. 

 23. Regarding "Record Date" Mr Imam, the learned counsel submitted that it has been argued by the Vice Chairman of the company that SEC Notification dated 26-11-2001 will be applicable in setting the record date of the company for the 24th ACM. Such an argument was placed before this Court earlier in ABM Khaliquzzaman vs United Commercial Bank reported in 28 BLD (HCD) 635. The above judgment of this Court has been upheld by the Appellate Division by Civil Appeal Nos. 319-321 of 2008. Further, following the above judgment, SEC published Notification Nos. SEC /CMRRCD/ 2008-183/ Admin/ 03-36 dated 05 October 2009 and Notification No. SEC/CMRRCD/ 2009-193/ Part II/ 35/ Admin/ 03-43 dated 4 May 2010 setting the record date. 

 24. Mr Imam further submitted that record date is the date declared by an insurer for identifying the owners of a certain class of securities listed in the Depository Register for the owners to be identifiable for participation in general meeting, extra ordinary general meeting etc to cast vote as for transfer of transmitting dividends, interests, proxies, financial reports, and other documentation to them. Dhaka Stock Exchange by its Notification dated 18-3-2010 (published on 31-03-2010) amended the provisions of the Regulation 36(a)(4) of the listing Regulation of DSE and defined record date in the following terms:— 

 "the words "book closing date" and 'book closer date' shall be replaced by the words, 'book closer date' or 'record date' as the case may be." 

 25. Thereafter, the SEC has defined record date in its latest Notification No. SEC/ CMRRCD/ 2009-193/ part-II/ 35/ Admin/ 03-43 dated 4-5-2010 which provides as follows:— 

 a) The record date or commencement of book closure period of the listed security issuers shall be as per requirements in the listing regulations of the stock exchanges. 

 b) Annual General Meeting (AGM) shall be held by the listed security issuers within 45 (forty five) working days from the record date or completion of book closure period, as the case may be.

In this respect paragraph 6.016 of Palmer's Company Law (Sweet & Maxwell's Loose leaf Filing Guide: Palmer Release 125: April 2010) read that: 

 "6.016: there is a presumption that the rights attaching to shares rank pari passu so that the holders participate equally in the benefits of membership. But this presumption is displaced when different shares carry different rights. Those shares then constitute different classes of shares. [-------]. 

 56. Classification of shares by way of attaching different rights thereto is recognized in our jurisdiction as well. This is why section 71 of the Companies Act, 1994 provides protection of variation of rights attached to different classes of shares. From meticulous reading of section 71 of the Companies Act, 1994, I am fully convinced that classification of shares is allowed to be created by way of attaching different rights, obligations or restrictions to the shares. Section 71(1) of Companies Act, 1994 states as follows:— 

 57. 1 am also convinced from the plain reading of the provision of section 71 of the Companies Act, 1994 that the legislature under the said section 71 has given protection to the rights attached to the shares উক্ত শ্রেনীর শেয়ারের সহিত সংশ্লিষ্ট অধিকার which manifests that such rights attached thereto run with the shares. In other words if such class of shares are transferred then such rights are also transferred along with the shares and subsequent transferee shall enjoy the said rights. These rights are covenant in rem, because such rights will not be extinguished by way of transfer of the shares. 

 "The truth of the matter is that an enormous variety of different rights, relating to dividends, return of capital, voting, conversion into ordinary shares, redemption and other matters, may be attached to classes of shares, all of which are conventionally described as "preference" shares. [--------]. 

 59. Such preferential rights are attached to shares. So such rights, which stem form the preferential shares, are convenient in rem that runs with the shares and change of holder of such shares does not vary the force of such right attached to such class of shares.

Now, whether any particular share is ordinary shares or preferential share or any other class of share depend upon the construction of the Articles of Association of the company or other instrument for issuing or creating such shares. For this purpose Court can have recourse to various "cannons of construction" of documents for interpreting the same. I have perused the Articles of Association of the respondent No. 1 company and other documents annexed in the both matters. Articles 6, 49 and 54 of the Articles of Association of the respondent No. 1 company empowers the respondent No. 1 company to attach any special right or privilege to any share and creation of preferential share and variation of rights attached to different classes of shares.  "6. Subject to any special rights or privileges for the time being attached to any issued shares, the new share shall be issued upon such terms and conditions and with such rights and privileges annexed thereto as the resolution creating them shall direct, and if no direction be given, as the Directors shall determine and in particular such shares may be issued with a preferential or qualified right to dividends and in distribution of assets of the Company and with a special or without any right of voting."

This Article 6 of Articles of Association of the respondent No. 1 company protects existing preferential shares and other classes of shares with any right or privilege attached thereto and this Article 6 also empowers the respondent No. 1 company to issue/allot new preferential shares or various classes of shares with various rights and privileges. This Article 6 does not ipso facto create any preferential share or classes of shares. On perusal of the Articles of Association and other documents annexed by both petitioners and other parties. I have not found any provision in the Articles of Association creating any preferential share or classes of shares attaching different rights thereto. Neither I have come across any other documents creating any preferential shares or classes of shares in the respondent No. 1 company. All the shares held by the promoters/ sponsor share-holders of the company and the public through IPO are ordinary shares having equal rights and privileges, or obligations attached thereto. In view of the matter, through I find force in the submission of Mr Karim that any right attached to shares does not extinguish in the event the script shares are converted into dematerialized shares through Central depository System, but I find it redundant and academic to address in the instant case to the issue whether categorizations/ classifications of shares are blurred in the event the script shares are converted into dematerialized form through Central Depository System and whether Central Depository Bangladesh Limited (CDBL) has failed to manage a system to identify the different classes of shares in dematerialized form, since in the instant case the respondent No. 1 Company has not issued different classes of shares or preferential shares. Hence I hold that all the shares so far issued by the respondent No. 1 company are ordinary shares. 

 62. As opposed to attaching rights to shares, often Articles of Association of the company or other instruments such as special resolution of the company attach special rights expressly or by necessary implication, to a particular person or set of persons. Such person or persons enjoy the rights attached to them so long they remain in the company and such right does not run with the shares. For instance, a particular share-holder is named in the Articles of Association to remain life long Chairman or Managing Director or Auditor etc.; or Articles of Association provides or special resolution or agreement provides that unless a particular share-holder or a particular number of share-holders from a defined set of share-holders appears in the meeting, there will not be any quorum for meeting; or Article of Association or other instruments creates a right that existing share-holders or particular named share-holder/ share-holders shall be offered first in the event of allotment of new shares or in the event of transfer of shares by other share-holders i.e. a pre-emptive right, or a right to right to refuse first is created. Even section 155 of the Companies Act, 1994 creates a pre-emptive right for offering the existing share-holders first in pro rata in the event of allotment of new shares to the existing share-holders. These are examples of rights attach to share-holders. These rights are not attached to the shares. So such rights do not run with the shares. In other words, the subsequent transferee of shares does not acquire such rights of the transferor who would earlier enjoy such rights. Such rights are covenant in personam. If the share-holder enjoying such special rights transfers his shares, then the ultimate transferee shall not able to enjoy the said rights. By way of attaching different rights to the share-holders, different class of share-holders are created. In our jurisdiction such classification of share-holders are also recognized, which gets legal footing from section 85(1)(e) of the Companies Act, 1994. Section 85(1)(e) states that share-holders shall enjoy the same rights and be subject to the same liabilities as all other share-holders of the same class. Section 85(1)(e) of the Companies Act, 1994 allows different classes of share-holders and amongst the own class the share-holders will enjoy same rights and be subjected to same obligations. Such classes of share-holders are created expressly or by necessary implication. Whether there is different classes of share-holders depends upon construction of constitutive document of the company i.e. the Articles of Association or any other instrument creating such classification of share-holders by way of attaching different set of share-holders. For this purpose as well the Court can take recourse to various "cannons of construction" of documents for ascertaining whether there are classes of share-holders with different rights attached to them. Applicable laws may also expressly or by necessary implication, create different classes of share-holders having different rights attached to them. Now I shall consider whether the Articles of Association of the respondent No. 1 company and provisions of laws of the land applicable thereto or any other instrument, either expressly or by necessary implication, has created different classes of share-holders with different rights attached to them.

 74. Dr Zahir, the learned Counsel argued that in view of Rule 15B(1) of the Insurance Rules, 1958 public subscribers shall elect directors representing public subscribers as well as the directors representing sponsor share-holder, but sponsor share-holders shall not be eligible to elect directors representing public subscribers. I find it difficult to agree with the submissions made by Dr Zahir Rules 15B(1) does not speak that public subscribers shall also elect directors representing sponsor share-holders. Rule 15B(1) simply provides that public subscribers shall elect directors representing public subscribers. This means that the right of public subscribers to elect directors is confined to the election of directors representing the public subscribers. So the public subscribers cannot exercise their right of election beyond directors representing public subscribers i.e. they cannot elect directors representing sponsor share-holders. Rule 15B(1) not only exclude all other share-holders (i.e. sponsor share-holders) other than public subscribers to elect director representing public subscribers, but the said Rule 15B(1) in the same vein is restrictive clause upon public subscribers in electing directors representing public subscribers only. If the legislature had the intention only to debar the sponsor share-holders in participating election of directors representing public subscribers then the legislature would provide in the plain language to that effect stating that in clear language that the sponsor share-holders shall not be eligible to participate in electing directors representing public subscribers. So I am fully convinced that Rule 15B(1) completely attached rights to public subscribers to elect only directors representing public subscribers and also by necessary implication debars the public subscribers to participate in electing sponsor directors and also debars sponsor share-holders in electing public directors. 

 79. No Article of the Articles of Association of the respondent No. 1 company or Article 96 makes any provision that any person other than member of the company can be eligible to contest election for the office of directors; or that any person who is not member of the company can vote for electing a director of the company; or that election of the director can be held in the meeting of board or any other meeting except general meeting. Therefore, none of the provisions of the Articles of Association offends section 91(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 1994. Article 96 only provides that directors representing sponsor directors shall be elected by sponsor-director and director representing public subscribers shall be elected by public subscribers and by way of providing two groups of share-holders, Article 96 does not conflict section 91(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 1994 rather Article 96 is fully in conformity with section 91(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 1994 since during election in compliance of Article 96 a director must be a member of the company; a voter must also be a member of director, and election of director will be held in general meeting. In other way around section 91(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 1994 does not restrict or prohibit making two groups of share-holders, one group having no right to elect directors from other group and the same is mutually applicable in both groups. Further, Dr Zahir argued that each share shall have one vote and, as such, Article 96 offends Regulations 61, 81 and 81. I have found that Regulation 61 is not mandatory regulation. In any event Article 96 does not confront the principle one share shall have one vote, since once allowed to cast vote each share shall carry the weight one vote, and shares of none of the eligible voter in the respective group shall carry the weight of more than one vote. Further Regulations 80 and 81 relates to retirement by rotation and re-election. The Articles of Association of the company keeps provision of retirement by rotation. So none of the provision of the Articles of Association negates the effect of Regulations 80 and 81. Thus, I have not found any provision in the Companies Act, 194 which restricts or prohibits classification of share-holders into different classes. Different classes of share-holders are created by attaching separate rights or special rights to the different classes of share-holders. Rather I have found that Companies Act, 1994 inspires creation of classes amongst the share-holders and enforces enjoyment of same rights amongst the same group.  80. So it appears that the literal interpretation of section 85(1)(s) of the Companies Act, 1994 in a very simple language transpires that share-holder of same class shall enjoy same rights. So one share-holder or a particular class cannot raise objection that share-holder of different group are enjoying different rights, neither one share-holder of particular class can wield a right of another class of share-holders. Therefore, if attachment of different rights to different classes of shares are treated as ultra virus the Companies Act, 1994, as argued by Dr Zahir, the whole sanction of the provision under section 85(1)(ঙ) of the Companies Act, shall be frustrated, futile and negated. 

 "parliament has never sought to fetter the right of the company to issue a share with such rights or restrictions as it may think fit. There is no fetter which compels the company to make the voting rights or restrictions of general application and it seems to me clear that such rights or restrictions can be attached to special circumstances and to particular types of resolution. This makes mockery of section 148; all that Parliament was seeking to do thereby was to make an ordinary resolution sufficient to remove a director. Had Parliament desired to go further and enact that every share entitled to vote should be deprived of its special rights under the articles it should have said so in plain terms by making the vote on a poll one vote one share. Then, what about shares, which had no voting, rights under the articles? Should not Parliament give them a vote when considering this completely artificial from of ordinary resolution? Suppose there had here been some preference shares in the name of Mr Faith's wife, which under the articles had in the circumstances no vote; why in justice should her voice be excluded from consideration in his artificial vote?" 

 82. In the instant case as well, I have not found any restriction or prohibition in the Companies Act, 1994 in classifying two groups of share-holders namely sponsor share-holders and public subscriber mutually debarring each group from participating in election of directors of other group. Articles of Association in proper construction having mutually curtailed right to vote of one group in electing directors from other group, any provision of law cannot be interpreted to give vote to the former group. Section 91(b) of the Companies Act, 1994 does not state that all the members/ share-holders of the company must have participation in the election of director, neither does section 91(1)(b) restrict or prohibit making two groups of share-holders one having no participation in electing directors from other group. If the legislature had otherwise intention, then the legislature in plain language would prohibit giving different rights of different groups of share-holders and section 85(1)(ঙ) would not encourage different rights amongst different groups of share-holders.

The said case reported in 1 LG (2004) HCD 46 enunciated the proposition of law to the effect "any Act of Parliament or the Companies Act, 1994 or statutory instrument created thereunder" in sub silentio does invalidate a provision of the Articles of Association of the company or an action of the company. I have not found any provision of the Companies Act, 1994 or the Insurance Act, 2010 prohibiting or restricting classification of rights as to electing directing amongst the group of share-holders. Both Dr Zahir and Mr Akhter Imam argued that under section 76(2) the directors are to be elected in the manner as prescribed in the Rule and election of directors cannot be held as per Article 96 of the Articles of Association. I do not agree with the contentions made by Dr Zahir and Mr Akhter Imam. In the Insurance Rules there is no provision of election of directors of sponsor directors and, as such, this silent aspect of Insurance Rules does not invalidate the provisions of Articles of Association for electing directors as any of the provision of the Articles of Association is not inconsistent with Rule 15B of the Insurance Rules. Rather 15B in clear terms provides that the public subscribers shall elect public directors and they shall not elect a sponsor directors. Further, I find a logical conclusion can be drawn that it will be discriminatory if the public subscribers are allowed to elect sponsors directors when sponsors cannot elect public directors. The public subscribers are allowed to elect sponsor directors that will mean a preferential right given to public share-holders but the Articles of Association of the company has not given any such preferential right to any public subscribers on top of the sponsor share-holders. Therefore, I hold that Article 96 is fully consistent with Rule 15B of the side rules and sponsor share-holders shall elect sponsor directors and public subscribers shall elect public directors. 

 85. As such I do not find any force in the argument of Dr Zahir, the learned counsel that proviso to Article 96 giving separate rights to two different classes, namely sponsor share-holders and public subscribes, allowing to elect directors of their respective class only is ultra vires the Companies Act, 1994 and Insurance Act, 2010. 

 87. Mr Imam, the learned counsel argued that a portion of the shares from both classes of share-holders have been converted into dematerialized form. As such he argued, from the face the shares it cannot be ascertained whether the holder of shares is a sponsor share-holder or a public subscribers and for this reason the public subscribers cannot be debarred from participating in the election of directors representing sponsor share-holders. I do not find any substance in this submission advanced by Mr Imam. Whether a person is a sponsor share-holder can be mentioned on the face of the Articles of Association, because the persons who subscribed to the Memorandum and Articles of Association as promoters are named in the Memorandum and Articles of Association. Therefore, the sponsor share-holders can easily be traced out on the face of the Articles of Association. From the list of share-holders obtained from CDBL as on the date of record date, it can easily be ascertained how many shares in dematerialized form are being held by a sponsor share-holders. Therefore, the total number of shares held by a particular share-holders, be sponsor share-holder or public subscribers, can be ascertained with sufficient certainty. On the other hand, as I have found above, there is no classes of shares in the respondent No. 1 company and, as such, whether categorization or identity of shares in dematerialized form is lost is immaterial. Therefore, I am not at all convinced with the submission of Mr Akhter Imam that as a result of shares 63% shares held by the share-holders by the company from the stock Exchange are not aware as to whether they are holding sponsor shares or public shares. I hold that the shares held by sponsors cannot be termed as 'sponsor share' since as I have already held that there is no special rights attached to shares, in other words all shares are ordinary shares and so long the sponsors will hold the same will be shares of sponsors and when the shares will be sold to public, the said shares will be shares of public subscribers. Therefore, after transferring the shares of sponsors to public the shares will no longer be sponsors' shares but the same will be of public shares. In this regard I find full force with the submission of Mr Karim, the learned counsel that promoters shall remain sponsor share-holders till they cease to have their membership of the company by way of transferring their entire shares. It further appears to me that the submission of the petitioner in Company Matter No. 61 of 2010 is contradictory of prayer made by him. If there is no classification of share-holders with separate voting rights then the petitioner would not have asked for votes in two ballots. However, the company may trace and identify sponsor shares amongst of dematerialized shares of the company as per law and rules as well as Articles of Association and the holders of sponsor shares as per law and rules are to vote for sponsor directors from amongst their sponsor holdings and the public share-holders vote for public share-holder director. And in such case, the company may take assistance of CDBL and the respective stock exchange and supply the accurate list to the election commission for holding smooth and fair election of directors of all the groups. 

 88. The next issue relating to record date, Mr Karim, the learned counsel submitted that the board of directors will fix record dates as per the notification and laws of SEC. Both Mr Huq and Mr Ahmed adopted the submission of Mr Karim. I also find that in any event Court cannot fix a record date, since it is the duty of board of director to fix a suitable record date as per law, further unless there is violation of law relating to fixing a record date or an purported action, more than a mere assumption leading to violation of law relating to fixing a record date, the Court cannot pass an order even directing the company to fix a record date, since the Court cannot act in vacuum. However, it is obligatory on the part of the board of directors of the respondent No. 1 company that it shall in compliance with relevant laws and SEC's Notifications fix a record dates for the AGMs in its due course of business and the record date which was earlier fixed by the board of directors in the year 2004 will be changed and a new record date will be fixed in accordance with the Companies Act as well as Notifications of the Securities and Exchange Commission. 

 3. The board of directors is directed to comply with the relevant laws and SEC's Notifications in fixing record date for the AGM's including for the AGM of the calendar year 2004.

full_judgment:
5. But we should not be that myopic. There are other provisions also in the Constitution, high- lighting the rights of the people. Part II of the Constitution spells out the Fundamental Principles of State Policy, while, Part-III stipulates the Fundamental Rights of the people of Bangladesh. 

 6. Article II within Part II of the Constitution stipulates that the Republic of Bangladesh shall be a democracy in which fundamental human rights and freedoms and respect for the dignity and worth of the human person, shall be guaranteed. These are not mere empty flowery words. These are the dictates of the Constitution. This Article glorifies the State Policy, emburdening the Republic with the obligations, among others to protect the dignity of its citizens. The dignity of a citizen is no less important than his life or limb. This Article casts a duty upon the State to protect the dignity of its citizens. 

 8. Part III of our Constitution guarantees Fundamental Rights of the people of Bangladesh, such as, among others, equality before law (Article 27), equal rights of women with men [Article 28(2)], right to protection of law (Article 31), protection of right to life and personal liberty (Article 32) etc. 

 17. The Constitution not only imposes obligation upon the citizens but also protects them from the excesses as well as laches of the authorities. As such, the persons who are unable to file a formal application, cannot be without remedy in vindication of their rights guaranteed under the Constitution .and the laws of the land. If so, it would be in total negation of the spirits enshrined in our sacred Constitution. 

 19. We must appreciate that the fundamental rights guaranteed under the Constitution would be meaningless to the inhabitants of this country, if their remedy is impeded for want of a formal application. 

 25. Today orders or writs in the nature of prerogative writs are frequently issued by the superior Courts almost all over the globe including the Republics having written Constitutions, in order to establish and enforce the fundamental rights of its citizens and also to prevent illegalities. 

 47. In India, after initial hesitation, the Supreme Court made a bold assertion in the case of SP Gupta vs Union of India AIR 1982 SC 149 and held that any member of the public acting bona fide can move the Court. This decision was followed in People s Union for Democratic Rights vs Union of India AIR 1982 SC 1473 where the principle of Rule of Law was invoked in allowing locus standiin the PIL. 

 53. In a Monarchy, with or without a democracy, the Monarch is sovereign. In a Republic, the people are sovereign and the character of its government is essentially a democratic one. In order to run the Republic, a charter is required, which would recognize the existing sovereignty of the people with their rights and obligations. It also delineates the functions of the Republic. This charter creates the institutions and functionaries of the Republic, so that they can serve the people. This charter is the Constitution and the people themselves are the centrepiece of the Republic and its Constitution. Everything belongs to them, the four-corners of the State, the political rights and powers and so also their pre-existing fundamental civic rights, recognised and guaranteed under the Constitution. 

 54. In this manner, with this end in view, the Constitution of the United States of America was framed which was rather a short one. The Constitution of India is quite a long one while the Constitution of Bangladesh is in between. The purpose and focus is the same in all the Constitutions, it is the people around which the Constitutions wound around. The Constitutions project, protect and uphold the rights of the people. For them alone the Republic and its Constitution exist, their interest is the highest law. Not only the nation but the Constitution is also of the people, by the people, for the people. For them the notion of justice also rise high. 

 55. The Constitution of Bangladesh is no exception. Part III of the Constitution guarantees the fundamental rights of the people and Part II narrates the fundamental principles of State Policy which are also propeople. 

 58.The High Court Division, under Article 102 of the Constitution, may issue orders and directions in the. nature of prerogative writs, stated therein, in order to establish and to enforce the fundamental rights of the people, to ameliorate their sufferings, to provide redress from the high handedness of the people in authority and others and to establish the rule of law. The right to enforce a fundamental right is also a fundamental right. 

 60. The purpose of procedural law is for proper exercise and implementation of substantive law so as to avoid busybodies or meddlesome interlopers, otherwise, its real beneficiaries would be lost in their crowd. The procedural law in this case is to promote the substantive right of the people. It cannot hinder or frustrate its real purpose, the interest of the people. After all, the Constitution along with its Article 102 has been enacted, as an expression of the will of the people. The rights of the people cannot be overlooked or sacrificed in the rigour of procedure. The procedure is needed in order to streamline enforcement of the fundamental rights of the people but not to create impediment to its fulfillment. 

 61. The purpose of law is not to hinge on the web of procedure against the interest of the people, rather, the other way around. That is why the ancient rigour of the prerogative writs were modified and used for the benefit of the people. Two hundred years ago, Marshall, CJ, acted suasponte, may be even without thinking about it but it was done, and a history was made. In the case of Dr Mohiuddin Farooque vs Bangladesh, the procedural requirement of filing an application by an actual 'aggrieved person' took a back-seat and the rights of the people were glorified. 

 62. The learned Advocates, do not apparently have any doubts about the grievance of Shahida or her rights under the Constitution, their only objection is in respect of the lack of an application. 

 66. Why then did those apex Courts become so charitable in accepting those apology of applications for consideration? Because,' the learned Judges of those Courts know and appreciate the true spirit of law. They know the background and purpose of the Fundamental Principles of State Policy and the Fundam ental Rights of the people enshrined in the respective Constitutions. They know that the said rights are not restricted only to those fortunate few who can avail the services of the learned Advocates and come before the Court with 'perfect' applications but the sacred provisions of the Constitution are not that much discriminatory, those rights are equally open to the poor, to the down-trodden illiterate mass, many of whom are unfortunate sufferers of oppression, direly requiring the protection of the Constitution but they have no means. 

 67. It is not their fault that they have no means to come before the Court. Is Bangladesh not their country? Is it not their Constitution also? Have the framers of the Constitution kept them outside its ambit because of their misfortune? Far from it, it is very much their Constitution endowed them, entitled them, blessed them with all the rights spelt out therein. 

 70. In this connection, one should appreciate that an aggrieved person may or may not be an oppressed but an oppressed person is inevitably and invariably an aggrieved person. Should the Judges refuse to uphold the rights guaranteed under the Constitution to an oppressed person in such a situation? Can the purpose of the fundamental rights guaranteed under Part III of the Constitution be defeated by some provisions of the Rules, made under the Constitution? 

 74. I would not however, make a pretence that the letters, post-cards, telegrams and even newspaper reports are 'applications' within the meaning of the Rules. Those are exactly what they are. But those contain information. Information about violations of human rights, injustice and oppression. 

 76. The learned Judges on reading the news-item were, however, apparently satisfied about the fundamental rights of Shahida, its breach and also her grievance, but there was no application, which is a procedural requirement under Article 102, as argued by the learned concerned Advocates. 

 78. The last but not the least, the consideration of grievance and the discretion of Judges must not be lost in the haze of the procedure, they should not sport away the rights of the people, guaranteed under the Constitution, specially, the down-trodden ones, who are unable to come before the Court. A Judge must keep his eyes on the ultimate dispensation of justice, in his discretion, to the needy, the poor, the oppressed, to all who suffered injustice, on consideration of law in its proper perspective, highlighting: 

 88. Under the circumstances, the vindication of the rights of an oppressed outweigh the procedural requirement of filing of an application. 

 89. In the instant case, because of the uncalled for fatwa, Shahida suffered extreme humiliation and outrageous indignity. As such, her inalienable rights guaranteed under Articles 27, 28 (2), 31 and 32 of the Constitution, have been violated. Besides, the provisions of the Muslim Family Law Ordinance were also flouted. 

 90. Shahida, above all is a human being. Her right to life is not that of a chattel but that of a citizen of sovereign Bangladesh. As such, she enjoys her inalienable rights guaranteed under the Constitution and the laws adopted or made there- under. Her rights under those provisions of laws had been violated. No doubt, she is an aggrieved person. She has rights as well as great expectations from the Constitution as any other citizen of this country. 

 91. Should she continue to suffer the humiliation, the indignity and injustice since she was unable to come before the Court with an application in her hand. If so, what value our valued and sacred Constitution holds for her with all its guarantees, superbly phrased and gloriously spelt out therein? It would become stale and meaningless flowery hollow words to Shahida and the thousands of faceless unfortunate women like her in the far away hamlets. To her, to them, the Constitution with all its guarantees to the fundamental rights, would become mere worthless sheafs of paper although the Constitution stringently ensured that nobody would trifle with her, with them. 

 93. The words “ ....I will do right to all manner of people according to law.” in this respect mean, among others, the implementation of the rights guaranteed under Part III of the Constitution. 

 94. The Judges are bound by their oath to uphold the provisions of the Constitution including the fundamental rights of the people guaranteed therein. The mere procedural veil cannot smog and delude their conscience. They ought to rise to the occasion when the Constitution is violated or fundamental rights are endangered or even threatened. In the instant case, they indeed did, they rose to the occasion, they issued the Rule suo moto. 

 96. Let us visualize what would have had happened if this kind of social ills is ignored and not promptly addressed. This would have subjected not only Shahida but the whole community to utmost disgrace. This would also be an insult to humanity. Besides, the failure to halt the receding human values would have encouraged and emboldened others to commit such and other violations of law and human rights, specially in the far-flung areas. This would inevitably lead to further violations of decency, human values, violations of the Rule of Law and also the Constitution. This cannot be allowed in any ordered society. 

 105. It is only when the executive branch fails to uphold the law, address the problems and provide the necessary redress or to come to rescue the sufferers, the Judges of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court, are constrained to look into the matter, but only as a last resort, either on an application filed by an aggrieved per- son or by the oppressed or by any conscientious person or an institution, on his/her behalf, praying for appropriate relief or in an extreme situation even in the absence of any application, by being aware of the violations of any law or violations of human rights, from the electronic or print media, by issuing a Rule upon the perpetrators of illegality and also upon the concerned officials, because ultimately those officials of the government would do the needful, not the Court. But, by and large, the Judges should normally remain aloof from the policy decisions of the government of the day which generally represents the will of the people. 

 107. The Court may only over-see that law has been obeyed and the rights of the people, guaranteed under the Constitution, are upheld, This is in vindication of the Constitutional obligations of the learned Judges, not for any personal or even institutional aggrandizement. 

 144. However, with the advent of civilisation, the rights of the people, the best creation of God, in contradistinction to the powers of the Kings and other autocratic Rulers, are now acknowledged throughout the world. Now, no body rules, the Head of the State, the Head of the Government and other authorities serve the people. 

 "102.(1) The High Court Division on the application of any person aggrieved, may give such directions or orders to any person or authority, including any per- son performing any function in connection with the affairs of the Republic, as may be appropriate for the enforcement of any of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III of this Constitution. 

 159. Sub-Article (1) of Article 102 has dealt with the powers of the High Court Division to give such directions or orders to any person or authority, including any person performing any function in connection with the affairs of the Republic, as may be appropriate for the enforcement of any of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution "on the application of any person aggrieved." Again in clause (a) of sub-Article (2) of the Article, power has been conferred on the High Court Division to make order (i) directing a person performing any functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority to refrain from doing that which he is not permitted by law to do or to do that which he is required by law to do; or (ii) declaring that any act done or proceeding taken by a person per- forming functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority has been done or taken without lawful authority and is of no legal effect "on the application of any person aggrieved" on its satisfaction that there is no other equally efficacious remedy provided by law. In clause (b) of sub-Article (2), the High Court Division has been empowered to make an order (i) directing that a person in custody be brought before it so that it may satisfy itself that he is not being held in custody without lawful authority or in an unlawful manner; or (ii) requiring a person holding or purporting to hold a public office to show under what authority he claims to hold that office "on the application of any person." Thus it is clear that in the case of enforcement of any of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution, there is no need for the satisfaction of the High Court Division that there is no other equally efficacious remedy provided by law, but the condition precedent is "on the application of any person aggrieved." In the case of sub-clauses (i) and (ii) of clause (a) of sub-Article (2), the High Court Division is required to be satisfied that there is no other equally efficacious remedy provided by law before making any order as contemplated therein but that again "on the application of any person aggrieved." So far as the cases contemplated in sub-clauses (i) and (ii) of clause (b) of sub-Article (2) are concerned, the High Court Division may make an order "on the application of any person." In these two cases, the word "aggrieved" has been omitted, but like the cases as contemplated in clause (a), the High Court Division has to be satisfied that there is no other equally efficacious remedy provided by law. The framers of the Constitution have used the words "on the application of any person" in every contemplated areas/field of jurisdiction of the High Court Division under Article 102. In the context, "aggrieved" is not the lis; however, we shall consider the word "aggrieved" later on. 

 160. A close reading of Article 102 as a whole shows that in conferring jurisdiction on the High Court Division to issue orders and directions etc, for the enforcement of any of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution and for other remedies as contemplated in clauses (a) and (b) of sub-Article (2), the framers of the Constitution have specifically used the words/language "on the application of any person." It is also significant to note that the legislature instead of "on an application" used the words "on the application", that is, instead of an indefinite article, has used a definite article, namely: 'the' And it appears to me the object of using the definite article 'the' is to give stress of the necessity to file application to invoke the jurisdiction of the High Court Division under Article 102. So, in order to decide the question whether the High Court Division could issue the suo motu Rule in question, we need to see the proper meaning of the core word "application" used in Article 102. 

 166. When in Article 102 in all situations including the enforcement of fundamental rights as conferred in Part III of the Constitution, the framers of the Constitution have used the word "application", it has to be adhered to its plain meaning without imputing anything of our own. From a plain reading of the words used in sub- Articles (1) and (2) of Article 102, it also appears to me that the words "on the application" cannot be read in isolation, but have to be read along with the words "of any person." Person may be artificial or natural, but it can never be a news item published in a newspaper. 

 172. It is true that the Supreme Court as the Guardian of the Constitution is the protector of the rights, freedom and liberty of the People as enshrined in Part III of the Constitution, but when the framers of the Constitution, namely, the Constituent Assembly, in plain and unambiguous language/wordings stated that the High Court Division "on the application of any person" may give such directions or orders to any person or authority, including any person performing any function in connection with the affairs of the Republic, as may be appropriate for the enforcement of any of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution, so also in respect of the other remedies as mentioned in clauses (a) and (b) of sub-Article (2) thereto how then it can be read that such power would include a power of issuance of a suo motu Rule in the absence of any application. Can it be said that the framers of the Constitution were oblivious or unmindful of the fact that Bangladesh's formal justice system remains relatively inaccessible to the vast majority people and that vulnerable and disadvantaged groups of people viz. children, women. ethnic minorities, ultra poor, disabled people face difficulty in having excess to the justice and that the vast majority people of Bangladesh cannot afford to come to the High Court Division to seek redress against their grievance and that the fundamental rights as guaranteed in Part III of the Constitution and their other rights as contemplated in clauses (a), (b) of sub-Article (2) could be or would be violated or infringed, while specifically using the words "on the application of any per- son."? If we say in the positive, then we shall be questioning the wisdom of the Constituent Assembly, wisdom of the framers of the Constitution and we shall be putting something which they omitted. 'Yes', there is scope of interpreting the word or expression "aggrieved" appeared/used in Article 102 of the Constitution, i.e. as to the standing of a person in filing an application under the Article. And that has been interpreted in the case of Dr. Mohiuddin Farooq vs Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of irrigation, Water Resources and Flood as Control and others 49 DLR (AD) 1. 

 "any person aggrieved" meaning only and exclusively individuals and excluding the consideration of people as a collective and consolidated personality will be a stand taken against the Constitution .... The High Court Division cannot under the circumstances adhere to the traditional concept that to invoke its jurisdiction under Article 102 only a person who has suffered a legal grievance or injury or an adverse decision or a wrongful deprivation or wrongful refusal of his title to something is a person aggrieved .... Insofar as it concerns public wrong or public injury or invasion of fundamental rights of an indeterminate number of people, any member of the public, being a citizen, suffering the common injury or common invasion in common with others or any citizen or an indigenous association, as distinguished from a local component of a foreign organisation, espousing that particular cause is a person aggrieved and has the right to invoke the jurisdiction under Article 102." 

 181. So far as Article 44 of the Constitution is concerned, it has simply guaranteed the right of a person to move the High Court Division for enforcement of the rights conferred by Part III, but that too in accordance with clause (1) of Article 102, i.e. the vehicle to enforce the fundamental rights is Article 102, which speaks about availing the vehicle by filing the application. Article 108 has said that the Supreme Court shall be a Court ofrecord and shall have all the powers of such a Court including the power subject to law to make an order for the investigation of or punishment for any contempt of itself. And there can- not be any dispute that the power of issuing a contempt Rule is inherent in a Court's power, but that power is not comparable with the power under Article 102. It may be mentioned that Article 108 of the Constitution has not said anything about filing of any application. 

 II. By the impugned judgment, the fundamental rights of the appellant guaranteed under Articles 29, 40 and 41 of the Constitution have been taken away. The High Court Division directed another organ of the State to frame law and thereby violated the principle of separation of power and, as such" the impugned judgment should be set aside. In support of his contention, he has relied upon the cases of Government of Bangladesh and another vs Sheikh Hasina and another; 60 DLR (AD) 90 and Hefzur Rahman (Md) vs Shamsun Nahar Begum and another, 51 DLR (AD) 172. Though the Fatwa in question is wrong the High Court Division cannot examine its propriety under Article 102 of the Constitution. 

 IV. In exercise of its suo motu power, the High Court Division can issue suo motu Rule and such power cannot be curtailed in the interest of protection of fundamental rights of the citizens as well as for establishment of rule of law. 

 II. Fatwa violates the fundamental rights of the freedom: 

 IV. Fatwa should not be given against prevailing laws and judgments of the Court and should not be pronouncedaffecting fundamental rights of the citizens. 

 III. The awarding of' extra-judicial punishment is totally unconstitutional and violates not only the basic structure of the Constitution but also is repugnant to the fundamental rights of the persons to equality, equal treatment. under the law, non-discrimination, life, liberty, freedom from cruel and degrading treatment and punishment and to freedom of religion as guaranteed under Articles 27, 28, 31, 32, 35 and 41 of the Constitution. 

 II. Fatwa is violative of personal 'as well as fundamental rights of a citizen. 

 228. We have considered the submissions of the learned Senior Advocates for the appellants of both the appeals, the amici curiae, the" interveners, the Olayma Kerams, the impugned judgment and the materials on record. 

 278. The Family Courts Ordinance, 1985 provides for the settlement of disputes through conciliation or compromise after filing of a written statement in a pre-trial hearing as envisaged in section 10. The Court may initiate a pre-trial hearing to seek to settle the disputes relating to dissolution of marriage, maintenance and dower, restitution of conjugal rights as well as guardianship and custody of children. 

 292. Article 27 of the Constitution provides that all citizens are equal before the law and are entitled to equal protection of law. Sub-Articles (1) and (2) of Article 28 of the Constitution state that the State shall not discriminate against any citizen on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth and that woman shall have equal rights with man in all spheres of the State and or public life. According to sub-Article (3) of Article 28 of the Constitution, no citizen shall, on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex or place of-birth be subjected to any disability, liability, restriction or condition with regard to access to any place of public entertainment or resort or admission to any educational institution. According to Article 35(1) of the Constitution, no person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of a law in force at the time of commission of the act, charged as an offence, nor shall he be subjected to any penalty greater than, or different from, that which might have been inflicted under law in force at the time of commission of the offence. Sub-Article (5) of Article 35 of the Constitution provides that no person shall be subjected to torture or cruelty, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment. 

 302. From the examples cited, above, it appears that in order to perform rituals and other things; Fatwa may be necessary apart from legal matters. Fatwa as opinion on Islamic tenets has never been treated as a source of Islamic law and therefore, cannot be treated as part of Shariat, but Fatwa may be given with reference to Shariat. The newspapers have frequently reported about violation of human rights and perpetration of criminal offences in the name of Fatwa which invariably infringe on the rights of the citizens enshrined in Articles 31 and 32 of the Constitution and law enforcing agencies have been unable to check the evil effects of Fatwa. Even when a Fatwa does not impose a punishment, the person against whom Fatwa is directed suffers ignominy and is looked down upon in the society. 

 306. Therefore, we are of the opinion that Fatwa cannot be given contradicting or against the existing laws of our country; Fatwa on religious matters only may be given by the properly educated persons which may be accepted only voluntarily but any coercion or undue influence in any form is forbidden; but no person can pronounce Fatwa which violates or affects the rights or reputation or dignity of any person which is covered by the law of the land; no punishment, including physical violence and/or mental torture in any form, can be imposed or inflicted on anybody in pursuance of fatwa; the declaration of the High Court Division that the impugned Fatwa is void and unauthorized, is maintained. 

 314. Leave was granted to consider whether the High Court Division can issue a suo motu "102(1) The High Court Division on the application of any person aggrieved, may give such directions or orders to any person or authority, including any person performing any function in connection with the affairs of the Republic, as may be appropriate for the enforcement of any of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III. of this Constitution. 

 319. The Supreme Court of Bangladesh as the guardian of the Constitution is the protector of rights, freedoms and liberties of the people. Using tools of innovative and creative interpretation of the constitutional provisions, the Supreme Court of Bangladesh has consistently endeavored to further extend the horizon of rights and liberties and administered quality justice to the justice-seekers. Bangladesh's formal justice system remains relatively inaccessible to the vast majority of the people. Vulnerable and disadvantaged groups including women, children, ethnic minorities, ultra poor and disabled people face particular difficulty in having access to justice. 

 320. There is no gainsaying the fact that the majority of the people of Bangladesh cannot afford to come to the High Court Division to seek redressed of their grievances. If the fundamental rights of an indigent citizen is violated and if he does not have the means, should he be allowed to suffer only because of his inability to come before the High Court Division with an application. If a glaring injustice amenable to the writ jurisdiction is done to that person, what would be the fate of the oath of office administered to a Judge who is under the obligation to preserve, protect and defend the Constitution. The words, preserve, protect and defend the Constitution shall mean and include implementation of the provisions of the Constitution in their letter and spirit. Mere non-filing of an application cannot be a ground for not exercising power under Article 102 of the Constitution. This Division in the recent judgments has enlarged the meaning of aggrieved per-son, a shining example of which is in the case of Dr Mohiuddin Farooq vs Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Irrigation. Water Resources and Flood Control and others, 49 DLR (AD) 1. As a result, various Non-Governmental Organizations are coming forward to help the indigent people for redressal of their grievances; but it is not always expected that such Organizations will come forward to assist such people in each and every case. In such a situation, the Court cannot sit idle. 

 323. The limitations are that (a) there should be an application; (b) the application shall be verified by an affidavit by the petitioner or by any person who is competent to represent the aggrieved person with the prior leave of the court (c) the affidavit filed in support of the writ petition must be satisfactory and (d) the relief asked for must be one to enforce a legal right of the petitioner himself. The Supreme Court of India has, of late, admitted exceptions from the limitations relating to affidavit, locus-standi and the like in the case of a class of litigations which are being entertained in the nature of 'public interest litigation' that is to say, the public in general are interested in the vindication of some rights or the enforcement of some public duty and the action can be brought by anyone. This Division has accepted the principle and widened the jurisdiction of the High Court Division by way of giving the meaning of 'aggrieved person’ in Dr. Mohiuddin Farooq (ibid). 

 324. The Supreme Court of India has further expanded its jurisdiction by entertaining petitions under Article 32 of the Constitution not only from associations or organizations or individuals interested in a common cause or an advocate, even journalists but also on the basis of letters written by such persons containing a complaint of maltreatment of under-trial prisoners or women in police custody (Sheela Bose vs State of Maharashtra, AIR 1983 SC 378, Mukes Kumar vs State of MP AIR 1985 SC 1363). The court cautioned that the process of the court should not be abused or misused. Where the court is so satisfied, prima facie, it may not insist on the filing of an affidavit and may proceed to investigate into allegations with a view to meting out justice to the persons on whose behalf the communication is addressed particularly where to insist upon an affidavit at the initial stage may lead to perpetration of injustice or may give rise to a situation where from a practical point of view the doors of justice would be closed to the poor and the disadvantaged. It was further observed that the court should not object to the procedural technicalities being relaxed, that is to say, it should provide easy access to justice to the weaker sections' of humanity and to combat exploitation and injustice and to secure for the under-privileged segments of society their social and economic entitlements, to redress public injury, enforce public duty, protect social rights, vindicate public interest and rule of law. Referencesin this connection are the cases of State of WB vsSampalLal, AIR 1985 se 195, State of HP vs Parent of Student Medical College, AIR 1985 se 910 and Malik Brothers vs Narendra Dadich, AIR 1999 se 3211. 

 325. In an unreported case, namely, Syeda Rizwana Hasan vs Bangladesh, 18 BLC (AD 54, this Division held that if there is violation of fundamental rights causing common injury or common invasion affecting the people of a particular area, any public spirited person or organization of that locality can maintain a petition in the High Court Division. It was further held 'that when there is invasion of human rights which shocks the judicial conscience, the court should extend its jurisdiction. In the case in hand, Shahida, wife of Saiful was forced to marry her paternal cousin Shamsul, under a 'Fatwa' pronounced by one Haji Azizul Huq on the ground that her marriage was dissolved on an incident of altercations between the husband and wife. The husband, out of anger uttered the word ‘talak’ despite that they continued their marital tie. The incidents of this nature are common in the rural areas and sometimes, in the name of such 'Fatwa' victims are being subjected to whipping. These incidents are social crimes which are spreading in the society tremendously day-by-day. These social crimes should be eliminated and the courts should not remain a silent spectator, particularly the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, which is the guardian of the Constitution. It has a duty to protect these social rights. Though we do not encourage in the manner the High Court Division suo motu has exercised its writ jurisdiction in view of the language used in Article 102 of the Constitution, we treat the news item published in ‘he Daily Banglabazar Patrika’ on the issue of 2nd December; 2000 as an application under Article 102' of the Constitution and wave the procedural formalities to protect social rights and vindicate public interest and rule of law treating it as an exceptional case with a view to preventing social injustice in the society. 

 326. It was never the intention of the framers of the Constitution to imprison theenforcement of fundamental rights guaranteed by Part-III of the Constitution to a weird, ‘application’, occurring in sub-Articles (1) and (2) of Article 102 of the Constitution. Given the provisions of the fundamental rights guaranteed by Part-III of the Constitution, in. general, and sub- Articles (1) and (2) of Article 102 in particular, the framers of the Constitution never, intended to deprive the vast majority of the people of the country of getting their fundamental rights enforced. Denying the fundamental rights of the majority of the people amounts to denying our independence earned through the blood of the freedom-fighters and the sacrifices of the women who were ravished by the occupation force and they never thought of an independence limited to a small section of affluent people. 

 329. Therefore, a proper case where the fundamental right of a citizen is infringed, the High Court Division can issue suo motu Rule provided the infringement of right is amenable to the writ jurisdiction and is of great public importance. In this context, a news paper report, post-card, written material maybe treated as an application in order to-overcome the obstacle of application. But before issuance of suo motu Rule, the High Court Division must record its satisfaction in clear terms about exercise, of such power. The High Court, Division shall exercise such power sparingly. 

 330. Mustafa Kamal, J in his ‘Bangladesh Constitution: Trends and Issues' at page 170 had referred to a suo motu Rule issued by Md. Mozammel Haque And Mahfuzur Rahman, JJ. on the basis of a report in a vernacular daily (Daily Ittefaq) concerning a person Nazrul Islam who had been languishing in jail for long 12 years ever since he was 12 years old. As a 5-year old boy he was implicated ina few gang and dacoity cases from which he was acquitted and yet he was kept in wrongful imprisonment. He was put under bar- fetters (danda-beri) ever since he wastaken into custody and was put under that condition although out, The Court was shocked to see him in bar-fetters when he was brought before it. The Court found that the proceedings of the criminal cases were void ab initio as he was tried in contravention of the .Children Act, 1974. The Court found that the fundamental rights of the boy were violated for many years in the past. He was literally in shackles wrongfully and illegally without any cause or case. He was set free and the Court issued, various directions to the Ministry of Home Affairs in respect of other accused or persons like Nazrul Islam who may be in any other jail in Bangladesh. 

 331. Mustafa Kamal, J has further stated that he had the occasion to meet Nasir Aslam Zahid, the Chief Justice of the High Court of Sindh and found him sorting out numerous telegrams and letters seeking the Court's interference, treating some as regular constitutional petitions and sending others to authorities for redress. He said he received 50 telegrams a day complaining of human rights violations.
