full_judgment:
But we should not be that myopic. There are other provisions also in the Constitution, highlighting the rights of the people. Part II of the Constitution spells out the Fundamental Principles of State Policy, while, Part-Ill stipulates the Fundamental Rights of the people of Bangladesh. 

 5. Article 11 within Part II of the Constitution stipulates that the Republic of Bangladesh shall be a democracy in which fundamental human rights and freedoms and respect for the dignity and worth of the human person, shall be guaranteed. These are not mere empty flowery words. These are the dictates of the Constitution. This Article glorifies the State Policy. unburdening the Republic with the obligations, among others to protect the dignity of its citizens. The dignity of a citizen is no less important than his life or limb. This Article casts a duty upon the State to protect the dignity of its citizens. 

 Part III of our Constitution guarantees Fundamental Rights of the people of Bangladesh, such as, among others, equality before law (Art. 27), equal rights of women with men [Art. 28(2)], right to protection of law (Art.31), protection of right to life and personal liberty (Art.32) etc. 

 The Constitution not only imposes obligation upon the citizens but also protects them from the excesses as well as laches of the authorities. As such, the persons who are unable to file a formal application, cannot be without remedy in vindication of their rights guaranteed under the Constitution and the laws of the land. If so, it would be in total negation of the spirits enshrined in our sacred Constitution. 

 We must appreciate that the fundamental rights guaranteed under the Constitution would be meaningless to the inhabitants of this country, if their remedy is impeded for want of a formal application. 

 11. To- day orders or writs in the nature of prerogative writs are frequently issued by the superior Courts almost all over the globe including the Republics having written Constitutions, in order to establish and enforce the fundamental rights of its citizens and also to prevent illegalities. 

 In India, after initial hesitation, the Supreme Court made a bold assertion in the case of S.P. Gupta V. Union of India AIR 1982 SC 149 and held that 'any member of the public acting bona fide can move the Court'. This decision was followed in People's Union for Democratic Rights V. Union of India AIR 1982 SC 1473 where the principle of Rule of Law was invoked in allowing locus standi in the PIL. 

 In a Monarchy, with or without a democracy, the Monarch is sovereign. In a Republic, the people are sovereign and, the character of its government is essentially a democratic one. In order to run the Republic, a charter is required, which would recognize the existing sovereignty of the people with their rights and obligations. It also delineates the functions of the Republic. This charter creates the institutions and functionaries of the Republic, so that they can serve the people. This charter is the. Constitution and the people themselves are the centre-piece of the Republic and its Constitution. Everything belongs to then, the four-corners of the State, the political rights and powers and so also their pre-existing fundamental civic rights, recognised and guaranteed under the Constitution. 

 In this manner, with this ends in view, the Constitution of the United States of America was framed which was rather a short one. The Constitution of India is quite a long one while the Constitution of Bangladesh is in between. The purpose and focus is the same in all the Constitutions, it is the people around which the Constitutions wound around. The Constitutions project, protect and uphold the rights of the people. For them alone the Republic and its Constitution exist, their interest is the highest law. Nor only the nation but the Constitution is also 'of the people, by the people, for the people'. For them the notion of justice also rise high. 

 15. The Constitution of Bangladesh is no exception. Part 1ll of the Constination guarantees the fundamental rights of the people 'and Part 11 narrates the fundamental' principles of State Policy which are also pro-people. 

 The High Court Division, under Article 102 of the Constitution, may issue orders and directions in the nature of prerogative writs, stated therein, in order to establish and to enforce the fundamental rights of the people, to ameliorate their sufferings, to provide redress from the high handedness of the people in authority and others and to establish the rule of law. The right .to enforce a fundamental right is also a fundamental right. 

 These are extraordinary original jurisdiction of the High Court Division. Of necessity, access to this jurisdiction is some what restricted. In the absence of an equally efficacious remedy, which is a precondition, an aggrieved person is entitled to file an application before This High Tribunal, praying for appropriate The purpose of procedural law is for proper exercise and implementation of substantive law no as to avoid busybodies or meddlesome interlopers, otherwise, its real beneficiaries would be lost in their crowd. The procedural' law in this case is to promote the substantive right of the people. It cannot hinder or frustrate its real purpose the interest of the people. After all, the Constitution along with its Article 102 has been enacted, as an expression of the will of the people. The rights of the people cannot be overlooked or sacrificed in the rigour of procedure. The procedure is needed in order to streamline enforcement of the fundamental rights of the people but not to create impediment to its fulfillment. 

 16. The purpose of law is not to hinge on the web of procedure against the interest of the people, rather, the other way around. That is why the ancient rigour of the prerogative writs were modified and used for the benefit of the people. Two hundred years ago, Marshall, CS., acted sua sponte, may be even without thinking about it but it was done, and a history was made. In the case of Dr. Mohiuddin Farooque V. Bangladesh, the procedural requirement of filing an application by an actual 'aggrieved person' took a back-seat and the rights of the people were glorified. 

 The learned Advocates, do not apparently have any doubts about the grievance of Shahida or her rights under the Constitution, their only objection is in respect of the lack of an application. 

 Why then did those apex Courts become so charitable in accepting those apology of applications for consideration? Because, the learned Judges of those Courts know and appreciate the true spirit of law. They know the background and purpose of the Fundamental Principles of State Policy and the Fundamental Rights of the people enshrined in the respective Constitutions. They know that the said rights are not restricted only to those fortunate few who can avail the services of the learned Advocates and come before the Court with `perfect' applications but the sacred provisions of the Constitution are not that much discriminatory, those rights are equally open to the poor, to the down-trodden illiterate mass, many of whom are unfortunate sufferers of oppression, direly requiring the protection of the Constitution but they have no means. 

 It is not their fault that they have no means to come before the Court. Is Bangladesh not their country? Is it not their Constitution also? Have the framers of the Constitution kept them outside its ambit because of their misfortune? Far from it, it is very much their Constitution endowed them, entitled them, blessed them with all the rights spelt out therein. 

 In this connection, one should appreciate that an aggrieved person may or may not be an oppressed but an oppressed person is inevitably and invariably an aggrieved person. Should the Judges refuse to uphold the rights guaranteed under the Constitution to an oppressed person in such a situation? Can the purpose of the fundamental rights guaranteed under Part III of the Constitution be defeated by some provisions of the Rules, made under the Constitution? 

 I would not however, make a pretence that the letters, post-cards, telegrams and even news-paper reports are 'applications' within the meaning of the Rules. Those are exactly what they are. But those contain information. Information about violations of human rights, injustice and oppression. 

 The learned Judges on reading the news-item were, however, apparently satisfied about the fundamental rights of Shahida, its breach and also her grievance, but there was no application, which is a procedural requirement under Article 102, as argued by the learned concerned Advocates. 

 The last but not the least, the consideration of grievance and the discretion of Judges must not be lost in the haze of the procedure, they should not sport away the rights of the people, guaranteed under the Constitution, specially, the down-trodden ones, who are unable to come before the Court. A Judge must keep his eyes on the ultimate dispensation of justice, in his discretion, to the needy, the poor, the oppressed, to all who suffered injustice, on consideration of law in its proper perspective, highlighting : those canons of decency and fairness . which express the notions of justice of English-speaking peoples....' (Justice Frankfurter in Adamson V. California, 1947). We are not English-speaking people but the ideals of justice is same and similar all over the globe which inescapably impose upon the High Court Division, an exercise of judgment, based on the principles of Rule of Law. 

 Under the circumstances, the vindication of the rights of an oppressed outweigh the procedural requirement of filing of an application. 

 21. In the instant case, because of the uncalled for fatwa, Shahida suffered extreme humiliation and outrageous indignity. As such, her inalienable rights guaranteed under Articles 27, 28 (2), 31 and 32 of the Constitution, have been violated. Besides, the provisions of the Muslim Family Law Ordinance were also flouted. 

 Shahida, above all is a human being. Her right to life is not that of a chattel but that of a citizen of sovereign Bangladesh. As such, she enjoys her inalienable rights guaranteed under the Constitution and the laws adopted or made there-under. Her rights under those provisions of laws had been violated. No doubt, she is an aggrieved person. She has rights as well as great expectations from the Constitution as any other citizen of this country. 

 Should she continue to suffer the humiliation, the indignity and injustice since she was unable to come before the Court with an application in her hand. If so, what value our valued and sacred Constitution holds for her with all its guarantees, superbly phrased and gloriously spelt out therein? It would become stale and meaningless flowery hollow words to Shahida and the thousands of faceless unfortunate women like her in the far away hamlets. To her, to them the Constitution with all its guarantees to the fundamental rights, would become mere worthless sheafs of paper although the Constitution stringently ensured that no body would trifle with her, with them. 

 The sad and inhuman plights of Shahida was reported in a newspaper and two of the learned Judges of a Bench of the High Court Division, noticed the said new sitem. Should they keep their eyes shut, close their conscience and leisurely wait for an application, as stated in Article 102, when the whole world was collapsing around Shahida, if so, how are they going to mince and digest the sacred words of Part-III of the Constitution and their own oath of office? The words ".... I will do right to all manner of people according to law." in this respect mean, among others= the implementation of the rights guaranteed under Part III of the Constitution. 

 The Judges are bound by their oath to uphold the provisions of the Constitution including the fundamental rights of the people guaranteed therein. The mere procedural veil cannot smog and delude their conscience. They ought to rise to the occasion when the Constitution is violated or fundamental rights are endangered or even threatened. In the instant case, they indeed did, they rose to the occasion, they issued the Rule suo moto. 

 Let us visualize what would have had happened if this kind of social ills is ignored and not promptly ark! '..tssed. This would have subjected not only Shahida but the whole community to utmost disgrace. This would also be an insult to humanity. Besides, the failure to halt the receding human values would have encouraged and emboldened others to commit such and other violations of law and human rights, specially in the far-flung areas. This would inevitably lead to further violations of decency, human values, violations of the Rule of Law and also the Constitution. This cannot be allowed in any ordered society. 

 It is only when the executive branch fails to uphold the law, address the problems and provide the necessary redress or to come to rescue the sufferers, the Judges of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court, are constrained to look into the matter, but only as a last resort, either on an application filed by an aggrieved person or by the oppressed or by any conscientious person or an institution, on his/her behalf, praying for appropriate relief or in an extreme situation even in the absence of any application, by being aware of the violations of any law or violations of human rights, from the electronic or print media, by issuing a Rule upon the perpetrators of illegality and also upon the concerned officials, because ultimately those officials of the government would do the needful, not the Court. But, by and large, the Judges should normally remain aloof from the policy decisions of the government of the day which generally represents the will of the people. 

 The Court may only over-see that law has been obeyed and the rights of the people, guaranteed under the Constitution, are upheld. This is in vindication of the Constitutional obligations of the learned Judges, not for any personal or even institutional aggrandizement. 

 However, with the advent of civilization, the rights of the people, the best creation of God, in contradistinction to the powers of the Kings and other autocratic Rulers, are now acknowledged throughout the world. Now, no body rules, the Head of the State, the Head of the Government and other authorities serve the people. 

 "102, (1) The High Court Division on the application of any pemn aggrieved, may give such directions or orders to any person or authority, including any person performing any function in connection with the affairs of the Republic, as may be appropriate for the enforcement of any of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III of this Constitution. 

 40. Sub-article (I) of article 102 has dealt with the powers of the High Court Division to give such directions or orders to any person or authority, including any person performing any function in connection with the affairs of the Republic as may be appropriate for the enforcement of any of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution "on the application of any person aggrieved." Again in clause (a) of sub-article (2) of the article, power has been conferred on the High Court Division to make order (i) directing a person performing any functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority to refrain from doing that which he is not permitted by law to 'do or to do that which he is required by law to do; or (ii) declaring that any act done or proceeding taken by a person performing functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority has been done or taken without lawful authority and is of no legal effect "on the application of any person aggrieved" on its satisfaction that there is no other equally efficacious remedy provided by law. In clause (b) of sub-article (2), the High Court Division has been empowered to make an order (i) directing that a person in custody be brought before it so that it may satisfy itself that he is not being held in custody without lawful authority or in an unlawful manner; or (ii) requiring a person holding or purporting to hold a public office to show under what authority he claims to hold that office "on the application of any person." Thus it is clear that in the case of enforcement of any of the fundamental rights conferred by Fart III of the Constitution, there is no need for the satisfaction of the High Court Division that there is no other equally efficacious remedy provided by law, but the condition precedent is "on the application of any person aggrieved." In the case of sub-clauses (i) and (ii) of clause (a) of sub-article (2), the High Court Division is required to be satisfied that there is no other equally efficacious remedy provided by law before making any order as contemplated therein but that again "on the application of any person aggrieved.' So far as the cases contemplated in sub-clauses (i) and (ii) of clause (b) of sub-article (2) are concerned, the High Court Division may make an order "on the application of any person." In these two cases, the word "aggrieved" has been omitted, but like the cases as contemplated in clause (a), the High Court. Division has to be satisfied that there is no other equally efficacious remedy provided by law. The framers of the Constitution have used the words "on the application of any person" in every contemplated areas/field of jurisdiction of the High Court Division under article 102. In the context, "aggrieved" is not the /is; however, we shall consider the word "aggrieved" later on. 

 41. A close reading of article 102 as a whole shows that in conferring jurisdiction on the High Court Division to issue orders and directions etc, for the enforcement of any of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution and for other remedies as contemplated in clauses (a) and (b) of sub-article (2), the framers of the Constitution have specifically used the words/language "on the application of any person." It is also significant to note that the legislature instead of "on an application" used the words "on the application", that is, instead of an indefinite article, has used a definite article, namely: 'the'. And it appears to me the object of using the definite article 'the' is to give stress of the necessity to file application to invoke the jurisdiction of the High Court Division under article 102. So, in order to decide the question whether the High Court Division could issue the suo moat Rule in question, we need to see the proper meaning of the core word "application" used in article 102. 

 46. When in article 102 in all situations including the enforcement of fundamental rights as conferred in Part. III of the Constitution, the framers of the Constitution have used the word "application", it has to be adhered to its plain meaning without imputing anything of our own. From a plain reading of the words used in sub-articles (I) and (2) of article 102, it also appears to me that the words "on the application" cannot be read in isolation, but have to be read along with the words "of any person." Person may be artificial or natural, but it can never be a news item published in a newspaper. 

 49. It is true that the Supreme Court as the Guardian of the Constitution is the protector of the rights, freedom and liberty of the People as enshrined in Part III of the Constitution, but when the framers of the Constitution, namely, the Constituent Assembly, in plain and unambiguous language/wordings stated that the High Court Division "on the application of any person" may give such directions or orders to any person or authority, including any person performing any function in connection with the affairs of the Republic, as may be appropriate for the enforcement of any of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution, so also in respect of the other remedies as mentioned in clauses (a) and (b) of sub-article (2) thereto how then it can be read that such power would include a power of issuance of a sue morn Rule in the absence of any application. Can it be said that the framers of the Constitution were oblivious or unmindful of the fact that Bangladesh's formal justice system remains relatively inaccessible to the vast majority people and that vulnerable and disadvantaged groups of people viz. children, women ethnic minorities. ultra poor, disabled people face difficulty in having excess to the justice and that the vast majority people of Bangladesh cannot afford to come to the High Court Division to seek redress against their grievance and that the fundamental rights as guaranteed in Part III of the Constitution and their other rights as contemplated in clauses (a), (b) of sub-article (2) could be or would be violated or infringed, while specifically using the words "on the application of any person."? If we say in the positive, then we shall be questioning the wisdom of the Constituent Assembly, wisdom of the framers of the Constitution and we shall he putting something which they omitted. 'Yes', there is scope of interpreting the word or expression "aggrieved" appeared/used in article 102 of the Constitution, i.e. as to the standing of a person in filing an application under the article. And that has been interpreted in the case of Dr. Mohiuddin Farooq Vs Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Irrigation, Water Resources and Flood as Control and others 49 DLR(AD) I. In that case A.T.M. Afzal, C.J. agreeing with Mustafa Kemal, J. said: 

 "any person aggrieved" meaning only and exclusively individuals and excluding the inconsideration of people as a collective and consolidated personality will be a stand taken against the Constitution. . . .The High Court Division cannot under the circumstances adhere to the traditional concept that to invoke its ,jurisdiction under article 102 only a person who has suffered a legal grievance or injury or an adverse decision or a wrongful deprivation or wrongful refusal of his title to something is a person aggrieved.. Insofar as it concerns public wrong or public injury or invasion of fundamental rights of an indeterminate number of people, any member of the public, being a citizen, suffering the common injury or common invasion in common with others or any citizen or an indigenous association, as distinguished from a local component of a foreign organisation, espousing that particular cause is a person aggrieved and has the right to invoke the jurisdiction under Article 102." 

 55. So far as article 44 of the Constitution is concerned, it has simply guaranteed the right of a person to move the High Court Division for enforcement of the rights conferred by Part III, but that too in accordance with clause (I) of article 102, i.e. the vehicle to enforce the fundamental rights is article 102, which speaks about availing the vehicle by filing the application. The learned Judge is also under the obligation to do right to all without fear or favour or lost of Bangladesh & Om (Seed Mahnned Howain, J)67 The Supreme Court of Bangladesh as the guardian of the Constitution is the protector of rights, freedoms and liberties of the people. Using tools of innovative and creative interpretation of the constitutional provisions, the Supreme Court of Bangladesh has consistently endeavored to further extend the horizon of rights and liberties and administered quality justice to the justice-seekers. Bangladesh's formal justice system remains relatively inaccessible to the vast majority of the people. Vulnerable and disadvantaged groups including women, children, ethnic minorities, ultra poor and disabled people face particular difficulty in having excess to justice. 

 119. There is no gainsaying the fact that the majority of the people of Bangladesh cannot afford to come to the High Court Division to seek redressal of their grievances. If the fundamental rights of an indigent citizen is violated and if he does not have the means, should he be allowed to suffer only because of his inability to come before the High Court Division with an application. If a glaring injustice amenable to the writ jurisdiction is done to that person, what would be the fate of the oath of office administered to a Judge who is under the obligation to preserve, protect and defend the Constitution. The words, preserve, protect and defend the Constitution shall mean and include implementation of the provisions of the Constitution in their letter and spirit. Mere non-filing of an application cannot be a ground for not exercising power under article 102 of the Constitution. This Division in the recent judgments has enlarged the meaning of aggrieved person, a shining example of which is in the case of Dr. Mohituldin Farooq vs. Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of 

 The limitations are that (a) there should be an application; (h) the application shall be verified by an affidavit by the petitioner or by any person who is competent to represent the aggrieved person with the prior leave of the court; (c) the affidavit filed in support of the writ petition must be satisfactory and (d) the relief asked for must be one to enforce a legal right-the right of the petitioner himself. The Supreme Court of India has, of late, admitted exceptions from the limitations relating to affidavit, locus-standi and the like in the case of a class of litigations which are being entertained in the nature of 'public interest litigation' that is to say, the:public in general are interested in the vindication of some rights or the enforcement of some public duty and the action can be brought by anyone. This Division has accepted the principle and widened the jurisdiction of the High Court Division by way of giving the meaning of `aggrieved person' in Dr. Mohiuddin Faroog(ibid). The Supreme Court of India has further expanded its jurisdiction by entertaining petitions under Article 32 of the Constitution not only from associations or organizations or individuals interested in a common cause or an advocate, even journalists but also on the bas4 of letters written by such persons containing a complaint of maltreatment of 'under-trial prisoners or women in police custody (Sheela Bose V. State of Maharashtra, AIR 1983 SC 378, Mukesh Kumar V. State of MP., AIR 1985 SC 1363). The court cautioned that the process of the court should not be abused or misused. Where the court is so satisfied, prima facie.it may not insist on the filing of an affidavit and may proceed to investigate into allegations with a view to meting out justice to the persons on whose behalf the communication is addressed particularly where to insist upon an affidavit at the initial stage may lead to perpetration of injustice or may give rise to a situation where from a practical point of view the doors of justice would be closed to the poor and the disadvantaged. it was further observed that the court should not object to the procedural technicalities being relaxed, that is to say, it should provide easy access to justice to the weaker sections of humanity and to combat exploitation and injustice and to secure for the under-privileged segments of society their social and economic entitlements, to redress public injury, enforce public duty, protect social rights, vindicate public interest and rule of law. References in this connection are the cases of State of W.B. V. Sampal Lal, AIR 1985 SC 195, State of H.P. V. Parent of Student Medical College, AIR 1985 SC 910 and Malik Brothers V. Narendra Dadich, AIR 1999 SC 3211.

No.200 of 2004, this Division held that if there is violation of fundamental rights causing common injury or common invasion affecting the people of a particular area, any public spirited person or organization of that locality can maintain a petition in the High Court Division. It was further held that when there is invasion of human rights which shocks the judicial conscience, the court should extend its jurisdiction. In the case in hand, Shahida, wife of Saiful was forced to marry her paternal cousin Samsul, under a 'Fatwa' pronounced by one Haji Azizul Huq on the ground that her marriage was dissolved on an incident of altercations between the husband and wife. The husband, out of anger uttered the word talak' despite that they continued their marital tie. The incidents of this nature are common in the rural areas and sometimes, in the name of such 'Fatwa' victims are being subjected to whipping. These incidents are social crimes which are spreading in the society tremendously day-by-day. These social crimes should be eliminated and the courts should not remain a silent spectator, particularly the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, which is the guardian of the Constitution. It has a duty to protect these social rights. Though we do not encourage in the manner the High Court Division suo motu has exercised its writ jurisdiction in view of the language used in Article 102 of the Constitution, we treat the news item published in 'The Daily Banglabazar Patrika' on the issue of 2m December, 2000 as an application under Article 102 of the Constitution and wave the procedural formalities to protect social rights and vindicate public interest and rule of law treating it as an exceptional case with a view to preventing social injustice in the society. 

 It was never the intention of the framers of. the Constitution to imprison the enforcement of fundamental rights guaranteed by Part-III of the Constitution to a word, 'application:. occurring in sub-articles (I) and (2) of Article 102 of the Constitution. Given the provisions of the fundamental rights guaranteed by Part-Ill of the Constitution, in general, and sub-articles (I) and (2) of Article 102 in particular, the framers of the Constitution never intended to deprive the vast majority of the people of the country of getting their fundamental rights enforced. Denying the fundamental rights of the majority of the people amounts to denying our independence earned through the blood of the freedom-fighters and the sacrifices of the women who were ravished by the occupation force and they never thought of an independence limited to a small section of affluent people. 

 120. 4. The trial court having decreed the suit and that having been affirmed by the lower appellate court by the impugned judgment and decree, and proceeding on the premise that both the courts below have decreed the suit on a misconception of law and gross misreading of materials on record, the Petitioner now contends that this has led to an error of law manifested in an erroneous decision occasioning a failure of justice. It is submitted specifically that inasmuch as according to the provisions of Section 48 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 earlier sale deeds take precedence over subsequent ones, the plaintiffs did not acquire any right, title and interest in the suit land on the basis of their subsequent alleged sale deeds of July 1978 (Exhibit- '1 series') as the sale property had already been sold to the predecessor-in-interest of the defendants by a registered sale deed dated 24.6.1960 (Exhibit-'M'). As executed, amongst others, by the alleged vendor of the plaintiffs, this relative status of the 1960 deed is submitted to be further enhanced by the very fact of it being a registered document that has a presumption of genuineness attached to it under Section 60 of the Registration Act, 1908, unless the contrary is proved which, it is submitted, has not been the case in this instance. In this regard, it has also been submitted in this Application that the suit is not maintainable without a concomitant prayer made for the cancellation of the sale deed of 24.6.1960 relied upon the defendants. It is also contended that both the courts below lost sight of the fact that the genealogy of the suit property given by the plaintiffs stood disproved given that P.S. Khatian No. 277 (Exhibit-'N') in respect of the non-disputed land clearly proved that Ramzan Ali had a son named Kala Miah who along with his two nephews executed the Exhibit 'M' sale deed of 24.6.1960 but which Kala Miah's existence is denied by the plaintiffs. It is submitted further that the impugned judgment not being in terms of Order 41, Rule 24 of the Code is not a proper judgment of affirmation in the eye of law inasmuch as the lower appellate court has endorsed the views of the trial court without any independent discussion and appreciation of materials on record. 

 5. Heard the learned Advocates for both parties and perused the Application and the Lower Court Records. 

 6. It is noted at the outset that the judgment of the trial court though having erroneously recorded the actual date of dispossession as claimed by the Opposite Parties but having touched upon various issues pertaining to the genealogy of the suit property and the issue of adverse possession makes clear substantive findings on the factual and legal consequences following upon the execution of the 1960 sale deed and why on a due examination of documentary and oral evidence adduced by the Plaintiffs-Respondents-Opposite Parties in substantiation of their claim to possession and title there remained no justification to grant primacy to the 1960 sale deed as relied upon by the Defendant-Appellant-Petitioner. That finding, it is noted, has been confirmed by the lower appellate court and has emerged as the focal point of concurrence between the two courts below. 

 7. It is on the above premise that this Court has had to consider the submissions of the learned Advocates of both parties as to the sufficiency or otherwise of the concurrent judgments of the courts below. The learned Advocate for the Petitioner Mr. Mahmudul Islam has submitted that the registered kabala of 1960 is pivotal to an understanding of this case. Mr. Islam submits that the courts below erred in not finding that in light of there being a registered kabala of 1960 the vendor consequentially had no saleable interest in 1978. Rather, he submits, the courts below went in a roundabout manner in finding that the kabala of 1960 had not been acted upon. It is submitted that the Opposite Parties having in fact not made out a case in the plaint that the Petitioner's 1960 kabala was not acted upon, the trial court travelled well beyond the pleadings in that regard by finding on this issue. The learned Advocates for the Opposite Parties Dr. M. Zahir and Mr. Junayed Ahmed Chowdhury have submitted in response that the Opposite Parties had no direct or indirect knowledge of the existence of the 1960 sale deed prior to or during the institution of the suit even notwithstanding the fact that they otherwise remained diligent in examining the relevant records of rights and rent receipts that go to establish the title and possession of the vendor. It is pointed out in this regard, that it was the Petitioner himself who as defendant first introduced the fact of the existence of the 1960 sale deed in his written statement on the basis of which the trial court framed Issue No. 2 pertaining to determining the plaintiffs' title and interest in the suit land. That the trial court could so frame such an issue is clearly evident from the provisions of Order 14, Rule 3 of the Code that sanctions issues to be framed on the basis of all materials taken together as may be placed before the trial court in terms of pleadings and documentary evidence. As argued by the learned Advocates for the Opposite Parties the said Issue No. 2 so framed is sufficiently comprehensive as to bring within its ambit an examination and determination of the fact whether the 1960 sale deed had or had not been acted upon. This Court is satisfied that an enquiry in this regard was essential to determine the right and title of the Opposite Parties as would also necessarily entail adjudging on the validity of the 1978 sale deeds. It is in that context that the trial court undertook an examination of evidence as would establish the claim to possession of the suit land of one or the other of the parties. Taking the existence of the 1960 sale deed as a given, the trial court at the outset noted that not much evidence other than the registered kabala was forthcoming from the Petitioner in establishing the consequential exercise of possessory rights. In this regard, the trial court noted in particular both the failure of either the vendee Zakir Hossain and/or his sons to appear in court to prove the said sale deed as well as the absence of care evident in the failure to produce any other witness to prove the 1960 sale deed or to substantiate the fact of the vendee or his successors-in-interest ever having gone into possession of the suit land pursuant to such deed. That finding of the trial court is further fortified by its finding that the Petitioner at no point could establish the payment of rent on any material date for the material period given the failure in this regard to produce the relevant rent receipts before the court. On the other hand, the trial court aptly enquired into all documentary evidence produced by the Opposite Parties in evidence of the exercise of their possessory rights over the suit land as concomitantly established to the satisfaction of the court an unbroken chain of title and possession as stems from Fazlul Haque and continues down to the Opposite Parties. In this regard, the trial court took note of the record entries in the field survey khatian (Exhibit-'3K') as pertains to among others the Opposite Parties' predecessor-in-interest Fazlul Haque as well as Exhibit-'3 L' which is a mutation khatian favouring the Opposite Parties. In addition the trial court has found on the fact of the payments of rent for the suit land from the Exhibit- '4 series' rent receipts that show the Opposite Parties' predecessor-in-interest having continuously paid rent on the suit land from 1375 B.S. to 1382 B.S. that is, from approximately 1968 to 1975. It is evident further that the subsequent payments of rent have been made by the Opposite Parties themselves, a fact that is evident from the relevant rent receipts themselves as produced in evidence. In this Court's opinion, therefore, there is no reason why, and subscribing to the judgments in, for example, Akbar Ali and others v. Zahiruddin Kabri and others reported in 30 DLR (SC) 81 as well as Sultanuddsin Chowdhury v. Government of Bangladesh reported in 32 DLR (1980) 252 a presumption of possession from the above referred entries in the relevant records of rights may not arise given particularly where the correctness of such entries remain unimpeachable. Similarly unqualified would be the sanctity of such a presumption arising in the facts and circumstances from the fact of the production of the rent receipts as above noted (Erfan Ali v. Joynal Abedin reported in 35 DLR (AD) 216). 

 8. Pertinently, further, the trial court came to a finding that the presumption of possession as consequentially operates in favour of the Opposite Parties, though rebuttable, was not in fact rebutted by the Petitioner. It is also noted that this lapse on the part of the Petitioner had a bearing on the extent to which the fact of the dispossession of the Opposite Parties on 25.12.1978 could not be disproved to the satisfaction of the courts below. Indeed, as the learned Advocate for the Petitioner Mr. Mahmudul Islam has submitted before this Court, if the fact of such dispossession remains unsubstantiated the attendant presumption shall be of the Petitioner being in continuous possession since 1960. It has been asserted on behalf of the Petitioner in this regard that the Opposite Parties having produced no evidence of dispossession and thereby having not discharged their onus of proving the sale, the courts below erred by finding instead that the Petitioner had failed to discharge his burden in disproving the fact of dispossession. Though Mr. Mahmudul Islam has submitted that the Opposite Party No. 1 was evidently not a first-hand witness to the fact of dispossession as comes across in his statements given in cross-examination as P.W. 1, and the fact that the P.W. 2 did not depose at all on this issue, this issue has to be considered overall in the proper context of the fact, and as noted by the trial court itself, that the deposition and claim of the P.W.1 as to dispossession having remained unchallenged and uncontested on account of evidence to the contrary not being forthcoming from the Petitioner at all, the oral evidence given by the Opposite Parties as above remained acceptable as a given. It is noted that though the D.W.1 in his examination-in-chief denied the fact of dispossession, the vary fact of his acquaintance with the Petitioner dating back to only as recently as 1990, appropriately in the eyes of the courts below belied the veracity of his statements to that effect and made his credibility questionable. This Court therefore, finds itself in agreement with the trial court's finding on the issues of possession and dispossession as above. In this regard, this Court finds that given the fact that the Opposite Parties having discharged their burden of proof on the pleadings and that of adducing evidence with respect to possession and dispossession, that burden consequently shifted to the Petitioner not only to prove his continued possession from 1960 through to 25.12.1978, but concomitantly to disprove the dispossession of the Opposite Parties on 25.12.1978. This, and as is evident from the records made available to this Court, the Petitioner failed to do. These failings, in the view of this Court, thereby, cumulatively operated to establish in the minds of the courts below that the sale deed or kabala of 1960 was not duly acted upon by the Petitioner. That in these facts and circumstances the Petitioner's failure would inexorably lead to such unfavourable substantive consequences with the two courts below applying the judicially sanctified principles of discharge of burden of proof on the pleadings and the burden of proof on evidence, is well evident from the following enunciation in Kumbhan Lashmanna v. Tangirala Venkateshwarlu reported in 2 DLR 83 (PC): 

 9. Much has been said on behalf of the Petitioner in this Court on the issue of whether the courts below in their ostensible zeal for travelling beyond the pleadings made yet another case on the issue of adverse possession. Given that on a perusal of the judgments of the courts below it is evident to this Court that no finding on adverse possession was arrived at by the courts below as in any way detracts from or adds to the substantive findings on possession in particular and the merits of the case in general, this Court notes that it was indeed the learned Advocate of the defendant at the time taking a cue from the written statement itself who argued and submitted on the question of adverse possession that led the trial court, in addition to issues framed in the regular course, to also frame an additional issue on adverse possession, albeit by way of an observation. The actual and substantive findings of the trial court, and as endorsed by the lower appellate court as above quoted, in the view of this Court operate wholly and exclusively of the issue of adverse possession. In that regard, this Court finds itself to be in agreement with Dr. Zahir's argument that upon dwelling on these peripheral issues the learned Advocate for the Petitioner Mr. Mahmudul Islam has perhaps adopted a far too technical approach at deconstructing the judgments of the courts below. This Court therefore, finds itself to be equally in agreement with Dr. Zahir's submissions that the courts below did not err in identifying and deciding on the core issue of establishing and proving possession of the suit land. In this regard, this Court finds that both the courts below appropriately found for the Opposite Parties on the basis of uncontested oral and documentary evidence and presumptions that arise there from and which were not rebutted by the other party. That being the case this Court also finds that the lower appellate court at all times remained substantially in agreement with the trial court's judgment on these core issues and, therefore, there was no necessity for the said appellate court to proceed to further resettle any of the issues and, thereby, proceed to find otherwise than what had been arrived at by the trial court. By that reason this Court finds no justification as to how and why the provisions of Order 41, Rule 24 of the Code, as submitted on behalf of the Petitioner, can be said to be attracted to this case. 

 "48. PRIORITY OF RIGHTS CREATED BY TRANSFER: Where a person purports to create by transfer at different limes rights in or over the same immoveable property, and such rights cannot all exist or be exercised to their full extent together, each later created right shall, in the absence of a special contract or reservation binding the earlier transferees, be subject to the rights previously created. 

 11. The provisions of Section 78 above clearly applying to instances where elements of gross neglect are found (Lloyds Bank Ltd. v. R E Guzdar Co. reported in AIR 1930 Calcutta, 22) and also having been found to apply to instances of sale (S. Arunachalam Asari and others v. Sivan Perumal Asari and another reported in AIR 1970 Madras, 226), it is not, therefore, difficult for this Court to subscribe to the ratio decidendi of the judgment in the Arunachalam Asari Case that the principle underlying Section 78 in applying to transactions of sale would accordingly operate to postpone the priority of a prior sale transaction should the prior vendee transferee be guilty of gross negligence. It is in that light that Mr. Junayed Ahmed Chowdhury has in particular submitted that the postponement of the rights created by the prior sale of 1960 shall operate in the facts and circumstances of this case given the Petitioner's gross negligence as evidenced in not acting upon the 1960 sale deed by taking the physical possession of the suit land at any material time or date, not being vigilant in amending the record of rights, thereby, allowing the name of the Opposite Parties' vendor to remain thereon and thereafter to be substituted by mutation in due process by the names of the Opposite Parties, and enabling at all material times the Opposite Parties' vendor and later the Opposite Parties, to pay rent for the suit land. These circumstances inexorably lead to the further conclusion that the Petitioner's indolence and/or negligence as above effectively allowed the vendor of the Opposite Parties to be in possession of the suit land for over twelve years i.e., eighteen years, till the execution of the above-referred deeds of 1978 favouring the Opposite Parties. This Court in this regard, finds merit in the submission so made and finds no reason why Section 48 of the Transfer of Property Act shall be relied on in these circumstances to operate in favour of the Petitioner. It has also been argued on behalf of the Petitioner that by the time that the 1960 sale deed was produced before the trial court it qualified as a document to which certain presumptions attach pertaining to due registration under Section 60 of the Registration Act, 1908. On a perusal of the judgments of the courts below it is noted that there is no finding thereon that deny to the 1960 sale deed its status as a duly registered instrument. However, competing presumptions that have been found to operate in favour of the Opposite Parties' possessory rights, and duly so in the view of this Court, operate to discourage the attachment of any further significance to that act of registration of the 1960 sale deed as can otherwise create a dent in the relative strength of the presumptions duly found to be operating in favour of the Opposite Parties. 

 14. Send down the Lower Court Records at once.
